**What `?&` means here, and what it does not (W-b).** `jsonb ?& text[]` answers one question: whether every listed string exists as a top-level key (or as a string element of an array). For an existing JSON object that lacks one listed key the result is **false**. If the left operand is itself SQL NULL (the key `risk_acceptance` is absent from `detail`, so `detail -> 'risk_acceptance'` is SQL NULL) the result may be **NULL**. A key whose value is a JSON null still exists, so `?&` is **true** for it: JSON null is not SQL NULL (`jsonb_typeof` returns the text `null` for the former and SQL NULL for a missing key). A JSON array that contains the nine key names as strings also makes `?&` true. Key existence and value validity are therefore two separate checks: `?&` states existence only, `jsonb_typeof` and the format predicates state validity, and the predicate **never** judges validity by `?&` alone. `IS NOT TRUE` over the whole `<RESOLVED_VALID>` maps both **false** and **NULL** to 'not valid', so a missing key (false), an absent or non-object `risk_acceptance` (NULL or false) and a JSON null (false through `jsonb_typeof`) all enter the anomaly index, whereas a plain `NOT (...)` would drop the NULL case. The migration may spell the operators as the equivalent functions `jsonb_exists_all` and `jsonb_exists` so that no `?` character reaches the driver's parameter parsing (PostgreSQL documentation, not run here). **Index-predicate purity (revision 17; verified, §13.1).** An index predicate may contain only IMMUTABLE functions. `to_jsonb` is STABLE (`provolatile = 's'`), so `to_jsonb(pid)` is **forbidden in every index predicate** and PostgreSQL refuses `CREATE INDEX … WHERE (…) = to_jsonb(pid)`; this fact is stated here only. The one spelling of the integer `pid` comparand is `(pid::text)::jsonb`, which is the canonical SQL fragment `PID_JSONB_SQL` (a name for that text, not a placeholder and not a separately rendered constant): it is written literally in the `<RA_VALID>` block, and `<RESOLVED_VALID>`, the `<ANOMALY_KIND>` `CASE`, the helper and project-wide queries, `ix_executions_tracked_unresolved`, `ix_executions_tracked_anomaly`, migration `0005`, the model's index definitions and the repository queries all take it through the rendered blocks (§7.5 item 7, `RISK_ACCEPTANCE_SCHEMA`) and never by hand copy. A test compares the frozen migration text, the model text and the query text byte for byte (§13). The cast compares as a number: `((1000)::text)::jsonb` equals `'1e3'::jsonb`. Which other functions and operators of these blocks are accepted, and whether `CREATE INDEX` accepts the whole U and anomaly predicates, is recorded in §13.1 as a verified set and a not-run set. `<TRACKED_ISH>` guards with `jsonb_typeof(detail) = 'object'`, so a `detail` that is SQL NULL or not a JSON object is outside every rule like a legacy row (no writer produces one: the column is a mapped dict, `tables.py:270`).

**Project-wide query shape (revision 18, CMIN-1; verified, §13.1).** Every query that applies the canonical blocks to a whole project (the U query `<PROJECT_U_QUERY>`, the A query `<PROJECT_A_QUERY>`, `has_unresolved_or_anomalous_for_project`, `risk_batch_targets`, the project-wide page block `<PROJECT_U_PAGE>`, the sweeper candidate query, the diagnostics and report project queries and any other repository query that uses a canonical block) reads `executions` as the **only** outer `FROM` table and restricts it with `<PROJECT_SCOPE>` (`task_id IN (SELECT id FROM tasks WHERE project_id = :project_id)`); `<U>`, `<RESOLVED_VALID>` and `<ANOMALY>` are combined with it **unchanged** and no alias is added to their text, so the partial indexes keep single-table predicates with the canonical text. *Why:* the blocks name `id`, `pid`, `finished_at` and `detail` without a table qualifier and `tasks` also has `id` (`tasks` has no `pid`, `detail` or `finished_at`, so `id` is the only collision, `tables.py:83-95`, `:248-270`): `executions e JOIN tasks t ON … WHERE t.project_id = $1 AND (<ANOMALY>)` fails on PostgreSQL 18.4 with an ambiguous column `id`, with and without aliases, while the `IN` subquery form and an `EXISTS` form execute (§13.1). The `IN` form is chosen because its subquery is a scope of its own, so the canonical text never needs an alias. **A `JOIN` of `tasks` and `executions` in one outer `FROM` is forbidden** for these queries (an architecture test and a PostgreSQL detection test, §13). Task-level conditions that a candidate scan needs (`<JUDGEABLE>`) are written as correlated `EXISTS` subqueries for the same reason. The queries were executed on tiny tables only; no cost, plan or index-use claim is made (§13.1).

**Cursor vocabulary (revision 22; normative, the one definition: every other place uses these words and refers here).** *Row stages.* A row is **fetched** when the database returned it; **classified** when its U, A or resolved classification (§6.1) was done in Python (a `decode_error` row counts as classified); **selected** when it was chosen into the current batch; **processed** (also **settled**) when its guarded state transition was executed; **committed** when the commit of that guarded transaction completed; **no-write proven** when the same fenced classification and re-read prove that no write is needed (a `decode_error` row, a row whose OS state cannot be proven and which is left untouched, or a row whose guarded UPDATE matched 0 rows and whose re-read shows that another writer settled it). A row is **decided** when it is committed or no-write proven; a rolled-back row, a row whose commit is uncertain and a row that was never processed are not decided. *Positions.* `pass_start_cursor` is the committed cursor at the start of the current pass (`null` means the first page); `scan_cursor` is the read-side position inside a pass, the id of the last classified row (the last position up to which the read has safely decided what happens to every row: each of them was selected or skipped without a write); it is the value of `:last_seen_id`, is internal to the pass and is never kept between passes (the 'last classified id' of the rules of this paragraph is this value); `committed_cursor` is the position the **next** pass may safely skip to. *Rules of `committed_cursor` (the only place that states them).* (1) It never advances on a fetched, a classified or a selected row alone. (2) It advances only up to rows whose guarded transaction **committed**, or that are **no-write proven**. (3) It never passes a rolled-back row, a row whose commit is uncertain or a row that was not processed. (4) The sweeper uses **per-row guarded transactions** (each target in its own short transaction, sweeper bullet of this section) and never one transaction for a whole batch; no rule of this document mixes the two models. The cursor is therefore tied to the commit boundary of each row and moves over the **exact committed prefix**: it is the id of the last row of the decided prefix of the ascending batch (rows that are committed or no-write proven, up to the first row that is not), it passes classified rows that were skipped without a write only when every selected target below them is decided, and it never passes a rolled-back row. *Worked example:* three targets t1 < t2 < t3, t1 commits, t2 commits, t3 rolls back → the committed cursor is t2, t3 is the failure candidate, the next pass re-judges from t3 (it starts after t2), and t1 and t2 are not state-changed again (a repeated judgement of them matches 0 rows). A rollback of the **first** row leaves the cursor where it was (there is no committed prefix). **C-9 (normative sentence):** the committed cursor is a promise that every row at or below it is committed or no-write proven; it is never derived from what was fetched, classified or selected.

**Candidate scan: keyset cursor, page size, result states and caps (revision 18, CMIN-2; cursor, page size and page timeout revision 19).** `risk_batch_targets`, the project-level discovery and the orphan sweeper read their candidates through one keyset procedure; none of them uses `OFFSET` and none uses a fixed over-fetch multiple of the batch size. *Why:* SQL cannot see a `decode_error` (§7.5 item 7): such a row is a SQL candidate of U that Python then reclassifies as A, so a fixed `LIMIT` (or a fixed multiple of it) would be filled by undecodable rows with the lowest ids and would starve every valid row behind them. *Cursors (the scan cursor is revision 19; the committed cursor and discard-and-restore are revision 20, decided by the user).* A sweeper pass has two cursors. The **scan cursor** is the **id of the last execution whose Python classification completed in the current pass**: it is temporary and internal to the pass, it is the value of the bind `:last_seen_id` in the page procedure of this paragraph, and it is neither the last row of the batch nor the last row fetched (a cursor defined as 'the last row included in the batch' would read classified-but-excluded rows, a `decode_error` row or an anomaly that cannot be proven automatically, again in every pass). The **committed cursor** is the id after which the next normal pass starts: it moves only after a batch was **completely collected** and every target that rule (g) lets it pass was **decided** (committed or no-write proven; rule (g) and 'Cursor vocabulary' of §7.4), it is the only cursor that survives from one pass to the next, and its value at the start of a collection is recorded as `pass_start_cursor`. *Rules of the scan cursor:* (a) a row's id becomes the scan cursor immediately after its classification completed, and a `decode_error` row counts as classified, so the scan cursor passes it; (b) the scan cursor never advances to an id that was fetched but not yet classified; (c) it is monotonic and never moves backwards within a collection; (d) the end of the candidate set is reached only by a page with fewer rows than its `page_size` (rule (g) says when this resets the committed cursor); (e) both cursors live in memory only (`risk_batch_targets`: inside one call, so every call starts with no cursor and has no committed cursor; sweeper: in `_sweeper_task`); if they are lost, for example by a restart, the scan restarts at the first page, which keeps safety and idempotence because every processing of a row is a guarded re-processing (§6.1 and the sweeper bullet of this section: a row that was already settled matches 0 rows and is re-read, never written twice). *(f) Discard and restore (revision 20).* **The sweeper processes only completely collected batches.** A collection is complete only if every page query **and** the Python classification of every row of the pass succeeded. On `QUERY_FAILED` (a query error, a statement timeout or a classification error that is not isolated per row), on a classification exception or on cancellation, the pass **discards every target gathered in it**, restores the scan cursor to `pass_start_cursor` and ends; the intermediate scan cursor of the failed pass is **never used** by the next pass; there is no processing of a partial batch and no partial cursor commit. For the sweeper `TARGETS_READY` therefore never outranks `QUERY_FAILED`: targets gathered before a failure are not processed. The risk batch keeps its fail-closed rule (after a failure no target and no risk option, §7.5 item 2) and has no committed cursor. *(g) Commit (revision 20).* After a completely collected batch the sweeper processes its targets, each in its own short guarded transaction (sweeper bullet of this section; per-row commit, not batch atomicity), and then sets the committed cursor only as far as the decided rows allow: (i) to **'no cursor'** (wrap-around) when the end of the candidate set was traversed successfully in this collection and every selected target was decided; (ii) to the **scan cursor at the end of the collection** when a full batch or a row or time cap ended the collection (`TARGETS_READY` or `SCAN_LIMIT_REACHED`) and every selected target was decided; (iii) to the **id of the last decided target** when `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS` was spent before every target was decided (the unreached targets are dropped from the batch, are not processed in this pass and are collected again by the next pass; no processing of a row is started once the budget is spent, the committed cursor never passes a target that is not decided, and **zero decided targets leave the committed cursor unchanged**, rule (h)); (iv) **to the id of the last row of the committed prefix** when the processing of the batch failed (an exception that is not isolated per row, a rolled-back row transaction, cancellation, shutdown): the cursor moves only over rows that are already decided, never passes the rolled-back or undecided row and stays where it was when no row of the batch was decided; the failed row is the failure candidate, and the next pass starts after the committed prefix and judges that row again (rule (4) of 'Cursor vocabulary' gives the t1, t2, t3 example). *Contract for half-decided batches:* every row's guarded transaction is atomic, so a batch can end with only a prefix decided; it moves the committed cursor under (iii) or (iv), in both cases only over the decided prefix, the rows of such a batch that were not decided are collected and processed again in the next pass, and a row that was processed and left unproven (no-write proven) is processed again **only when the committed cursor has not passed it** (the row lies behind the decided prefix of a failed pass, or no row was decided) **or after the next wrap-around**; once the committed cursor has passed it, the immediately following pass does not read it again: **a duplicate re-processing is allowed, a duplicate state change never** (a settled row matches 0 rows under its guard and is no-write proven, an unsettled row is processed by the same rules). A wrap-around (reset to 'no cursor') happens **only** after the end of the candidate set was traversed successfully **and** every selected target was decided under (i); a failed pass never resets the cursor. *Cost of the re-read.* A failed collection is repeated from `pass_start_cursor` and a failed processing from the committed prefix, so the same rows are read again; missed-row avoidance is preferred over speed, and the cost is bounded by the limits of every pass: at most `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` rows scanned per pass, at most `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS` elapsed per pass, at most `CANDIDATE_PAGE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` per page query, one pass per `ORPHAN_SWEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS` and one sweeper at a time (only the Runner that holds the advisory lock sweeps). Stated honestly: a failure that recurs at the same place (a permanent classification error, a page that always exceeds its timeout) keeps the committed cursor in front of that place; the sweeper does not skip it, B2 does not promise progress behind it, and every failed pass is logged with ids and the reason code only. *Page size (revision 19).* `page_size = min(CANDIDATE_PAGE_ROWS, remaining_scan_rows, remaining_target_rows)`, where `remaining_scan_rows = CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS − scanned_rows` and `remaining_target_rows = target_batch_size − accepted_targets`; the target batch size is `PROCESS_RISK_MAX_TARGETS` for the risk batch and `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BATCH_ROWS` for the sweeper (both reused, no new constant). *Page procedure (the same for all three consumers):* (1) compute `page_size`: `remaining_target_rows = 0` means the batch is full and the scan ends with `TARGETS_READY`, otherwise `page_size = 0` ends the scan by the row limit; (2) check the remaining overall scan time and compute the statement timeout of the page (the page-level time limit, §7.4 'Page-level database time limit'); no time left means no query and the end by the time limit; (3) fetch one page ordered by execution `id` ascending: the first page has no cursor and each later page adds `id > :last_seen_id` (`<RISK_PAGE_OWN>`, `<RISK_PAGE_REST>`, `<PROJECT_U_PAGE>` or `<SWEEP_PAGE>`, chosen per consumer by the table 'Per-consumer queries' after the result-state table); the bind name `:last_seen_id` is kept so that the canonical blocks stay unchanged, and the value passed is the **scan cursor**, the last classified id (at the start of a collection `pass_start_cursor`); (4) classify each row in order (§6.1, per-row isolation); (5) advance the scan cursor to that row's id immediately after its classification completed; (6) a `decode_error` row is not added to the batch (it still counts as scanned) and the scan cursor passes it; (7) an eligible row is added to the batch; (8) stop when the batch reaches the target size; (9) a page with fewer rows than `page_size` means the end of the set; reading exactly `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` rows with full pages does **not** show the end, so the state is then `SCAN_LIMIT_REACHED` (`cap = ROW`) even if the set happens to end there, and `NO_ELIGIBLE_TARGETS` needs a page shorter than its `page_size` (a set one row shorter than the budget ends on a short page). Because `page_size <= remaining_target_rows` and each row adds at most one target, the batch cannot fill in the middle of a page and leave an unclassified suffix in the normal contract. *Defence:* if an implementation change ever creates an unclassified suffix, the scan cursor (and through it the committed cursor) advances only to the last classified row, never unconditionally to the last fetched or last returned row and never to 'the last eligible batch row', so the next pass reads the suffix. Further rules: (10) the scan never deletes, modifies or writes a `decode_error` row and never logs or returns its `detail`: only the ids and the fixed reason code are kept; (11) every page is a short read of its own and no lock is held between pages beyond the locks of the caller (the decision-time predicate runs the procedure under the Task and project locks it already holds, §7.5 item 4; the sweeper uses its own read transactions); (12) the caps of the whole scan are `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` rows and `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS` seconds, and the database cost of one page is bounded by its statement timeout only (the paragraph 'Page-level database time limit' of this section), never by its row count. *Interaction of the two cursors with the 12 steps (revision 20).* Before step (1) the collection records `pass_start_cursor` and starts its scan cursor there; steps (3) to (6) read with the scan cursor and advance **only** the scan cursor; steps (1), (2), (8), (9) and (12) end a collection without a failure (a full batch, the end of the set, the row cap or the time cap); a query error, a statement timeout, a classification exception or a cancellation at any of the steps (2) to (7) is a failure: it discards the batch and restores the scan cursor (rule (f)); no step touches the committed cursor, which moves only under rule (g), after the rows it passes were decided. *Candidate set per consumer (three consumers; the query block of each is named in 'Per-consumer queries' after the result-state table):* `risk_batch_targets` reads **U rows only** (RESOLVED_VALID and A rows are never risk targets, and a `decode_error` row is A) in the batch order of §7.5 item 5, realised by **two phases** instead of a composite cursor: phase 1 reads the resumed Task's own rows (`<RISK_PAGE_OWN>`); when phase 1 reached the end of its set (a page shorter than its `page_size`) before the batch is full, phase 2 reads the other rows of the project (`<RISK_PAGE_REST>`) with a first page of its own (no cursor); each phase keeps its own cursor, the last classified id of that phase; the two row sets are disjoint (`task_id = :task_id` versus `task_id <> :task_id`), so the order equals 'own rows first, then `id` ascending', no row is read twice, and the caps count the rows of both phases together. The sweeper reads the judgeable U rows (`<JUDGEABLE>`, the W3 condition of the sweeper bullet of this section) and all A rows, across all projects, as one ascending stream (`<SWEEP_PAGE>`); it skips a `decode_error` row (the scan cursor passes it), continues with the later eligible rows and never closes, proves or rewrites it. *Result states (one table for the risk batch and the sweeper; the project-level discovery maps its outcome to the same states; internal discriminators: `cap` ∈ `ROW`, `TIME` for `SCAN_LIMIT_REACHED`, the row budget being checked first, and `failure` ∈ `PAGE_TIMEOUT`, `TRANSIENT`, `PERMANENT` for `QUERY_FAILED`; the API reasons are the contract of §7.5 item 2; precedence when several hold: `QUERY_FAILED`, then `TARGETS_READY`, then `NO_ELIGIBLE_TARGETS`, then `SCAN_LIMIT_REACHED`; `QUERY_FAILED` outranks `TARGETS_READY` for both consumers: the targets gathered by a pass that failed are discarded (sweeper) or never offered (risk batch), rule (f)):*

| State | Meaning | `risk_batch_targets` | Orphan sweeper |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TARGETS_READY` | at least one eligible target was found (the batch may be smaller than the target size when the set ended or a cap was hit; the rest stays in place) | returns the targets; the risk options follow §7.5 item 1 | processes the targets of a completely collected batch; the committed cursor then moves under rule (g) of 'Candidate scan' (only over decided rows, never before) |
| `NO_ELIGIBLE_TARGETS` | the whole candidate set was read to its end and no row is eligible (empty, or only `decode_error` rows) | no target and no risk option; `options_hidden` reason `NO_ELIGIBLE_TARGETS`; the project stays `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED` | nothing to process; the end of the set was traversed successfully, so the committed cursor is cleared (wrap-around, rule (g)(i)); this state needs a page shorter than its `page_size`: exactly `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` rows read with full pages never give it |
| `SCAN_LIMIT_REACHED` | the row budget or the overall time budget was exhausted before the end and no eligible target was found (internal `cap` = `ROW` or `TIME`); more candidates may remain (exactly `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` rows read with full pages have not shown the end of the set and give this state with `cap = ROW`); **never read as 'no targets'** | no target and no risk option; `options_hidden` reason `TARGET_SCAN_ROW_LIMIT_REACHED` (`cap = ROW`: a new scan starts at the first page and meets the same rows, so only changed data helps) or `TARGET_SCAN_TIME_LIMIT_REACHED` (`cap = TIME`: a slow database may recover, so a retry can succeed); both `retryable = true` with `next_available_at` null | no row is written; the collection ended without a failure, so the committed cursor moves to the last classified id (rule (g)(ii)) and the next pass continues after it |
| `QUERY_FAILED` | a database error or a classification error that is not isolated per row (a single undecodable `detail` is isolated and is not this state); internal `failure` = `PAGE_TIMEOUT` (SQLSTATE `57014`), `TRANSIENT` or `PERMANENT` | fail closed: no target, no risk option, `continue` stays hidden (on the DIRTY gate `continue` is offered only when U and A are both empty); no request row is written; logged with ids and the reason code only; `options_hidden` reason `TARGET_PAGE_TIMEOUT` (`retryable = true`), `TARGET_QUERY_FAILED` (a transient database error, `retryable = true`) or `TARGET_CLASSIFICATION_ERROR` (a permanent contract or classification error, `retryable = false`) | no row is changed and **no gathered target is processed**: the pass discards its targets, restores the scan cursor to `pass_start_cursor`, leaves the committed cursor unchanged and ends (rule (f)); the next pass (the normal interval) starts at `pass_start_cursor` and makes at most one attempt again under the same row, time and page-timeout caps: each pass is bounded and the total number of retries is not limited; the failure is counted in the stall record and the retry delay follows the capped backoff ('Sweeper stall visibility', revisions 21 and 22) |

**Processing order and pass budget (revision 21, CM-2; vocabulary revision 22).** *Order (rule (h)).* The sweeper processes the targets of a completely collected batch **one at a time, in ascending execution `id`**: the page queries return rows in ascending `id` (`ORDER BY id`), the collection keeps that order, and the Python processing takes the targets in exactly that order, one row at a time. The order is never changed and the targets are never processed in parallel (no `gather`, no concurrent processing tasks); a mutation test that reverses the order must fail. *Cursor discipline.* No cursor advances before the row is decided ('Cursor vocabulary' of §7.4): the committed cursor is never moved past a target that is not decided and never past a row that was not processed. When the pass budget `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS` runs out, no new processing is started and the committed cursor is set only to the id of the **last decided row**; the targets that were not reached stay behind it and are collected again by the next pass. If **no** target was decided (zero decided rows, for example because one processing step or the database is slow), the committed cursor stays unchanged; this is a pass without progress: it is counted in the stall record with the fixed code `SWEEP_NO_PROGRESS` ('Sweeper stall visibility'), it is no error of a row and it skips nothing. The committed cursor is fixed only over decided rows; on a failure **of the collection** (a query failure, a statement timeout, a classification error that is not isolated per row, an exception or a cancellation) nothing was processed, the scan cursor is restored to `pass_start_cursor` and the committed cursor stays unchanged (rule (f)); on a failure **of the processing** it moves only over the committed prefix (rule (g)(iv)). *Budget relation, stated without a guarantee.* The validator requires `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS` < `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS` **strictly** (both > 0 and finite; equality is rejected). The margin exists for the cleanup, the rollback and the recording of the state after the collection. This relation does **not** guarantee that at least one target is decided: the collection may use its whole scan budget, one processing step may need up to `JOB_CLOSE_SETTLE_SECONDS` + `PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS`, and a slow database or a slow Python step can leave zero decided rows. The document makes no minimum-one-decision claim (a contract test checks the text and the validator for this).

**Isolation per row (revision 21, W-3).** A processing or classification error is *isolated per row* exactly when it can be converted into a safe, row-local anomaly that the classifier already defines: a `detail` that cannot be decoded or classified becomes the anomaly `OTHER_SCHEMA_INVALID` with `sub_reason = decode_error`, caught by the per-row `try/except Exception` of §7.5 item 7. Such a row counts as classified, the scan cursor passes it, the batch continues and the pass does not fail. Every other error is **not isolated** and fails the **whole pass**: a database error, a statement timeout (SQLSTATE `57014`), a contract violation or an unexpected exception outside the per-row conversion, and a cancellation. A non-isolated error during the collection discards every target of the pass, restores the scan cursor to `pass_start_cursor`, leaves the committed cursor unchanged (rule (f)) and counts toward the stall record; during the processing it ends the pass, the committed cursor moves only over the committed prefix (rule (g)(iv)) and it counts toward the stall record as well. The rows that stay in the sweeper stream are therefore the isolated ones (the scan cursor passes them) and, after a non-isolated error, the row at which it occurred (the scan does not pass it and does not skip it).

**Per-consumer queries (revision 21, CM-3; user decision: `<PROJECT_U_PAGE>` is a canonical block of its own and the OWN and REST blocks are not reused for project discovery).** Each consumer uses its own query block; no consumer borrows the block of another, and no block is reused to hide a difference in the candidate set:

| Consumer | Query block(s) | Candidate set | Order and partition | Cursor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| risk batch (`risk_batch_targets`: the decision-time predicate and the worker pre-check) | `<RISK_PAGE_OWN>`, then `<RISK_PAGE_REST>` | the U rows of one project, partitioned by Task: phase 1 the resumed Task's own rows, phase 2 the rows of the other Tasks | own rows first, then ascending `id`; one cursor per phase | none across calls (the call owns it) |
| project discovery (the `continue` option decision, the project-level diagnostics discovery and every other project-level consumer without a resumed Task) | `<PROJECT_U_PAGE>` | all U rows of one project through `<PROJECT_SCOPE>`, as one stream | ascending `id` only; no Task partition and no resumed-Task-first order | none across calls (the call owns it) |
| orphan sweeper | `<SWEEP_PAGE>` | the judgeable U rows (`<JUDGEABLE>`) **and** all A rows, across all projects | one ascending `id` stream | the committed cursor of `_sweeper_task` |

The candidate sets differ on purpose: `<RISK_PAGE_OWN>` and `<RISK_PAGE_REST>` are U rows with a Task partition (their union is the U set of the project, but each read is ordered 'own rows first'); `<PROJECT_U_PAGE>` is the whole U set of one project in plain id order, without a resumed Task; `<SWEEP_PAGE>` adds the A rows and the judgeable condition and spans all projects. The binds are `:project_id` (every project-scoped block), `:task_id` (the two risk blocks only), `:last_seen_id` and `:page_size` (every page block; the first page has no `AND id > :last_seen_id`); the appended `:bounded_limit` of 'TrackedBlock …' belongs to the two helper queries only and never to a page block. The page procedure, the page size formula, the caps, the statement timeout and the result states are the same for the three consumers.

**Page-level database time limit (revision 19, C4).** The row count and the Python elapsed time do not bound the database cost of a page, and this document does not claim they do. Every page query runs inside a transaction with a **transaction-local statement timeout**, set with `select set_config('statement_timeout', :ms, true)`, the mechanism that `app/services/recovery_transaction.py:168-169` already uses (`Database.transaction()` rolls back on any exception, `app/db.py:22-26`; the literal `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` is equivalent and both forms ran in r19, §13.1). *Value:* `page_timeout = min(CANDIDATE_PAGE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, remaining_scan_seconds)`, where `remaining_scan_seconds` is `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS` minus the scan time already spent, recomputed before every page; it is finite and > 0, and its millisecond value is an integer ≥ 1 and ≤ `MAX_PG_TIMEOUT_MS` (`policies.py:89`, the rule of `validate_recovery_timeouts`, `validators.py:21-33`); `CANDIDATE_PAGE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` = 2 is a design default, unverified (relations in 'Constants and validator' in this section). *No time left:* when the remaining scan time is below 1 ms the query is **not run** and the scan ends by the time limit. *Restoring the setting:* the setting is local to the transaction, so a scan that shares its transaction with other work (the decision-time scan) reads `current_setting('statement_timeout')` before its first page and restores it with `set_config(…, true)` after its last page, so that later statements of that transaction are not limited by a page timeout (a test, §13). *Result mapping (the one place):* the Python overall scan deadline gives `TARGET_SCAN_TIME_LIMIT_REACHED`; the row budget gives `TARGET_SCAN_ROW_LIMIT_REACHED`; a PostgreSQL statement timeout, SQLSTATE `57014` (read as `exc.orig.sqlstate`; `exc.orig.__cause__` is asyncpg `QueryCanceledError`, observed in r19), gives `TARGET_PAGE_TIMEOUT`; any other transient database error gives `TARGET_QUERY_FAILED`; a contract violation or a permanent classification error gives `TARGET_CLASSIFICATION_ERROR`. **A query timeout is never read as 'no targets' and never as `NO_ELIGIBLE_TARGETS`.** *Aborted transaction:* a statement timeout aborts the transaction, and PostgreSQL answers every later statement with SQLSTATE `25P02` ('current transaction is aborted', observed in r19); therefore nothing — no audit write, no Approval decision, no state change, no savepoint-and-continue — runs after it in that transaction, and the transaction is **rolled back**, never committed. In r19 the row locks of the timed-out transaction were already released by the abort itself, before the explicit rollback; the rollback is still mandatory because the connection must leave the aborted state and nothing may be written on it. *Decision-time scan and locks:* the decision-time predicate may run the scan while it holds the Approval → Task → Project locks (`human_gate_service.py:144,159`, `project_recovery_effect.py:40`); `project_lock_service.py` sets no statement timeout (a grep of `app/` finds `statement_timeout` only in `config.py`, `container.py`, `runner.py`, `policies.py` and `recovery_transaction.py`). The **overall decision scan deadline bounds only the scan's own hold of these locks** (the later risk-target lock phase has its own budget, §7.4 'Risk-target lock phase'): every page timeout is ≤ the remaining decision deadline (`CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS`, counted from the start of the scan), so the scan adds at most that deadline plus one page's round trip and classification, which a statement timeout does not cover (`recovery_transaction.py:17-18` says the same of COMMIT and the network); the rest of the decision transaction is not bounded by this paragraph. On a timeout or a failure the transaction rolls back and releases its locks, the Approval stays PENDING and the outer boundary answers with the defined conflict `409 OPTION_NOT_AVAILABLE`, whose details carry (proposed shape) the `reason_code` and `retryable` of the corresponding `options_hidden` entry, so the client re-reads; no partial decision, partial risk acceptance, request row or `RESUME` is ever written, and the next request is not affected. *Read-time scan:* the options read runs each page in its own short read transaction (rule 11); a timed-out page is rolled back and its session released before the result is built.

**Risk-target lock phase (revision 22; every constant is an unverified design default).** The final lock of the risk snapshot (§7.5 item 4, `<RISK_TARGET_LOCK>`) runs in the decision transaction under the Approval → Task → Project locks and has its **own** time budget, separate from the scan budget `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS`: the scan reads, the lock phase waits for other writers' row locks, and one shared budget would let a slow scan starve the lock phase or the reverse. *Constants (§9.2; central validator `validate_process_timing_limits()`).* `PROCESS_RISK_TARGET_LOCK_SECONDS` = 3 (total budget of the phase), `PROCESS_RISK_TARGET_LOCK_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` = 2 (`statement_timeout` ceiling of one lock statement) and `PROCESS_RISK_TARGET_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` = 1 (`lock_timeout` ceiling of one lock statement). *Why 3 s.* The rows are held only by single-row writers that do no OS work under a row lock (§7.5 item 15), so a healthy wait is expected to be milliseconds (a design expectation, unverified); the decision path already holds the Approval, Task and Project locks during the scan (up to the 5 s scan budget plus one page) and the phase adds at most 3 s on top, a bounded and short extra hold, while a row that stays contended for longer is better answered with a retryable `409` than with a longer hold of three upper locks. *Validation.* All three are finite and > 0; each has an integer millisecond value >= 1 and <= `MAX_PG_TIMEOUT_MS` (`policies.py:89`); the `lock_timeout` ceiling is strictly below the `statement_timeout` ceiling; the statement ceiling is <= the total budget; the construction of the Runner is refused on a violation (R31-9). These are policy ceilings: **the relations do not guarantee that the lock succeeds**, and a contended row can still end the decision with a timeout. *Per statement.* Immediately before **each** lock statement the remaining deadline `remaining = deadline - now` is recomputed (`deadline` = the start of the phase plus the total budget); when it leaves fewer than 2 ms the statement is **not** run and the phase ends as a timeout; otherwise `statement_ms = min(statement_ceiling, remaining)` and `lock_ms = min(lock_ceiling, remaining)` as integer milliseconds, and `lock_ms` is lowered to `statement_ms - 1` when it is not already smaller, so that both are <= the remaining deadline and `lock_timeout` < `statement_timeout` always holds. The lock phase is exactly **one** ordered `FOR UPDATE` statement per decision (`<RISK_TARGET_LOCK>`, §7.5 item 4), so this computation runs once; the INSERT and the commit are **not** claimed to be bounded: after the restore of 'On success: restore before the INSERT' they run under whatever the upper transaction has, and B2 adds no upper whole-decision deadline (none exists today: a grep of `project_lock_service.py` and `human_gate_service.py` finds no statement timeout; stated, not changed). *Mechanism.* In the risk-target-lock transaction both settings are applied as transaction-local values: the implementation form is `select set_config('statement_timeout', :ms, true)` and `select set_config('lock_timeout', :ms, true)` (the mechanism that `app/services/recovery_transaction.py:168-169` already uses for `statement_timeout`, read again in revision 22); `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` and `SET LOCAL lock_timeout` have the same semantics for **both** settings and are not used in code. When both are set, the smaller one fires first (r22): `lock_timeout` ends a lock wait with SQLSTATE `55P03`, `statement_timeout` ends the statement with `57014`; they are told apart by `exc.orig.sqlstate`, never by the exception class. *Mapping (decision).* SQLSTATE `57014` → the existing external reason `TARGET_PAGE_TIMEOUT` (`retryable = true`); SQLSTATE `55P03` → the existing external reason `TARGET_QUERY_FAILED` with `retryable = true` and the **internal** sub-reason `TARGET_LOCK_TIMEOUT` (logged and tested, never an API value); a budget already spent before a statement starts is treated like `57014` (`TARGET_PAGE_TIMEOUT`, internal sub-reason `TARGET_LOCK_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED`). **No new external reason is added:** the fourteen reasons and the priority table of §7.5 item 2 are unchanged, and the internal sub-reasons never appear in `options_hidden` or in a response. *On error.* The whole decision transaction is rolled back: no partial Approval decision, no risk request, no marker and no `RESUME`; **no further SQL runs inside the aborted transaction** (`25P02`, r22); after the rollback the outer boundary answers `409 OPTION_NOT_AVAILABLE` with the `reason_code` and `retryable` of this paragraph. *On success: restore before the INSERT.* Before overriding, the phase reads the current transaction values explicitly with `select current_setting('statement_timeout'), current_setting('lock_timeout')`; after the lock statement returned (a statement that returned 0 rows included) and **before** the risk-request INSERT it restores each value with `set_config(name, previous, true)`; it never sets `0` blindly, which would erase the upper transaction's own policy (a `0` is written back only when the previous value read was `0`). The INSERT and the commit then run under the previous values; r22 read back `7s` and `2500ms` (and `0` and `0`) exactly as before. *Where the sweeper meets this.* The sweeper's page queries are plain `SELECT`s that lock no row, so its mapping is unchanged: `57014` → `SWEEP_PAGE_TIMEOUT`, `55P03` → `SWEEP_QUERY_FAILED` (the sweeper takes no `lock_timeout` of its own; a row-lock wait in its per-row guarded `UPDATE` is bounded only by the short holders of §7.5 item 15).

**Sweeper continuation and restart (CMIN-2; cursor semantics revision 19).** The sweeper keeps its committed cursor only in the memory of `_sweeper_task` (the scan cursor is internal to a pass; both are defined in 'Candidate scan', rules (a) to (h)). A pass that ended on a full batch or on `SCAN_LIMIT_REACHED` continues after the committed cursor in the next pass once the rows it passes were decided; a pass that ended on `QUERY_FAILED`, on a classification exception or on a cancellation during the collection leaves the committed cursor unchanged, so the next pass starts again at `pass_start_cursor` and collects the rows of the failed pass again: the targets of a failed collection were discarded and not processed, so none of them is lost; a pass whose batch processing failed (a rolled-back row, an exception, a cancellation) keeps the cursor at the end of the committed prefix, so the next pass starts after that prefix and judges the failed row again (a duplicate re-processing is allowed, a duplicate state change never); reaching the end of the set successfully, with every selected target decided, resets the committed cursor, so the next pass starts at the first page and revisits rows that stayed unproven. The cursors are never stored; a restart of the Runner or of the task begins again at the first page. That is safe because every processing of a row is idempotent under its guard: a closing write is `WHERE id = :id AND finished_at IS NULL`, a re-processing of a closed row uses the proof-and-disposition guard and an anomaly uses the compare-and-swap on the exact `detail` it read (§6.1, the sweeper bullet of this section), so a row that was already settled matches 0 rows and is re-read, never written twice and never mishandled. Stated honestly: the rows that never leave the sweeper stream are the `decode_error` rows **and** every anomaly or unproven row whose state cannot be proven automatically; because the committed cursor passes every classified row of a batch whose selected targets were all decided, later passes of one incarnation go further even when such rows exceed `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS`, but one pass cannot get past more than that many of them and after every restart the scan begins at the first page again, so B2 does not promise that the sweeper ever reaches eligible rows behind that many permanently stuck rows. **`decode_error` and CLEAN.** While any `decode_error` row exists in the project the project is never CLEAN (A is non-empty): resolving valid U rows, whether by risk acceptance or by the sweeper, does not resolve a `decode_error` row; its operational exit is stated once, in §7.5 item 7. **Constants and validator (§9.2).** `CANDIDATE_PAGE_ROWS` = 50, `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` = 1000, `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS` = 5 and `CANDIDATE_PAGE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` = 2 are design defaults, unverified on any host. `validate_process_timing_limits()` requires: page size ≥ 1; the target batch sizes `PROCESS_RISK_MAX_TARGETS` and `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BATCH_ROWS` ≥ 1 (their existing rules); `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` ≥ `CANDIDATE_PAGE_ROWS`, ≥ `PROCESS_RISK_MAX_TARGETS` and ≥ `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BATCH_ROWS`; `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS` > 0 and finite and ≤ `PROCESS_RISK_ROW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and **strictly less than** `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS` (equality is rejected, rule (h), revision 21); `CANDIDATE_PAGE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` > 0 and finite and ≤ `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS`, with an integer millisecond value ≥ 1 and ≤ `MAX_PG_TIMEOUT_MS`; the construction of the Runner is refused on a violation (R31-9). These arithmetic relations are policy relations between independent ceilings, not a guarantee of database cost: the 5 s database scan budget and the 10 s OS row timeout bound different work and neither depends on the other; and the strict relation to the pass budget leaves a margin without guaranteeing that a target is decided ('Processing order and pass budget'). Every page reads at least one new row or ends the scan, the scanned rows never exceed `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` and each page runs under its own statement timeout, so a scan neither loops forever nor reads without bound.

**Sweeper stall visibility (revision 21, CM-1; position model and transitions revision 22; every default here is an unverified design default).** The rule 'never skip a row' is unchanged: every failed collection, even a single transient one, discards its targets, restores the scan cursor to `pass_start_cursor` and leaves the committed cursor unchanged (rule (f)), and a failed processing moves the committed cursor only over the committed prefix (rule (g)(iv)); the cursor never follows anything that did not commit. The stall state adds visibility and a bounded retry rhythm, nothing else. *Failure causes (fixed safe codes).* `SWEEP_QUERY_FAILED` (a database error other than a timeout, SQLSTATE `55P03` included), `SWEEP_PAGE_TIMEOUT` (a statement timeout, SQLSTATE `57014`), `SWEEP_CLASSIFICATION_ERROR` (a classification or contract error that is not isolated per row), `SWEEP_EXCEPTION` (any other exception of the pass), `SWEEP_CANCELLED` (a **child operation that the pass created**, such as a page query or the processing of one row, was cancelled unexpectedly while the sweeper task itself was not cancelled; the cancellation of the top-level task is never recorded under this code: a normal stop and a failed-start settlement are not failures, and an unexpected end of the top-level task belongs to the Runner supervisor, 'Explicit cancel reason' (§7.4) and table rows 14 to 20, 27 and 28), `SWEEP_NO_PROGRESS` (a pass in which targets were selected and none was decided: targets existed, zero decided; 'Processing order and pass budget'; it counts toward the threshold, table row 13) and `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` (a configuration invariant violation found by the entry-time policy snapshot of §9.1 SUP-28, described in 'Retry rhythm and overflow guard'; it **replaces the failure representation of the same pass**, it is never a second, accumulated failure and it never carries a raw value; table rows 22 to 26, 29 and 30; row 28 is not a `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` row, it is the abnormal exit of the fallback itself). No other text is ever stored or exposed. The sweeper's page queries lock no row, so `55P03` cannot come from them; the mapping is listed for completeness and is not changed by the risk-target lock phase (§7.4 'Risk-target lock phase'). *Position model.* A failure has a **position**. `failure_candidate_id` is the id of the target that failed or, when the pass failed without naming a row, the first selected target that was not decided (for `SWEEP_NO_PROGRESS` the lowest selected id); it is `null` when the page query failed **before returning rows**. `failure_page_after_cursor` is the value of `:last_seen_id` of the page whose query failed before returning rows (`null` when that page was the first page and had no `id >` bound); it is recorded only when `failure_candidate_id` is `null`. A failure during the classification or the processing of a row names that row: its id is the `failure_candidate_id`. The **failure position** of one failure is `failure_candidate_id` when it is not null, otherwise `failure_page_after_cursor` (`null` ranks below every id). Every failure position has a **kind** that decides how it is cleared: `CANDIDATE` for a `failure_candidate_id` (the position is a row that failed while it was classified or processed) and `PAGE_AFTER` for a `failure_page_after_cursor` (the position is **not** a failing row but the boundary just before a page that could not be read, so processing the rows up to and including it has not passed the failed page); the kinds are kept in the internal fields `first_failure_kind` and `current_failure_kind` and are not part of the external view, whose position fields are documented as 'a failing row id or the boundary before an unread page'. `first_failure_cursor` is the failure position that **created the current record** (the first failure after the record was started or replaced); `current_failure_cursor` is the failure position of the **most recent** failure; the two are never confused: while a stall is pinned the current position, the failure code, `last_failure_at`, `next_retry_at` and the `pass_start_cursor` of the latest failed pass are updated to the latest values, and `first_failure_cursor` and `stalled_since` are kept. No raw SQL, no `detail` and no exception string is ever recorded. *Internal state and external view.* The six fields of revision 21 cannot express this, so the **internal** state is split from the external DTO: the pure class `SweeperStallState` (new file `app/services/sweeper_stall.py`, no I/O; the Runner owns one instance and the transition table of this paragraph (rows 1 to 32) is its specification) carries `stalled`, `stalled_since`, `pass_start_cursor`, `consecutive_failures`, `first_failure_cursor`, `current_failure_cursor`, `failure_candidate_id`, `failure_page_after_cursor`, `last_failure_code`, `last_failure_at` and `next_retry_at`, plus the persistent `config_invalid_*` fields of CI-1; the **external** frozen view `SweeperStallSnapshot` (runtime status) and its API model `SweeperStallOut` (the diagnostics cause only, see 'Exposure' in 'Retry rhythm and overflow guard') expose only the safe subset `stalled`, `stalled_since`, `pass_start_cursor`, `first_failure_cursor`, `current_failure_cursor`, `consecutive_failures`, `last_failure_code`, `last_failure_at` and `next_retry_at` (the two component fields, the two position kinds and the internal `config_invalid_*` fields of CI-1 stay internal; the exposed subset of CI-1 is carried only by the diagnostics cause). Positions are execution ids (UUID) or `null`, ordered like `executions.id` (PostgreSQL `uuid` order equals Python `uuid.UUID` order: observed on 500 random values, r22, and pinned by a test, §13). *Counting.* A failed pass whose `pass_start_cursor` equals that of the record increments `consecutive_failures`; a failed pass with another `pass_start_cursor` **replaces** the record with a new one (count 1, new first position, `stalled` false) when the record is not stalled and is **pinned** when it is stalled: the record is not replaced, the count keeps counting and only the current fields are updated. When `consecutive_failures` reaches `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STALL_THRESHOLD` (default 5) `stalled` becomes true and `stalled_since` is set. Reaching the threshold changes **nothing** about the scan: the problem row is **not** skipped, no target of the failing pass is processed, the cursors do not move and the bounded retry continues after the threshold. *Clearing (by position kind).* The record (count and stall) is cleared when a pass that ended **without a failure**, is **not** `SWEEP_NO_PROGRESS` and **advanced the committed cursor or wrapped around** has passed **both** the first and the current failure position, each by the rule of its own kind. A `CANDIDATE` position is passed when `committed_cursor >= failure_candidate_id` (equality counts: the committed cursor is the id of the last decided row, so equality means that the failure candidate itself is decided). A `PAGE_AFTER` position is passed only when `committed_cursor > failure_page_after_cursor` (**strictly**: equality means only that the rows up to the boundary are decided, which says nothing about the page after it that could not be read). The first-page position (`failure_page_after_cursor = null`, which ranks below every id) is passed when the pass advanced the committed cursor by at least one row **successfully** or confirmed the end of the candidate set (a wrap-around); a repeated failure of the first page never clears. The rule is one sentence: **the record is cleared when every recorded failure position (the first and the current one) has been passed by the rule of its own kind, and it is kept when not every recorded position has been passed (only some of them, or none of them).** A wrap-around (the whole candidate set read successfully from `pass_start_cursor` to its end with every selected target decided, an empty candidate set read from the first page included) makes the committed cursor 'no cursor', which is the end of the set and ranks above every id, so every position of both kinds, `null` included, is passed (rows 9 and 10 of the transition table of this paragraph). A record whose first and current positions are of different kinds is cleared only when each satisfies the rule of its own kind (row 7), and when not every position satisfies its rule the record is kept (row 8). One `>=` for every kind is wrong: it would clear a `PAGE_AFTER` record at `committed_cursor = failure_page_after_cursor` although the page after that boundary was never read successfully (the superseded rule; a mutation test detects it, §13). If the failure candidate was settled or deleted by another path it simply leaves the stream, and the record is cleared by the next successful pass that passes its position by the rule of its kind (or that wraps around). A success at another position (a commit below the failure position by the rule of its kind) never clears an existing stall and does not change the count, and a pass without a failure that advanced nothing and did not wrap leaves the record and the count unchanged (row 11). The in-memory state is lost when the process or the `Runner` object is replaced and is kept across a stop and start of the same object (§9.1 SUP-11); the limitation of a memory-only state is kept. *State-transition table (the specification of `SweeperStallState`; `T` = `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STALL_THRESHOLD`, `f` = the position of the new failure, `P` = the `pass_start_cursor` of the new pass; a failed pass is any pass that ends with one of the failure codes listed under 'Failure causes' of this paragraph). **Order of application (the rows are not claimed to be mutually exclusive):** (1) the cancellation rows 14 to 19 and 27 first decide whether an event is a failure at all; (2) when the entry-time policy snapshot fails, `now + ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` is computed first (a failure there is row 28 and nothing is written, so a failing snapshot together with a corrupted fallback leaves the record and the count unchanged); then rows 22 and 23 apply and replace the failure representation of the pass and write the persistent configuration-invalid state (CI-1 to CI-6) (row 22: the failing entry is counted and positioned as row 2 or row 4 by state, because an earlier pass left a record; row 23: it is counted and positioned as row 1 or row 3, because no record exists or its recorded `P` differs from `pass_start_cursor`; the choice depends only on the record and on `pass_start_cursor` and never on whether the previous pass failed, so a pending record that row 8 or row 11 kept after a pass without failure gives one outcome: row 22 (count +1, same position, the trigger code by the rule of CI-1) while `pass_start_cursor` equals `P`, otherwise row 23 (replacement as row 3); no pass body ran in either case); (3) a failed pass is handled by rows 1 to 4 (rows 13 and 16 name the code); (4) for a pass without a failure, a wrap-around is handled first (rows 9 and 10 give the same result for an empty candidate set, so either may be named, and a wrap-around passes every position, so it takes precedence over rows 5 to 8), then rows 5, 6 and 7, then row 8 as the remainder ('not every recorded position was passed': some of them or none of them), then row 11 (no advance and no wrap-around); rows 25 and 26 are the `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` cases of rows 5 to 11 and give the same result; (5) rows 12, 20, 21, 24, 31 and 32 describe events and apply to whatever state exists; (6) rows 28 to 30 handle the corrupted fallback and the persistent configuration-invalid state, which no row of 1 to 12 reads or changes (CI-4)):*

**Persistent configuration-invalid state (revision 26; rule IDs CI-1 to CI-7; it replaces the revision-25 rule that keyed the warning `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` on `last_failure_code`; design only, not implemented or run).** The warning is `config_invalid_active`, not the latest failure code: a later failure with another code used to hide a configuration error that had not been fixed. The persistent state is separate from the ordinary failure context of the stall record and lives in the Runner-owned `SweeperStallState` (in memory; lost when the process or the `Runner` object is replaced; kept across a restart of the sweeper task, §9.1 SUP-8, and across a stop and start of the same object, §9.1 SUP-11).

- **CI-1 Fields (internal or exposed; revision 27 renames two of them).** The **ordinary** failure context (`last_failure_code`, the position `current_failure_cursor` and the other fields of the stall record) is separate and is never a `config_invalid_*` field. **Four different fields are never confused:** the ordinary latest failure code (`last_failure_code` of the stall record: the code of the latest failed pass, `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` after a detection); the original failure code that triggered the state (`config_invalid_trigger_failure_code`, internal); the public representative code (the fixed code `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` that the exposed `last_failure_code` and the warning `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` show while the state is active; it is never the trigger code); the current validation result (`config_currently_valid`, §9.1 SUP-29). `config_invalid_active` (bool; exposed as the fixed warning code and in the diagnostics cause). `config_invalid_detected_at` (exposed in the diagnostics cause). `config_invalid_trigger_position` (the position of the pass that **first activated** the state or that last replaced the trigger context: its kind, `CANDIDATE` or `PAGE_AFTER`, is **internal**, and the candidate or page-after cursor is exposed in the diagnostics cause only, never in `/health` or in the report). `config_invalid_trigger_failure_code` (**internal**; the original failure code that triggered the state: the `last_failure_code` that the record held immediately before the detecting entry-time snapshot failure, taken only when it is not `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`, otherwise the stored trigger code is kept (`null` when no record existed and nothing is stored); a later ordinary failure never changes it and it is never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` itself; the r27 name of the r26 field `config_invalid_original_failure_code`, itself the r25 `original_failure_code`). `config_invalid_next_retry_at` (exposed in the diagnostics cause; not null while active; an **audit value**: the end of the wait that the trigger pass started, not a schedule once CI-7 applies). `config_invalid_reasons` (an optional bounded set of the fixed reasons of `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID_REASONS`, §9.4: `TYPE`, `NON_FINITE`, `OUT_OF_RANGE`, `RELATION`, `OVERFLOW`, `DATETIME_LIMIT`; internal and in the diagnostics cause; never free text, never a constant name and never a value). 'Exposed in the diagnostics cause' means the additive model `SweeperConfigInvalidOut` on the `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` cause only. The fields of this model and of the other sweeper objects are listed once, in §14.2, which also says how `next_retry_at` of the stall snapshot (the ordinary schedule) differs from `config_invalid_next_retry_at` (the audit value of the trigger pass).
- **CI-2 Detection (rows 22 and 23).** `consecutive_failures` (the failure count that is also the stall counter) rises **at most once per pass**: a pass whose entry-time snapshot fails runs no pass body and is counted once. The first step of a detection is `now + ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS`: when that cannot be computed the detection writes nothing (row 28). Then, in one atomic step, `last_failure_code` becomes `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` (the public representative code), the count rises once, and the position and the trigger failure code of the **trigger pass** are stored in the `config_invalid_trigger_*` fields (the trigger code by the rule of CI-1: the record's code unless it is `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`, otherwise the stored one is kept); no second failure accumulates. An entry-time snapshot failure while `config_invalid_active` is false is the **first activation**; one while it is true is a **new event** (CI-3, row 30).
- **CI-3 Later passes and the replacement of the trigger context (rows 29 and 30).** While `config_invalid_active` is true, a pass that fails with **another code** (not an entry-time snapshot failure) at the **same, an earlier or a later** position than `config_invalid_trigger_position` neither clears the state nor touches the trigger context: only the ordinary `last_failure_*` fields change (rows 1 to 4), the warning stays, and the state clears only after the recorded trigger position has been passed by the rule of its kind (CI-5). The trigger context is replaced **exactly when the entry-time snapshot itself fails again** at the entry of a pass (rows 22 and 23 while the state is active, row 30): the replacement is atomic and complete (the position and kind, the trigger failure code by the rule of CI-1, the detection time, `config_invalid_next_retry_at` and the reasons of the new detecting pass), because a repeated snapshot failure is the freshest proof that the configuration is still invalid and its position is the one that must be passed; a failure for another reason never replaces the context, and its trigger failure code is never read as the current code.
- **CI-4 Independence.** Rows 1 to 12 (the ordinary stall record) never read or change a `config_invalid_*` field: rows 5 to 10 remove the stall record without clearing the configuration-invalid state, and row 3 replaces the ordinary record only. Rows 22 to 26, 29 and 30 own the persistent state (row 28 writes no `config_invalid_*` state and is not `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`: it is the abnormal exit of a corrupted fallback; row 32 only requests a wake-up and changes none of its fields); row 21 (a replaced process or a new `Runner` object) resets it; rows 20, 27 and 31 (a task restart, and a stop followed by a start of the same object) keep it.
- **CI-5 Clearing requires all three.** (1) The current configuration validation passes (the entry-time snapshot of the clearing pass passed). (2) The recorded `config_invalid_trigger_position` has been passed by the rule of its kind ('Clearing (by position kind)' of 'Sweeper stall visibility': a `CANDIDATE` at `committed_cursor >= position`, a `PAGE_AFTER` only at strictly `>`, the first-page `null` position by an advance of at least one row or a wrap-around). (3) The passing is a **successful cursor commit** or a confirmed end of the candidate set (the equal progress evidence of rows 9 and 10), not a failing or skipping pass and not a pass without an advance (row 11). The state is **not** cleared by a different failure code, by editing the configuration, by a wake-up (CI-7), by the stall record clearing or by a pass that has not run. It is exposed **immediately** in `/health.warnings`, the report `warnings` and the diagnostics, whatever the stall threshold says (`stalled` may be false).
- **CI-6 Honest limits.** (W5) Rows 22 to 26, 28 to 30 and 32 are reachable only when a constant is changed or injected on a live Runner (row 28 writes no `config_invalid_*` state, see CI-4): the validators of §9.3 refuse every such shape at the construction of the Runner (R31-9), before a Runner runs, so the guard exists to keep a changed constant from leaking an exception, not because a normal deployment reaches it. (W4, revised in r27) `config_invalid_next_retry_at` keeps the value computed at detection (the detection time plus `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS`, 24 hours) until the state clears, but it is an **audit value and not a schedule once CI-7 applies**: when the configuration becomes valid again the sweeper is woken once instead of waiting for it, and the first pass of a new generation starts after `startup_mutation_done` (R31-4). After a fix the real wait is therefore the wake-up contract of CI-7, neither `ORPHAN_SWEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS` nor 24 hours.
- **CI-7 Configuration-fixed wake-up (revision 27, decision D27-5).** *Real boundaries (read from the code).* There is **no run-time reload of `Settings`**: `get_settings()` runs once in `create_app` (`main.py:68`) and the `policies.py` constants are module literals, so a configuration can become valid again only at the boundaries RV-1 to RV-3: (RV-1) the start of a new Runner generation (§9.1 SUP-11), whose new sweeper task has no long wait and starts a fresh pass **after `startup_mutation_done`** (R31-4; the stored `next_retry_at` values stay as audit values and the first pass validates its snapshot at its entry and then passes or keeps the recorded trigger position by the normal rules of CI-5); (RV-2, revised in r29) the policy snapshot of §9.1 SUP-28, built and validated at the **entry** of every pass before any value is consumed (superseded in r29: the revision-25 'guard at the end of every pass'; no end-of-pass check remains, because no value is read after the entry; 'Retry rhythm and overflow guard' and row 23 follow the same rule); (RV-3) an explicit **recheck call**, the private Runner method `_recheck_sweeper_configuration(generation, policy)` (revision 28, decision D28-6; it has no `validate_*` name because `validate_*` functions live in `app/validation` with one allow-listed exception, `app/services/artifacts.py` (`ALLOWED_VALIDATE_OUTSIDE`, `tests/architecture/test_rules.py:162`; the check is `:165-174`; revision 33, D33-13)), with no HTTP endpoint, no timer, no hot reload of `Settings` and **no production caller today**: it is a contract for tests and for a future in-process operator boundary that changes a constant on a live process, and this design assumes no reload feature that does not exist; the supervisor never calls it. *Rule.* When RV-3 finds the policy snapshot valid while `config_invalid_active` is true (an **invalid-to-valid transition**, detected there and nowhere else), the sweeper's long wait is ended **once**: the execution schedule ignores `next_retry_at` and `config_invalid_next_retry_at`, which stay unchanged as audit values (the database holds no copy; they are exposed as they were). (1) At most one wake-up is pending: `wake_pending` is a boolean, and a request while it is set is coalesced, not queued. (2) The wake-up pass starts no earlier than `BACKGROUND_WAKEUP_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS` after the start of the previous pass or wake-up, so there is no busy loop; a request inside that interval delays the single pass to its end. (3) The wake-up **does not clear** `config_invalid_active` and does not change the warning: the state clears only under CI-5, after the recorded trigger position has been passed. (4) A pass that fails after the wake-up follows the normal failure policy (rows 1 to 4 and the ordinary backoff of 'Retry rhythm and overflow guard'; an entry-time snapshot failure is a new event, row 30, with the long fallback again). (5) A wake-up that races `stop()` or a generation change starts **no** pass: the sweeper re-checks lifecycle, generation and stop signal in the same synchronous section that consumes `wake_pending`, and a new generation clears the flag (SUP-11). (6) A wake-up is not a restart and touches no supervisor budget (row 32). *Contract of the recheck (revision 28).* `_recheck_sweeper_configuration(generation, policy)` takes the generation of the caller and a policy snapshot (or explicit policy values) and returns a `ConfigWakeResult` (§9.1 SUP-30 is the one contract; superseded in r29: the r28 list with `NOOP` and the lifecycle map that ignored the generation): the first matching result of this precedence: `STALE_GENERATION` (the argument is not the current generation, in every lifecycle), `NOT_RUNNING` (the lifecycle is not `RUNNING`), `STILL_INVALID` (the policy snapshot of SUP-28 fails and nothing is woken), `NO_SWEEPER_TASK` (no live sweeper task exists, so no wake-up is recorded), `NO_INVALID_STATE` (revision 30, C3: the configuration is valid and `config_invalid_active` is false, so nothing is woken and an ordinary failure backoff is not ended early), `ALREADY_PENDING` (the wake-up was already pending and the request is coalesced) and `WAKE_SCHEDULED` (a valid configuration, `config_invalid_active` true, a live sweeper task and no pending wake-up: one wake-up was requested). By lifecycle with a matching generation: `STOPPED`, an IDLE unit, `STARTING`, `STOPPING` and `STOP_INCOMPLETE`: no-op (`NOT_RUNNING`); `RUNNING`: the recheck and at most one wake-up; a stale generation: no-op (`STALE_GENERATION`) whatever the lifecycle. **Lock scope:** the lifecycle lock is held only for the lifecycle and generation check and for setting `wake_pending`, in one synchronous section; the policy snapshot is computed from the policy that was passed in, without the lock; no database I/O and no sleep ever happen while the lifecycle lock is held. A configuration that becomes valid never clears the warning by itself: `WAKE_SCHEDULED` only asks for one pass, and only passing the trigger position clears the state (CI-5).

**Reset table of the persistent state (CI-R; the three sets of CI-4: (i) reset at the start of a new ordinary pass, (ii) reset when the state clears under CI-5, (iii) replaced when a new configuration-invalid event occurs under CI-3).**

| Field | (i) at the start of a new ordinary pass | (ii) when the state clears (CI-5) | (iii) on a new event (row 30) | Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `config_invalid_active` | not reset | set to false | set to true | fixed warning code; diagnostics cause |
| `config_invalid_detected_at` | not reset | cleared (`null`) | replaced with the time of the new detecting pass | diagnostics cause |
| `config_invalid_trigger_position` (kind and cursor) | not reset | cleared | replaced with the position and kind of the new detecting pass | cursor in the diagnostics cause; kind internal |
| `config_invalid_trigger_failure_code` | not reset (rows 2 to 4 never reset it) | cleared | set by the rule of row 22 (the record's code unless it is `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`, then the stored code is kept; `null` when no record existed and nothing is stored) | internal |
| `config_invalid_next_retry_at` | not reset (keeps its old value as an audit value, CI-6) | cleared | replaced with `now + ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` | diagnostics cause |
| `config_invalid_reasons` | not reset | cleared | replaced with the reasons of the new detecting pass | internal and diagnostics cause |
| `wake_pending` (CI-7) | consumed when the wake-up pass starts | cleared | not applicable (a detection never sets it) | internal |
| per-pass scratch (the pass's own positions, the target and stage identification, the 'counted in this pass' flag, the per-pass failure code) | reset | not applicable | not applicable | internal |
| ordinary failure context (`last_failure_code`, the stall record's positions, counts and times) | not reset at the pass start; changed only by rows 1 to 4, 13, 16 and, for `last_failure_code`, by rows 22 and 23 (entry-time snapshot failures) | not touched | `last_failure_code` is set to `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` by rows 22 and 23 | as 'Exposure' of 'Retry rhythm and overflow guard' |

**Stall meaning (revision 26; rule IDs STALL-1 to STALL-4; it replaces the earlier wording that called a configuration error 'permanent' after `T` passes).** (STALL-1) Only consecutive failed passes that make **no progress at the same failure position** (the same `pass_start_cursor`, rows 2 and 4) increase the count that meets `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STALL_THRESHOLD`; a failed pass with another `pass_start_cursor` means that the committed cursor advanced, and it replaces a pending record (row 3: the count restarts at 1 at the new position). (STALL-2) While a backlog drains (failure-free passes that advance the cursor, or failed passes that first commit rows) it is not a stall: reaching the threshold means **sustained no-progress at the same position**, never elapsed time and never the number of passes alone. (STALL-3) A stalled record is **pinned** (row 4): once the threshold has been reached the flag stays until a clearing pass (rows 5 to 10), and after that the pinned count only counts failed passes under the record and is not a claim of no progress; the current-position fields show the latest failure. (STALL-4) The configuration-invalid warning (immediate, CI-5) and the stall-threshold warning `SWEEPER_STALLED` (after `T` passes of sustained no-progress) are **different signals**; when the entry-time snapshot fails the pass body does not run and that pass commits no row; a failure position that differs from the recorded `P` comes only from the committed cursor of the **previous** pass (row 23 then applies), and a pending record then restarts at count 1.

**Configuration guard coverage and a corrupted fallback (revision 26; rule IDs CG-1 to CG-3).** (CG-1) The configuration guard of 'Retry rhythm and overflow guard' (since r29 the entry-time policy snapshot of §9.1 SUP-28) validates, in its one `try` block, every constant that enters the wait or the restart of the sweeper and, since r29, every other constant that the pass body consumes (the next paragraph): the counts `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP` and `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STALL_THRESHOLD` (each a non-bool `int` in its validated range) and the time constants `ORPHAN_SWEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS`, `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BACKOFF_MIN_SECONDS`, `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BACKOFF_MAX_SECONDS`, `ORPHAN_SWEEP_LOG_THROTTLE_SECONDS`, `ORPHAN_SWEEP_MAX_INTERVAL_SECONDS`, `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS`, `CANDIDATE_SCAN_MAX_SECONDS`, `CANDIDATE_PAGE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_WAKEUP_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS` (each a non-bool finite `int` or `float`), the arithmetic relations between them (§9.2) and the `now + timedelta(seconds=delay)` computation; **the backoff computation itself runs inside the same `try`**. Membership of the pass snapshot is not decided here (revision 35, final decision Q2-2): it is the sentence of SUP-28, 'the members of the pass snapshot are the constants that §9.3 validates as sweeper pass inputs and whose validation failure it maps to `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`', and the names listed here restate §9.3 for reading and are not a member list (a difference is resolved by §9.3 and the decision rule of its vocabulary paragraph). For every one of these constants a bool, `None`, a string, NaN, plus or minus infinity, a huge integer such as `10**400`, zero or a negative value where the constant requires a positive one, an out-of-range value and a violated relation is classified as `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` (the verdict per constant is the judgement table of §9.3; zero is **valid** for `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP`) and **never raised out of the guard**; `OverflowError`, `TypeError`, `ValueError` and any other `ArithmeticError` raised anywhere in the block map to the same code, with the fixed reasons of CI-1 and no value. The supervisor-only constants (`BACKGROUND_MAX_RESTARTS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_CAP_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP`, `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX`) are **not** in this guard: they are validated at the construction of the Runner (R31-9) and copied into the supervisor's own state, and an unusable value in that copy makes the component DEGRADED at once (§9.1 SUP-3, SUP-5, SUP-28 'Consumers', SUP-T T16), never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`, because the sweeper guard cannot run in a component that is not running. (CG-2) **Corrupted fallback.** `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` stays a code-policy constant and is not runtime-configurable. If it is itself invalid or uncomputable when it is used (a bool, `None`, a string, NaN, infinity, zero, a negative value), the `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` path is **not** entered again: the error propagates as a top-level exception of the pass, which the supervisor treats as an abnormal exit (§9.1 SUP-2 (d), row 28): bounded restarts within the per-component budgets of SUP-5 with the delay of SUP-3, then DEGRADED; never an infinite wait and never an immediate infinite retry. (CG-3) The validators refuse all of these shapes at the construction of the Runner, before a Runner runs (§9.3), so the guard and row 28 are reachable only when a constant is changed or injected on a live Runner (W5); the tests inject them (a monkeypatch of the constants to `None`, `'x'`, NaN and a bool, §13). **Count constants and the entry snapshot (revision 28; renamed in r30, because since r29 these constants are inside the snapshot and not outside a guard).** `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BATCH_ROWS`, `CANDIDATE_PAGE_ROWS` and `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` do not enter the wait or the restart computation but are consumed by the pass body, so since r29 they **are** in the CG-1 list through the entry snapshot (§9.1 SUP-28): an invalid value of one of them (a bool, `None`, a non-`int`, zero, a negative value or a huge integer) is `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` before any database read (superseded in r29: the revision-28 verdict 'a top-level exception handled by the supervisor as an abnormal exit, never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`'); only a corrupted fallback (CG-2) still ends the pass as an abnormal exit; the validators refuse every such value at the construction of the Runner, before a Runner runs (§9.3).

**Explicit cancel reason (revision 24; user decision: a normal stop and a failed-start settlement are never inferred from the lifecycle; revision 25 limits `SWEEP_CANCELLED` to child operations and adds rule (8), the supervisor).** Whether the cancellation of the top-level task `_sweeper_task` is a normal stop, a failed-start settlement or something else is **recorded before the cancellation, not inferred afterwards**. The reason is a **new field owned by the Runner and its sweeper** with the fixed values `STOP`, `FAILED_START` and `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN` (a new enum, for example `SweeperCancelReason`); it is **not** the recovery enum `CancelReason` of `app/services/runner.py:95-99` (`NONE`, `CALLER_CANCEL`, `OPERATION_DEADLINE`, `SHUTDOWN`), which describes a recovery operation only and stays unchanged. *Rules.* (1) `_shutdown_resources` (`runner.py:393`, run by `stop()`, `runner.py:330-360`) records `STOP` **before** it cancels the sweeper task, the way it cancels the loop task today (`runner.py:404`); `_settle_failed_start` (`runner.py:296`) records `FAILED_START` before it cancels the task; between recording the reason and `task.cancel()` there is **no other `await`** (one synchronous block), and the reason is bound to the identity of the task it was recorded for. (2) A cancellation for which no reason was recorded has the reason `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN`: it is the value when the field is empty, so a caller's cancel of the task, an unexpected `CancelledError` of the task and a cancel by code that does not know the field are all read as `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN` (an unexpected top-level end, rule (5)); none of them is recorded as `SWEEP_CANCELLED`. (3) The reason is cleared when the task has ended (where `_sweeper_task` is cleared) and again when a task is created, and a task never reads a reason bound to another task, so a restarted task (§9.1 item 6) never inherits the reason of its predecessor. (4) The lifecycle and the generation (`runner.py:209`, bumped at `:247` and `:347`) are **defensive cross-checks only**: when the generation captured at task creation differs from the current one, the sweeper looks for a recorded shutdown-family reason (`STOP` or `FAILED_START`); it **never invents** `STOP` from the lifecycle or the generation, and a changed generation without a recorded reason stays `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN` (row 17).
