The `APPLIED → NEEDS_REDECISION` supersede of rows 6, 12 and 13 is deliberate and records `result.supersede` (item 4): the Task was re-gated or failed, so the request must not read as live authority; it is the one allowed exception to terminal immutability.

**Row 3 duplicate prevention (C-a).** Today row 3 (`workflow_service.py:267-274`) calls `HumanGateService.open_recovery` whenever `_recovery_unsafe` reports a problem, and neither it nor `open_recovery` (`human_gate_service.py:82-102`) looks at the Task's PENDING approvals; the only database back-stop is `uq_approvals_project_dirty_pending`, which covers `PROJECT_DIRTY` only (`tables.py:307-309`). A replay (the first pass committed the gate and released the lease, the process died before `Runner.process` finished the RESUME, the recovery requeued it) therefore opens a second PENDING `EXECUTION_UNCERTAIN` gate. **Change:** in the same transaction, after the Task lock and **before** `open_recovery`, row 3 reads `ApprovalRepository.pending_for_task(task.id)` **without** its `type_` filter (`approval_repository.py:34-38`; the repository object is already in scope, `workflow_service.py:260`). No PENDING approval → open the `EXECUTION_UNCERTAIN` gate as today. Any PENDING approval (DESIGN, PERMISSION, RECOVERY, which includes a `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate, or a future type) → **no new gate**: the Task stays parked on the existing one, which is never updated; the lease is released (`leases.release`, `workflow_service.py:272`), `ctx.parked = True` and the outcome is `PARKED`, exactly as on the gate-creating path, so the forbidden state 'WAITING_APPROVAL, no valid gate, lease held, not parked' cannot arise; the current RESUME ends `DONE` through `Runner.process` (`runner.py:1003`) and a replay finds the same gate. This follows the pattern of `Runner._park_uncertain` (`runner.py:1027-1030`) with one difference stated honestly: `_park_uncertain` filters the pending list on `ApprovalType.RECOVERY`, so a PENDING DESIGN or PERMISSION approval does not stop it from opening a RECOVERY gate. Row 3 and the worker use the broader any-type check; `_park_uncertain` is outside this change and stays as it is (a possible follow-up, not part of B2). **Implementation scope:** `WorkflowService._resume_from_approval`, row 3, only; `open_recovery`, the approval repository and the schema are unchanged. **Tests (§13):** gate creation when no approval is PENDING; a crash after the gate commit (the RESUME stays `CLAIMED`) and the replay of the old RESUME → no second gate; an existing PENDING DESIGN approval, PERMISSION approval and RECOVERY approval with `reason_code` `PROJECT_DIRTY` → no new gate, parked on the existing one, lease released; after every case at most one PENDING approval of the Task exists.

11. **Gate creation, reuse and the new `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate (m2).** **Facts of today's code (`project_lock_service.py:342-354`):** `_open_dirty_gate` looks only at the Task's PENDING approvals and filters on `reason_code == PROJECT_DIRTY`; it compares neither `project_id` nor `dirty_epoch`, so it **reuses a stale gate**; `uq_approvals_project_dirty_pending` is one PENDING per `task_id` for `reason_code='PROJECT_DIRTY'`. **Existing `ensure_for_step` path — one optional lineage argument added (C-b, the paragraph after this item):** without it the path is unchanged and keeps that reuse; a stale reused gate is handled by the options of item 1 (CLEAN project: `continue` resumes; DIRTY and stale: `refresh_gate`/`abort`). **New paths (worker result transaction, handler rows 8–13) go through a dedicated path of `HumanGateService`** (the `EXECUTION_UNCERTAIN` default of `open_recovery` is unchanged) with these rules: they run only when the Task has **no PENDING approval** (otherwise row 5: park on the existing gate) **and the lineage lookup of item 11 finds no successor** (otherwise row 15 or 16); a stale PENDING gate is therefore never replaced by a stale-superseding UPDATE (M1) — a stale gate is left PENDING and is resolved by the operator through `refresh_gate`, whose decision marks it DECIDED in the normal lock order and opens the current-epoch gate; so no lock edge is added and the one-PENDING-per-Task index is respected. The previous approval of the resume path is already DECIDED, so the index cannot collide. **Fields, one by one:** `checkpoint_step_key` — **copied** from the previous Approval (`open_recovery` requires it and the next `_resume_from_approval` maps it through `STEP_TASK_STATE[approval.checkpoint_step_key]`); `target.reason_code` — `PROJECT_DIRTY`; `target.project_id` and `target.dirty_epoch` — **recomputed** from the locked project row (never from the old payload); `target.step_id` — `None`; `target.resume_step_key` — the copied checkpoint; previous `approval_id` and process-risk request id (= the previous `approval_id`) — **copied**; refusal or redecision code — the code of item 6 (`LIVE_PROCESS_PRESENT` is shown as `OPERATOR_OVERRIDE_REFUSED_LIVE_PROCESS`); `target.baseline_ref` (last 16 characters of the current `baseline_fingerprint`), `detail.project` (the project's current name) and `detail.baseline_version_ok` (`is_current_version(...)` of the current baseline) — **recomputed** from the locked project row, **not copied**, so a stale baseline is never presented as current authority; `request_payload` also carries the human-readable `reason` and the **static options snapshot** (`continue`, `abort`; an audit record only). Because `open_gate` leaves a Task that is already `WAITING_APPROVAL` in that state, the new gate keeps it waiting without a state transition. The stored options are never authority: reads and decisions recompute them (item 1). **Approval lineage (C7: replay idempotence).** *What it solves:* a RESUME `R1` of approval `A1` replays after a handler, the worker or the ordinary `ensure_for_step` path created a gate `G2` for it and a new RESUME `R2` exists for `G2`; without a lineage the handler could open a spurious gate `G3`. *Storage (decision):* the lineage lives **in the Approval's own `target` JSON, written once in the INSERT** (through the `target_extra` parameter that `open_recovery` already has, `human_gate_service.py:82-85,99`): `supersedes_approval_id` (the approval this gate follows), `lineage_root_id` (the first approval of the lineage; absent on a root gate), `lineage_dirty_epoch` (the project's `write_epoch` when the gate was created, null without a project) and `lineage_origin` (`HANDLER`, `WORKER`, `REFRESH_GATE`, `ENSURE_FOR_STEP` or `LINEAGE_CONFLICT`). It is **not** a new column of `approvals` and **not** on `process_risk_requests`, because: (1) `approvals` rows are updated only by `mark_decided` (`approval_repository.py:40-41`) and `consume_permission` (`:67-71`), never `target`, so an INSERT-time lineage keeps the rule 'no Approval UPDATE other than the ordinary decision' and adds no lock edge; (2) a gate created by `refresh_gate`, by the handler or by the worker's defensive path has **no** `process_risk_requests` row, so a column there cannot describe it; (3) a follow-up *request* needs no column of its own: its id equals its approval id (item 4), so it inherits the lineage of that approval, and a separate `supersedes_request_id` is not needed ("a follow-up process-risk request exists" is `by_approvals(successor ids)`); (4) the existing partial unique index on `approvals` already keys on a `target` expression (`uq_approvals_project_dirty_pending`, `tables.py:307-309`). *Order is never inferred:* "latest" is never decided by `created_at`, `decided_at` or UUID order, only `supersedes_approval_id` links count. *Index (decision):* migration `0005` creates `uq_approvals_lineage_successor`, a partial **unique** expression index on `approvals ((target ->> 'supersedes_approval_id')) WHERE (target ->> 'supersedes_approval_id') IS NOT NULL` (raw SQL literal key, W5, §7.4); it serves the successor lookup and forbids a second direct successor. A partial unique index for *active* successors only was evaluated and **rejected**: whether a successor is active depends on its Approval status, which changes by UPDATE and must not be mirrored into lineage data, and an index cannot see it. Uniqueness over **all** direct successors is correct because one approval has exactly one decision (`uq_approval_decisions_approval`, `tables.py:324`) and one decision yields at most one follow-up gate. The Task-scoped lookup needs no further index: the Task's approvals come from the existing `approvals.task_id` index (`tables.py:289`; a Task has few approvals). *Successor lookup:* under the Task lock, **before** any gate-creating row and before the proceed row 14 (T9, item 10): `SELECT … FROM approvals WHERE (target ->> 'supersedes_approval_id') = :current_id` (the predicate text equals the index predicate). One row → row 15, `IDEMPOTENT_DONE`. This single check covers every case — a PENDING successor (normally caught earlier by row 5, which parks), a DECIDED successor, a `RESUME` created from it (`execution_requests.approval_id` is a foreign key to that approval), a follow-up process-risk request (`process_risk_requests.approval_id` likewise) and a follow-up recovery created through the lineage-aware gate path — because each of them hangs off the successor Approval. *Branching:* two or more direct successors of one approval (possible only if the unique index is absent, for example after a restore) or a successor that belongs to another Task is abnormal: row 16, `APPROVAL_LINEAGE_CONFLICT`, whatever the request status (`APPLIED` or not). No successor is chosen and nothing is picked automatically: the transaction opens **one** `EXECUTION_UNCERTAIN` gate that is itself a lineage **root** (`lineage_origin = LINEAGE_CONFLICT`, no `supersedes_approval_id`, so it adds no successor and cannot enlarge the conflict), only when the Task has no PENDING approval, with `detail.lineage_conflict = {approval_id, successor_ids}` listing **all** conflicting ids as the audit; request rows and existing approvals are untouched. *No gate loop:* the conflict gate is created at most once per replay and only when no PENDING approval exists (row 5 precedes); the RESUME that triggered it ends `DONE` and a `DONE` RESUME is never claimed again (`execution_requests.approval_id` is UNIQUE); the conflict gate's own `continue`/`retry`/`abort` is an ordinary RECOVERY decision (rows 1–3 only) and never enters rows 4–16. An `IntegrityError` on the unique index while a gate is inserted (it cannot happen under the Task lock) rolls the transaction back, the RESUME is requeued and the next pass finds the successor (row 15). The worker uses the same lookup before opening any gate (item 6). Row 3 (`_recovery_unsafe`) keeps today's check and gains the any-type PENDING guard before it opens a gate (C-a, item 10): without it a replay could open a second PENDING `EXECUTION_UNCERTAIN` gate because `open_recovery` has no pending check (`workflow_service.py:267-274`, `human_gate_service.py:82-102`); with it the replay finds the gate of the first pass and parks on it.

**Lineage through the ordinary `ensure_for_step` path (C-b, revision 14).** *Why:* the gate that a resumed Task meets next is created by the ordinary path, not by the handler or the worker. The real path, read from code: `Runner.process` claims the RESUME and calls `WorkflowService.run_task(lease, task_id, resume_approval_id=request.approval_id, request_id=request.id)` (`runner.py:990`); `run_task` creates the `RunContext` (`workflow_service.py:97-106`, built at `:129` or `:132`) and calls `_resume_from_approval` (`:135`, `:256-282`); the loop then dispatches the handler of the Task state (`:144`); a changing step enters `_agent_step`, which calls `self.locks.ensure_for_step(ctx.lease, task.id, step_key, self.gates)` (`:313`); that calls `_acquire_once` (`project_lock_service.py:224`, `:238`), which calls `_open_dirty_gate` for a project that is not CLEAN (`:251`, `:342-354`), which calls `open_recovery(…, target_extra=…)`. Without a lineage on that gate, a replay of the old RESUME `R1` after the new gate `G2` was decided finds neither a PENDING approval nor a successor, passes row 14 and would resume the Task a second time (or, after the `continue` of the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate `G2` changed the epoch, open a spurious `G3` through row 12). *Ownership and flow:* (1) `Runner.process` passes only `request.approval_id` and `request.id`; a client never supplies lineage. (2) `_resume_from_approval` stores `ctx.resumed_from_approval_id = approval.id` and `ctx.lineage_root_id = approval.target.get("lineage_root_id") or approval.id` in the `RunContext` **in the lineage restoration step L, before the Task-state early return** (revision 15, M-1; item 10, paragraph 'Lineage restoration before the Task-state early return'), and only for a risk-option decision whose RESUME, approval, decision, request, lineage fields and successor lookup were verified under the Task lock; the earlier version, which set them only at row 14, lost them whenever the run was entered again with the Task no longer `WAITING_APPROVAL`. Both new fields default to `None`; no other path sets them (a DESIGN, PERMISSION or ordinary `continue` resume leaves them `None`) and neither is ever taken from a request body. A separate `resumed_from_request_id` is not needed: the process-risk request id equals the approval id (item 4), the RESUME is `ctx.request_id` (`:104`), and a successor request or RESUME is found through the successor Approval. (3) `_agent_step` builds a `GateLineage(supersedes_approval_id, lineage_root_id)` from the context when `ctx.resumed_from_approval_id` is set and passes it as one new **optional** argument `lineage` of `ensure_for_step`, which hands it unchanged to `_acquire_once` and `_open_dirty_gate`; every call without it (all existing callers and tests) is the legacy path. (4) `_open_dirty_gate(…, lineage=None)`: **absent → the code path is today's, with `target_extra` and `detail` byte-identical (golden test)**; **present → the NEW Approval's `target` additionally carries, written once in the INSERT through `target_extra`,** `supersedes_approval_id`, `lineage_root_id`, `lineage_dirty_epoch` (the project's `write_epoch` read under the project row lock, the same value as `dirty_epoch`) and `lineage_origin = ENSURE_FOR_STEP`. The minimum content of such a gate is therefore: `reason_code = PROJECT_DIRTY`, `project_id`, `dirty_epoch`, `baseline_ref`, `resume_step_key` (the checkpoint step key, the `step_key` argument), and the four lineage keys. (5) **No Approval UPDATE and no new lock edge:** the lineage is part of the INSERT; `ensure_for_step` and `_acquire_once` already hold Task → TaskRun → Project, and the INSERT of an `approvals` row, with its entry in the unique lineage index, waits for nothing that holds a lock on those rows, because the only other writer of the same key would be a second successor of the same approval, which needs the same Task lock. (6) **Reusing an existing PENDING gate never writes or overwrites a lineage:** `_open_dirty_gate` finds a PENDING `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate and only releases the lease, as today. If a lineage is passed and the reused gate carries a different `supersedes_approval_id` (or none), the code does not UPDATE it; it logs a warning `LINEAGE_REUSE_MISMATCH` and uses the gate as it is. This is a **stated limitation**, not a handled case: it cannot arise from the documented producers, because a PENDING approval makes the run park (row 5) and a parked run never calls `ensure_for_step`, and a second run of the Task cannot exist while the lease is held; were it to arise, the only consequence is that the successor lookup does not link that gate to the earlier approval, while row 5 and the one-PENDING-per-Task index still prevent a duplicate. (7) The successor lookup (T9) of this item runs under the Task lock for every decision of the risk branch that passed T1–T7, before rows 8–14: **a PENDING successor gate, a DECIDED successor gate, a successor RESUME and a successor process-risk request all lead to `IDEMPOTENT_DONE`**, decided only by the `supersedes_approval_id` links and never by time or UUID order. The one reconciliation, stated in item 10: a PENDING successor is caught by row 5 first and ends `PARKED`, because the replaying run's lease must be released; the effect on gates and requests is the same.

**Lineage unique-constraint conflict on the ordinary path (C-7, revision 16).** *Facts read from code:* no code under `app/` inspects an `IntegrityError` today (a search of `app/` for `IntegrityError`, `constraint_name` and `23505` finds nothing), so the extraction of this item is new and is pinned by a PostgreSQL test. In the installed stack (SQLAlchemy 2.1.6 with asyncpg 0.32.0) the path is **verified on PostgreSQL 18.4 for exactly these versions** with a real partial unique expression index and an ORM flush inside `session.begin()` (§13.1): a unique violation raised through the SQLAlchemy asyncpg engine is an `IntegrityError` whose `exc.orig.sqlstate` is `'23505'` and whose `exc.orig.__cause__` is an `asyncpg.exceptions.UniqueViolationError` (`sqlstate == '23505'`) whose `constraint_name` is the name of the violated unique constraint. This is the internal exception structure of two libraries, not a documented contract, so it is version-specific and the defences of this item stay: the sqlstate and the constraint name are checked together, and if the structure is not as verified here (`__cause__` missing or of another type, no constraint name) the exception is **not** treated as idempotent success and the original error propagates. *Contract:* `ensure_for_step`, outside the `async with self.db.transaction()` of `_acquire_once` (so the failed transaction has already rolled back), catches `sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError` around the call that can insert a lineage-carrying gate and treats it as the lineage race **only if** the sqlstate is `23505` **and** the violated constraint name is exactly `uq_approvals_lineage_successor`. If the name cannot be read, or is another name (`uq_approvals_project_dirty_pending`), or the violation is a check or a foreign key, the exception **propagates unchanged**: never are all `IntegrityError`s idempotent success. On the lineage race a new short transaction takes the Task lock, verifies the lease and re-reads the successor of `lineage.supersedes_approval_id` (the T9 lookup): (a) the successor is a PENDING approval of the Task: release the lease in that transaction and return `GATE_OPENED` (the run parks, PARKED); (b) the successor is DECIDED, or only its RESUME or request exists: the lineage was consumed by another pass, so this run opens no gate and continues the `ensure_for_step` loop **with the lineage dropped** (the legacy path of item 11); (c) no successor is visible (the other writer rolled back): the loop retries once with the lineage, bounded by `PROOF_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (`project_lock_service.py:209`). The Task lock stays the primary serialisation (a second successor needs the same lock); the unique index is the final backstop. *Which later path the run takes when step L refused the restoration because a successor exists:* the context lineage stays `None`, so the run proceeds through the table of item 10: a PENDING successor is row 5 (PARKED); a Task that is no longer `WAITING_APPROVAL` returns early at row 2 (`IDEMPOTENT_DONE`) and the loop then continues **as an ordinary run from the Task's current state**; a DECIDED successor, a successor RESUME or a successor request with the Task still waiting is row 15 (`IDEMPOTENT_DONE`, nothing created). In the ordinary-run case `_agent_step` calls `ensure_for_step` **without** lineage (the legacy path): a CLEAN ownerless project acquires normally; a project that is dirty again opens or reuses a `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate by `reason_code` with **no** lineage keys, so it cannot violate the unique index. A genuinely new dirty condition may therefore still let the run continue as an ordinary run and open a new, unlinked gate; the earlier wording that a replay always ends in `IDEMPOTENT_DONE` or `PARKED` is corrected: it holds for the rows of the table, not for the run that follows an early return. *Successor RESUME `CLAIMED` and two successive crashes:* (i) the successor gate `G2` was decided and its RESUME `R2` is `CLAIMED` when `R1` replays: L finds the successor and refuses, row 15 or row 2 applies, `R1` writes nothing and `R2` is untouched; (ii) crash A after row 14 committed the Task move, crash B after `G2` was opened and before the run parked, then `R1` and `R2` replay in either order: the one processed second finds the successor through the `supersedes_approval_id` link and L refuses; at most one direct successor exists (unique index); no `G3` is opened. All are tests (§13).

12. **Two approvals targeting the same executions (m8).** Requests A and B are independent rows with independent snapshots; neither overwrites the other, and their result transactions serialize on the project row lock. **Outcome A — `dirty_epoch` unchanged:** A's worker wrote the dispositions first and no baseline re-acceptance happened yet; B's worker re-reads the rows, counts them resolved and reaches `APPLIED` with its own `RESUME` for its own Task, fenced by its own Task and `dirty_epoch`. **Outcome B — `dirty_epoch` changed:** A's Task already completed `continue` (`accept_baseline` raised `write_epoch`/changed the state). If B's request was not yet `APPLIED`, its worker ends it `NEEDS_REDECISION(DIRTY_EPOCH_CHANGED)` (item 6); if it already was `APPLIED`, the handler supersedes it (row 12 of item 10). Either way B is **never** resumed from the old request; a new gate is opened with the current epoch through item 11, and because the project is now CLEAN, B's Task finds `continue` offered even on a stale gate and resumes with its own `continue` (CLEAN-first order of item 1). A `REFUSED_ALIVE` of one request deletes nothing of the other's audit (each `result` is its own). Neither Task is left in `WAITING_APPROVAL` without a request that is being processed or a valid gate.
13. **Operator visibility.** The request's state is returned in `ApprovalOut.operator_request` (item 2). While the worker is DEGRADED (§9.1 item 6, SUP-6) or the Runner is down the request waits: the Task shows `WAITING_APPROVAL` with a decided approval and a non-terminal request, diagnostics `RUNNER_STATE` names the degraded component, the existing cancel path still works, and a new Runner generation revives the worker, which re-discovers the request.
14. **Audit (m11).** The database is authoritative: the request rows (one per approval, never overwritten except the single `APPLIED → NEEDS_REDECISION` supersede of item 4, which keeps `result.supersede`; every recheck is its own row), the approval decision with its rationale, the lineage keys in the `target` of each new gate (item 11), `detail.reason_code` and `detail.risk_acceptance` on each accepted row. B2 publishes **no** event: `EventBus.publish` is keyed by task id only, and a project-scoped event would need a separate EventBus design. No session id or token is stored; pid and create time are not secrets. **One rule for everyone:** D4 `TEST_ONLY` has no separate path or option; its rows are ordinary tracked rows.
15. **Lock order (m6, M1, mi-2).** Decision (including `refresh_gate`, whose new Approval is an INSERT): Approval → Task → Project, then, for the two risk options only (revision 21), the execution rows of the final risk snapshot in ascending `id` (`<RISK_TARGET_LOCK>`, item 4), then the INSERT of the new request or gate row (nothing waits on a new row). Worker result transaction and the `_resume_from_approval` branch: Task → Project → request row → execution rows in ascending id; the claim and the retry bookkeeping take only the request row. Plain sweeper: execution rows only, one transaction per row. Two requests serialize on the project lock. The worker's `RESUME` INSERT and its gate INSERT touch `approvals` only as new rows or through the `execution_requests.approval_id` foreign key, which can take `FOR KEY SHARE` on the decided `approvals` row after the Task and Project locks; this does not recreate the M1 cycle, because the worker sees a request only after the decision transaction committed (so that transaction no longer holds the Approval row) and a replayed `decide` holds `repo.lock` (`FOR UPDATE`) briefly and returns without taking the Task lock, so it never waits for the worker. No B2 write is an UPDATE of an existing Approval other than the ordinary `mark_decided` of a decision; the lineage keys are part of the INSERT of the new Approval, and the successor lookup is a plain `SELECT` under the Task lock (no new lock edge). This is reasoned from the code, not run; the interleaving tests of §13 stay.

**Execution rows and deadlock freedom (revision 21, CM-4; ordered structurally in revision 22; reasoned from the code, the PostgreSQL behaviour is recorded in §13.1, r21 and r22).** Wherever one transaction takes both, the execution rows come **after** the Approval, Task and Project locks, so they add no edge from an execution row back to those locks. The global order is Approval → Task → Project → execution rows in ascending `id`: the decision transaction (Approval `human_gate_service.py:144` → Task `:159` → Project `project_recovery_effect.py:40` → execution rows) and the worker result transaction (Task → Project → request row → execution rows) are serialized with each other by the Project lock before either touches an execution row. *The ascending order is enforced structurally, not by convention.* Every place that locks **several** execution rows does it through one ordered-lock repository API in `TaskRepository`, `lock_executions_ordered(ids)` (plain) and `lock_risk_targets(project_id, target_ids)` (the `<RISK_TARGET_LOCK>` form), which (a) sorts and de-duplicates the ids itself, so the caller's order is irrelevant, (b) issues **one** statement `SELECT … WHERE id = ANY(:ids) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` (PostgreSQL locks the rows in the order the sort delivers them: plan `LockRows` over `Sort`, r22), (c) checks that the returned ids are strictly ascending and raises a contract error otherwise, and (d) returns the rows in that order; callers then iterate the **returned** sequence. No caller depends on the return order of another query (the shared `unterminated_executions` query has no `ORDER BY`, `task_repository.py:156-159`, and is never the lock order), and no code assumes that one `UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…)` locks rows in the order of the list. *Lease takeover (`lease_service.py:119-135`, Txn B).* Today the update loop (`:129-132`) runs in the order of `verdicts`, which comes from the unordered read at `:102-103`: two transactions that lock several rows in opposite orders deadlock (`40P01`, r21 and r22). B2 changes it as follows: (1) sort the target ids explicitly; (2) first lock them with `SELECT id FROM executions WHERE id = ANY(:ids) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` (the ordered-lock API; the guard `finished_at IS NULL` stays on the UPDATE); (3) then UPDATE iterating the **returned** ordered sequence. It takes neither the Project nor the Approval lock, so it never waits for a lock that the decision holds after taking a row. *Survey of every execution-row writer or locker (code read in revision 22):*

| Path (file:line) | Execution rows touched | Class | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| risk decision, `ProjectDirtyRecoveryEffect.apply` after the project lock (design, §7.5 item 4) | the final risk snapshot | multi-row | `lock_risk_targets`: ordered lock before the request INSERT |
| process-risk worker result transaction (design, §7.5 item 6) | the request's target rows | multi-row | `lock_executions_ordered` after Task, Project and the request row |
| lease takeover Txn B, `lease_service.py:129-132` | the stale rows of one Task | multi-row | sort the ids, `lock_executions_ordered`, then UPDATE in the returned order |
| orphan sweeper closing and anomaly writes (design, §7.4) | one row per transaction | single-row | one guarded `UPDATE … WHERE id = :id`, own transaction, nothing awaited afterwards |
| `on_started`, `step_runner.py:156-160` | one row | single-row | `UPDATE … WHERE id`, own transaction |
| `_record_start`, `step_runner.py:209` (the `add_execution` INSERT; the method starts at `:198`) | none (a new row) | insert only | a new `STARTING` row of an untracked agent-CLI execution; the Task is locked first (`:200`); no lock on an existing execution row and no `FOR UPDATE` on `executions` |
| `_record_finish`, `step_runner.py:215-234` | one row | single-row | locks the Task first (`:219`), then updates the execution and the Task: Task → execution, the global order; untracked rows are never locked by the risk paths |
| `_discard_result`, `step_runner.py:248-256` | one row | single-row | `UPDATE … WHERE id`, then the step state; no Task, Project or Approval lock is awaited after it |
| terminal settlement (`release_on_terminal`, `project_terminal.py`) and `ProjectLockService._reconcile_once` | none | read only | plain `SELECT`, no `FOR UPDATE` (§7.4) |
| recovery and cancel reads (`runner.py:860,873`, `_finalize_cancel`, `_recovery_unsafe`) | none | read only | plain `SELECT` of `unterminated_executions` |
| orchestrator test run, `workflow_service.py:776-780` | none | insert only | a new row; no lock on an existing row |

*Architecture and behaviour tests (§13).* (1) Only the two ordered-lock methods issue `FOR UPDATE` on `executions` (a text scan of the repository sources and the SQL blocks); (2) a source (AST) test fails when a function runs `update(Execution)` or a multi-row `UPDATE executions` inside a loop without an earlier call of an ordered-lock method in the same function and iteration over that call's result; an unordered id loop (a `for` over a `set`, over `verdicts` or over an unsorted query result) around an execution UPDATE is forbidden; (3) the ordered-lock method rejects a result that is not strictly ascending (a fake that returns a reversed list makes the test fail); (4) a PostgreSQL interleaving test: two transactions that use the ordered-lock API, or one that uses it against a session locking the same rows one by one in ascending order, never deadlock, while a mutation that locks in reversed order deadlocks against them (`40P01`; detection power: the test fails if the mutation does not deadlock); (5) the takeover test pins the sorted ids, the ordered `FOR UPDATE` before the first UPDATE and the iteration over the returned sequence. With one global order — Approval → Task → Project → execution rows in ascending `id` — and single-row writers that wait for nothing afterwards, no wait cycle exists (reasoned; the deadlock and no-deadlock interleavings ran on tiny tables, §13.1 r22).

## 8. Crash recovery: what the database can and cannot prove

Who performs OS work: **only the Runner / a recovery worker inside the Runner process** (`Runner.recover`, `_recover_rest`, `LeaseService.acquire` takeover, `Runner.stop`). Human Gate handlers run on the API request path (possibly an instance that does not hold the Runner advisory lock) and may only **record a request** that the Runner acts on. B2 does not change this and D4 must not add OS work to gate effects.

Proof is written by the same takeover path that already writes `finished_at` (`lease_service.py:129-132`); it does not depend on the old lease still being valid, and no step is parked just to write it. Required changes to that path (§14): the verdict step receives the whole execution row (today `Terminator` receives only a `ProcessIdentity`) through an injected tracked-verdict function (a plain callable, not a new Protocol); the closing write uses a **JSONB merge** (`detail || :proof`) instead of replacing `detail`, so `tracked`/`runner_process` survive; and the `pid IS NULL` guard of this item. Rows of terminal Tasks are evaluated by the orphan sweeper of §7.4. **Checkpoint after a crash:** when `Runner._park_uncertain` finds no RUNNING/INTERRUPTED step it reads `detail.checkpoint_step_key` of the Task's unresolved tracked row (`STEP_TEST` for test calls) before falling back to `resume_step_key`/`PLAN`, so a crash during `ids_before` re-enters TESTING, not PLANNING.

| Situation after a Runner/API crash (row has `detail.tracked`, `finished_at IS NULL`) | What recovery may conclude |
|---|---|
| `pid IS NULL` | I4: the process was never resumed, so no user code ran → close as `SPAWN_FAILED` with `proof=NEVER_RAN`, `reason=SUSPENDED_ORPHAN_POSSIBLE`. **Two guards make this sound:** the closing `UPDATE` carries `AND pid IS NULL` (a row whose identity was committed after Txn A read it is not closed; rowcount 0 → `HELD("takeover raced")`, re-evaluated on the next cycle), and the owner's own `on_started` update is fenced with `finished_at IS NULL` plus lease verification (§5.1 step 5), so an old coroutine whose row was closed can never resume its process. (A pid-less **untracked** agent-CLI row keeps today's UNCERTAIN rule.) |
| pid + create_time, Windows, **all of the following conditions hold** | confirmed: `termination=ALREADY_EXITED` (member of `CONFIRMED_GONE`), `detail.proof=JOB_KILL_ON_CLOSE_ASSUMED` (written in the same UPDATE as `finished_at`, §6.1) |
| pid reused (`IDENTITY_MISMATCH`) for the root | the recorded root is gone; the new process is not ours and is **not killed**; the other conditions still apply |
| any condition fails, or `ACCESS_DENIED`/`UNKNOWN` | `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`, never CLEAN; the existing RECOVERY gate applies |

Conditions for `JOB_KILL_ON_CLOSE_ASSUMED` (decision H3 — a **conditional OS guarantee**, labelled as such, never presented as database proof):

1. `detail.runner_process.host` equals this host's name.
2. The previous Runner process is **proven dead**: `check_alive(runner_process)` is `ALREADY_EXITED` or `IDENTITY_MISMATCH`. `STILL_ALIVE`, `ACCESS_DENIED`, `UNKNOWN` or a missing record → not proven (the handle may still be open).
3. The root is gone: `check_alive(pid, create_time)` is `ALREADY_EXITED` or `IDENTITY_MISMATCH`.
4. A bounded settle wait (`JOB_CLOSE_SETTLE_SECONDS`) finds **no live process whose `ppid` is the recorded root pid and whose create time is not earlier than the root's** (best-effort sweep; only direct children are reliable once the root is gone). Any survivor means the OS guarantee did not hold → `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`.

Residual risks, accepted only through H3: a Job handle inherited or duplicated by another process (guarded by the §5.1 step-1 test), teardown slower than `JOB_CLOSE_SETTLE_SECONDS` (only 1.5 s was observed, in a limited probe; 2.0 s is an unverified design default), a launcher outside the Job. A deployment that does not accept this switches the policy off and every crash then ends in `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`.

Clean stop: `Runner.stop` cancels in-flight tasks; each tracked run settles (§9) and its caller closes the row in `finally`, so a **normal** stop leaves no open tracked row (the closing write is lease-independent, §6.1, although `Runner.stop` has already revoked the lease). A run that did not settle within the stop budget is listed in `RunnerStopIncomplete` (existing mechanism); its row stays open and is evaluated by the crash-recovery table of §8 after the process exits.

## 9. Cancellation, natural exit and output draining

`CommandExecutor.run`/`_execute` are restructured so that after spawn there is a single settlement coroutine, named **`_settle_process`** (the existing `_settle` stays as is):

```
try:
    spawn → (tracked) assign → identity → resume        # the settlement try-block starts at the spawn, so a failing on_started also settles the tree
    wait for root exit (returncode) / cancel / timeout / idle
except BaseException as exc:          # including CancelledError
    outer = exc
settle = asyncio.ensure_future(self._settle_process(handle, reason))   # created once per run, idempotent
result = await shielded(settle)       # loops on repeated CancelledError, as _acquire_slot already does
tracked.result = result               # visible to the caller before anything is raised
if outer: raise outer                 # re-raised only after the tree is settled
```

- The root-exit check by `returncode` precedes the timeout/idle checks in every tick. The settlement try-block begins immediately after spawn, so an exception from `on_started` also settles the tree before it propagates (also for **untracked** commands: today's process leak on an `on_started` exception is fixed; the exception still propagates).
- Repeated `cancel()` while settling does not interrupt it (shield + remember + re-raise, the `_acquire_slot` pattern).
- cancel, timeout, idle and Runner stop converge on the same future; the first reason is recorded.
- A cleanup error and a `CancelledError` together: the **cleanup result is recorded first** (it may decide `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`), then the `CancelledError` is re-raised; a cleanup exception is logged and converted into `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`, never swallowed.
- **Output draining is bounded** (`PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS`, `policies.py`), for tracked **and untracked** commands: tracked — the Job is terminated first, then the pipes reach EOF; if EOF still does not arrive within the bound, the pumps are cancelled and awaited, `truncated=true`, `reason=PUMP_DRAIN_TIMEOUT`, and a tracked run whose pipes cannot be drained is `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED` only if the Job is not proven empty. Untracked — after the root exits the pumps get the bound, then are cancelled (result `tree=UNKNOWN`, `termination` unchanged); this ends today's unbounded hang and is a visible behaviour change for provider CLIs that leave background children.
- **Slot policy:** the slot is released in `finally` after settlement for every lifecycle, including `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED` (the executor no longer drives that command; holding the permit forever would starve all Tasks). The real limiter of unconfirmed runs is the project write ownership, which stays (§7.2). The executor exposes the count of retained unconfirmed Jobs for diagnostics and `RunnerStopIncomplete`.
- `_cancel_events[run_key]` is removed in `finally` after settlement; pump and waiter tasks are awaited, never abandoned.
- **User cancel must reach test commands.** `_watch_cancel` is generalised to a task-cancel watcher with a callback (the provider path keeps its exact behaviour and tests). For test commands the watcher is **started when a `tracked_scope` opens and lives for the whole scope** — `collect_ids`, the real test commands, the gaps between them and the result-collection phase — and is cancelled in the scope's `finally`, so `task.cancel_requested_at` calls `executor.cancel(scope_key)` at any moment of the scope, not only while a command is running.
- **Cancel must survive the gaps between commands.** A `tracked_scope(scope_key)` (context manager opened by the caller, `scope_key` of §7.1) makes `CommandExecutor.cancel` also record the cancel prefix as *cancelled* while the scope is open; `run()` refuses to spawn (`NOT_STARTED`, `outcome=CANCELLED`) any command whose key matches a cancelled prefix. The match is the same as the live one: a cancel prefix `P` refuses a key `K` iff `K == P` or `K` starts with `P + ":"`; a `cancel(P)` call is recorded while a scope with prefix `S` is open iff it would have matched some key under `S` (`S == P`, `S` starts with `P + ":"`, or `P` starts with `S + ":"`). **What is stored is `P` (the cancel prefix), never `S`**, so a cancel aimed at one command cannot refuse its siblings, whereas `cancel(run_id)` or `cancel(scope_key)` refuses every later command of the scope. The record lives in a **separate structure** (`_cancelled_prefixes`), never in `_cancel_events` (`tests/unit/test_command_executor.py:306,327` pin `_cancel_events == {}`). **Scope ownership:** one scope for `ids_before`; one scope for `tests.run` and `ids_after` together (inside `evaluate`); between the groups the tester CLI runs under its own watcher. Entering a scope first checks `Task.cancel_requested_at` (raises `TaskCancelled`), and a revoked lease already fails the registration transaction (`leases.verify`), which covers a cancel that arrived before the scope existed. Between the two scopes (while the tester CLI runs) a Runner stop or lease loss is covered by `leases.revoke` (called before `_cancel_cli`, `runner.py:483`) failing the next registration; a bare `cancel(run_id)` without a revoke is not a path in the code, and user cancel is covered by the scope-entry check of `cancel_requested_at`. The scope is removed when the group ends. This covers user cancel, Runner stop and lease loss for the time between two commands of one policy, where today no event exists.
- **Layering:** `TestPolicyService` keeps its constructor and stays free of the database. `WorkflowService` builds the `TrackedRun` objects (registration, fenced identity update, row closing, task-cancel watcher via the generalised `StepRunner` helper) and passes a factory into `tests.run`/`collect_ids`; no change to `container.py` is expected beyond the existing wiring (to be confirmed at implementation).
- `Runner.stop`/`_drain` cancel in-flight tasks; a cancelled run returns (or re-raises) only after the Job is proven empty or `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`; runs that did not finish within the stop budget are listed in `RunnerStopIncomplete`.

### 9.1 Background components and their settlement (n2, n8)

Components: `_sweeper_task` (orphan sweeper, §7.4), `_risk_task` (process-risk request worker, §7.5; woken by `Runner.notify()` with an idle polling fallback) and `_capability_task` (§6.2).

1. **Idempotent, guarded start:** one helper, `_ensure_background_tasks(generation, origin)` (revision 30, D30-4: the origins `START`, `RECOVERY` and `RESTART` and their rules are SUP-31), creates a missing task only once at a time (idempotent: an occupied slot is reused and never duplicated, a task that is `done()` while its exit event is not yet processed still occupies its slot, and this helper is also the creation path of a supervisor restart, SUP-3), and only while the lifecycle is `STARTING` or `RUNNING`, `_start_aborting` is false **and** `generation` equals the current lifecycle generation; the check and the task creation have no `await` between them, and `stop()` bumps the generation, so no task is created once a stop has begun. `_recover_rest` has one caller, `_finish_mutation(ctx, result, startup, checked)` (`runner.py:784`; today its call at `:804` passes only `summary`), which already holds `startup` and compares `ctx.generation` and the lifecycle state before it calls (`runner.py:800-803`). **Signature change (revision 15):** `_recover_rest(summary, generation, startup)` — `_finish_mutation` passes `ctx.generation` and its own `startup`; `_recover_rest` hands `generation` to `_ensure_background_tasks(generation, RECOVERY)` and uses `startup` to decide whether to wait for the first sweeper pass (item 2). The chain is `recover(startup=True|False)` (`runner.py:505`) → `_recover` (`:521`) → `_finish_mutation` (`:784`) → `_recover_rest` (`:842`) → `_ensure_background_tasks(generation, RECOVERY)`. Both startup recovery and the periodic `recover(startup=False)` reach it through `_finish_mutation`, so later calls reuse the running tasks; with the origin `RECOVERY` they create nothing for a unit that already exists in this generation (revision 30, SUP-31). Tests that touch these internals: `tests/integration_pg/test_runner_recovery_bounded.py` (`count_rest`, `:156-164`, wraps `_recover_rest` with an `async def rest(summary)` and replaces it with `monkeypatch.setattr(r, "_recover_rest", rest)`, so it must forward `(summary, generation, startup)`; a search of the `*.py` files finds no other reference to `_recover_rest`); tests that construct `RunnerStopIncomplete` positionally (for example `tests/unit/test_lifespan_shutdown.py`) stay valid because `components` is a keyword argument with a default.
2. **Only the startup recovery waits:** when `startup` is true, `_recover_rest` waits for the first pass of the sweeper task, bounded by `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS`, before `reconcile()`; when `startup` is false it only calls the guarded start with the origin `RECOVERY` (`_ensure_background_tasks(generation, origin)`, table SUP-O: a no-op while the tasks run) and **never waits**. The wait belongs to the same `generation` and the lifecycle guard: it ends early, and `reconcile()` proceeds conservatively, if the lifecycle leaves `STARTING`/`RUNNING` or the generation changes; the guarded start creates no task after `stop()` bumped the generation and never a duplicate for an occupied slot (a second `_recover_rest` call finds the tasks existing); `_settle_failed_start` and `stop` (`_settle_stop`; `runner.py:296`, `:362`) cancel and settle the tasks, and a waiting call is released with them. **Revision 29 (SUP-20):** this wait is only the startup recovery's wait for the first sweeper pass before `reconcile()`; it is **not** a READY condition and its expiry neither passes nor fails the start boundary. **Revision 30 (D30-3):** the components already exist when the startup recovery runs (they are created by `start()`, item 3 and SUP-31), so the `RECOVERY` call of `_recover_rest` finds every slot occupied and creates nothing; the first sweeper pass is held until the startup mutation is done (SUP-31).
3. **Start order (one order, decided in r30, D30-3; the full flow is SUP-19):** `start()` performs, in this order, (a) the entry critical section (`STARTING`, the generation bump, `_start_aborting` = false and the `start_failed` Future; `runner.py:240-248`), (b) `engine.connect()` and `pg_try_advisory_lock` (`:251-256`), (c) the capability `UNKNOWN` upsert (mandatory, fail closed), the self-test and the result upsert, in this order (§6.2, R31-11), (d) **only then** one synchronous section that creates the supervisor, registers the startup registry and creates the required component tasks, and (e) the startup recovery as the explicit task `startup-recovery`. No task therefore exists in an incarnation that does not own the lock: a start that ends in `RunnerAlreadyActive` at (b) leaves no task behind (test). Because the components exist while the startup recovery runs, the first sweeper pass is held until the startup mutation is done (SUP-31); the loop task is created later, in the `RUNNING` publication critical section (`:259`).
4. **Failed start (rewritten in r30, D30-1; SUP-19 and SUP-23):** every failure path of `start()` does only synchronous work before it hands over: it sets the plain bool `_start_aborting` (no `async with` on the lifecycle lock, because an `async with` in the failure path is itself a cancellation point) and writes the settling record of SUP-22 in the **same synchronous section**, then calls `_fail_start`. `_fail_start` creates **one** private settle task and awaits it through `_wait_shielded` (`runner.py:265-294`, `:447-463`). **Inside that one shielded settle task** run, in this order: the cancellation of every startup task that is not done, the wait for them (under the common deadline `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` for the components, the restart waiters and the supervisor, and under the own bounded wait of SUP-32 for `startup-recovery`) and then the existing `_settle_failed_start` (`:296-328`), which closes the lock connection only when the registry is empty. A caller cancellation during the settlement only adds a note and never aborts it; the final error is the first cancellation (the original one, or, when the original is a start failure, the first one that arrives during the settlement; `:280-294`), so a second cancellation can never leave the lifecycle in `STARTING`. A task that cannot be settled stays registered, is listed in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` and keeps the lifecycle `STOP_INCOMPLETE`, like an unclosed lock connection. The sweeper task is cancelled with the recorded reason `FAILED_START`, which is never a sweeper failure (§7.4 'Explicit cancel reason'). 
5. **Stop (rewritten in r29, SUP-23 and SUP-24):** `Runner.stop` cancels every component task, restart waiter and the supervisor and awaits them under **one** common deadline of `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (not within a per-component or an unbounded wait). Unfinished components are reported by **extending the existing error**: `RunnerStopIncomplete` gains the field `components: tuple[str, ...]` of canonical ids (SUP-24; run ids are never invented for them and its message lists the components); a repeated `stop()` retries the remaining components. `_shutdown_resources` records the reason `STOP` before it cancels the sweeper task (§7.4 'Explicit cancel reason'); a normal stop is never a sweeper failure. The backoff wait of a failing or stalled `_sweeper_task` is a cancellable `await` that the cancellation ends at once, so a stop never waits for the retry rhythm (§7.4 'Sweeper stall visibility'); an unsettled sweeper task appears in `components` by its id. Restart waiters and the supervisor are settled and reported the same way (SUP-7). 
6. **Failure and restart:** a component that ends abnormally (an exception, or an unexpected end of its task such as an unexpected cancellation of the task itself) is handled by the Runner's background supervisor under the **Supervisor restart contract** that follows item 7 (SUP-1 to SUP-18 as amended by SUP-19 to SUP-32, tables SUP-C, SUP-T, SUP-B, SUP-W and SUP-E): logged at critical level, then restarted through a restart waiter after a bounded exponential delay (SUP-3), within two **per-component** budgets, a consecutive-failure budget and a rolling-window budget, of which only a stabilization of `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS` resets the first (SUP-5); a normal stop and a failed-start settlement are not failures and start no restart, and an abnormal exit during `STARTING` is a failed start (SUP-4). The Runner lifecycle stays RUNNING (a stopped sweeper or worker only leaves rows unresolved, so the project stays `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED`, which is conservative; a stopped capability task lets the TTL expire into `STATUS_UNKNOWN`, which refuses Test-Run requests). When a budget is exhausted that component is DEGRADED (an internal component state, not a lifecycle value), reported by the diagnostics `RUNNER_STATE` item (`cause=BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`) and the `/health` warnings (SUP-6); only a new Runner generation revives it (SUP-11). A restart of `_sweeper_task` resets its in-memory cursors but keeps the sweeper stall record and the configuration-invalid state (§7.4 'Explicit cancel reason', rule (8)); a task or a waiter that a stop cannot settle is reported in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` (item 5, SUP-7).
7. **DB pool (what is and is not guaranteed):** the minimum pool size allowed by `config.py` is pool plus overflow = 2, and the advisory-lock connection `_lock_conn` (from `engine.connect()`) may occupy one of them, leaving one for dispatch, recovery, closing writes and all components. **Not guaranteed:** a connection reserved for the components, or the absence of starvation. **Guaranteed:** short DB transactions; no connection held across OS work or sleep; bounded batches; a shared semaphore (`BACKGROUND_DB_CONCURRENCY`, default 1) limiting all components together to one pool connection at a time; waiting bounded by `pool_timeout`; the closing writes of callers, dispatch and recovery are never throttled by the semaphore. A test at the minimum pool size observes dispatch latency and starvation while the components are active.

**Supervisor restart contract (revision 27; the single definition of how a background component is supervised and restarted, rule IDs SUP-1 to SUP-32, introduced in steps (revision 27: the first twelve; revision 28: SUP-13 to SUP-18 after table SUP-T; r29: SUP-19 to SUP-30; r30: SUP-31 and SUP-32) and amended in r31 by R31-1 to R31-8; design only: today `app/services/runner.py` has no supervisor, no `BACKGROUND_*` constant and no sweeper, so nothing here is implemented or verified).** It resolves reviewer finding CM-1 and replaces the one-sentence restart rule that item 6 used to hold. The guarded start of item 1 is idempotent (it never creates a second task for an occupied slot) and is also the creation path of a **restart** under SUP-3; the number of restarts is limited per component by SUP-5. **DEGRADED is an internal state of one component** (SUP-1, with the public warning of SUP-6): it is **not** a `RunnerLifecycle` value (the enum of `runner.py:117-125` has STOPPED, STARTING, RUNNING, STOPPING and STOP_INCOMPLETE, and B2 adds no value) and the end of one component never moves the Runner lifecycle, neither to IDLE nor anywhere else. 'Failed start' and `FAILED_START` mean a failed Runner start only. **The constants of this contract** are code literals of `app/validation/policies.py` with no environment variable (decision D27-1, §9.4): `BACKGROUND_MAX_RESTARTS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_CAP_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP`, `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX` and `BACKGROUND_WAKEUP_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS` (ranges and relations: §9.2 and the judgement table of §9.3); the constants of the start and of the settlement are `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_RECOVERY_SETTLE_MARGIN_SECONDS`, and `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_DB_CONCURRENCY` are the shared interval bound and the shared concurrency constant (§9.4).

- **SUP-1 Components, identifiers and state.** The supervised components are exactly those of this section: the orphan sweeper (id `sweeper`, `_sweeper_task`), the process-risk request worker (id `risk-worker`, `_risk_task`) and the capability updater (id `capability`, `_capability_task`); the constant `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_IDS` (§9.4) lists them. The supervisor itself is a **required lifecycle unit** (id `supervisor`) that `stop()` and `_settle_failed_start` cancel and await like a component, but nothing ever restarts it (SUP-10). The identifier of a component's task is its id; the identifier of its restart waiter is `<id>:restart-waiter` (for example `sweeper:restart-waiter`): this format is defined here once and is used by the component registry, by `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` and by the diagnostics. A component never gets an invented run id. The state of one component is the table SUP-C; its state machine is the table SUP-T (states IDLE, RUNNING, BACKOFF, DEGRADED and STOPPED).

- **SUP-2 Exit kinds.** (a) A top-level cancellation for which `STOP` or `FAILED_START` was recorded **before the handler read the field** is a normal end: not a failure, not a restart trigger, not `SWEEP_CANCELLED`. (b) Only an unexpectedly cancelled **child operation** of a sweeper pass is `SWEEP_CANCELLED` (discriminator: `asyncio.current_task().cancelling() == 0`; `Task.cancelling()` exists because the project requires Python >= 3.12; using it is an implementation choice that this design does not verify). (c) A component whose top-level task ends without a normal-termination condition (an uncaught exception, an unexpected top-level cancellation, the reason `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN`) is an **abnormal exit** that the supervisor detects. (d) An unhandled internal error that ends the component, for example an invalid `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` that propagates as a pass exception (§7.4 table row 28), is an abnormal exit and uses the same path. A supervised loop never ends by itself, so a return without the stop signal and without a recorded `STOP` or `FAILED_START` is also an abnormal exit.

- **SUP-3 Restart through the guarded start with a bounded exponential delay; the restart waiter is not an orphan sleep.** On an abnormal exit while the lifecycle is `RUNNING` the supervisor processes the exit event (SUP-9) and, when SUP-5 allows a restart, registers a **restart-waiter task** for the component in the component registry and records the lifecycle generation captured at that moment. The delay of the k-th consecutive restart is `min(BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_CAP_SECONDS, BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS * 2 ** min(k - 1, BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP))`, where `k` is the consecutive-failure count after the increment; with the defaults the delays are 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0 and 60.0 s (the fifth is capped). The `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_*` constants are the **only** restart-delay constants: they replace the single fixed `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_SECONDS` of revisions 25 and 26, which no longer exists, and `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BACKOFF_*` and `PROCESS_RISK_BACKOFF_*` are unrelated retry rhythms. The exponent is capped before the power, so the delay is finite for every count and never exceeds the cap. `stop()` and `_settle_failed_start` cancel and await the waiter like any task. When the delay has elapsed the waiter runs, in **one synchronous section with no `await` between the re-check and the registration**, under the same lifecycle synchronization that guards the first creation (item 1), this re-check: the lifecycle is `RUNNING`; the lifecycle generation equals the generation captured when the restart was scheduled; the stop signal is not set; the supervisor is not degraded (SUP-10); the component slot is empty; no other restart waiter is registered for the component and the caller is the registered current waiter itself (identity, table SUP-O). *Which checks can fail (revision 33, D33-15):* for a unit in BACKOFF the checks of the slot and of a duplicate waiter cannot fail without a defect (BACKOFF has no task, SUP-T T20 allows one waiter) and the identity of the caller fails only for a waiter of an older generation, which the generation check catches first; they are kept as defence, and the checks that can fail are the lifecycle, the generation, the stop signal and `supervisor_degraded` (SUP-T T14). When any check fails no component is created and the waiter deregisters; a restart scheduled in an older generation can therefore never create a component in a newer one. When all checks hold, the guarded start of item 1 creates the task (the same helper, not a second code path), the waiter deregisters and the state becomes RUNNING. A second supervisor or a second waiter for the same component is **refused** (the registration fails and nothing is created). **Origin (revision 30, D30-4):** the guarded start called by the waiter has the origin `RESTART` (SUP-31); it is the only origin that may create a component for a unit in BACKOFF, and only for the registered current waiter itself after the delay and this re-check, under every condition of table SUP-O (**superseded in r31:** the r30 wording named only the delay and the re-check; R31-1).

- **SUP-4 STARTING.** A required component, **or the supervisor**, that ends abnormally while the lifecycle is `STARTING` (the start has not crossed the success boundary) makes the start **unsuccessful**; no restart is scheduled and no budget is counted. **Revision 29 (superseded in r29: the first sentence of r27 and r28 that the exit 'routes into the failed-start settlement'):** the exit is recorded in `start_failed` and only `start()` settles (`_fail_start`, defined at `runner.py:265`, SUP-13); the supervisor never calls `_settle_failed_start` or `_fail_start`. The supervisor task is created in `start()` together with the components (SUP-19) and the success boundary requires it to be alive (SUP-21). The decision point is the moment at which the transition to `RUNNING` is published under the lifecycle lock, with the generation of that start as the basis: an exit observed before it is a STARTING exit, an exit after it is an ordinary supervisor case (SUP-3, SUP-5, SUP-10). 

- **SUP-5 Two budgets per component, stabilization and bounded history.** The budget key is the component id; there is no global count. (1) The **consecutive-failure budget:** `consecutive_failure_count` is incremented when an abnormal exit is processed (a restart that cannot be created is a further abnormal exit with its own event id and counts too; one exit is never counted twice, SUP-9). A restart is allowed while the incremented count is at most `BACKGROUND_MAX_RESTARTS` (default 5: five restarts, and the sixth consecutive abnormal exit degrades the component). (2) The **rolling-window budget:** `rolling_restart_timestamps` is a bounded record (a `collections.deque` with `maxlen` equal to `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX`) of the monotonic times (`exit_time` of the exit that scheduled the restart, SUP-15) at which a restart was scheduled. Before a restart is scheduled the entries older than `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_SECONDS` are dropped (expiry **by time only**); when `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX` entries remain the restart is **not** scheduled and the component is DEGRADED, otherwise the time is appended. A top-level crash consumes the rolling budget whether or not the previous run had stabilized. **Exceeding either budget degrades that component only** (SUP-6). **Stabilization.** The first normally returning pass of the sweeper (a handled `SWEEP_*` failed pass counts as returning normally, because the stall record of §7.4 tracks pass failures and the supervisor tracks task health), the first completed claim iteration of the risk worker and the first completed tick of the capability updater were the READY signal until r29 (superseded in r29: the READY signal is the initial entry point of the task, SUP-20); the READY signal sets `ready_seen` and `stable_since` **of that task** (SUP-15) and resets nothing. The consecutive-failure count is reset to 0 only when the component has **stayed alive** for `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS` (default 300.0) after `stable_since`; handled domain-failure passes count toward the alive time, because the supervisor measures the life of the task and not the success of its work. The condition is evaluated **lazily**: when the supervisor processes the next exit of that component, the **real exit time** that the done-callback stamped (`exit_time`, SUP-15) minus the `stable_since` of the same task decides whether the count is reset to 0 **before** the exit is counted (SUP-T T3; the supervisor's read time is never used), and a status read derives a `stable` flag the same way; no timer task exists. Creating a task or one pass never resets the count, and a failure before stabilization keeps and increments it. Stabilization **never** deletes an entry of the rolling window. **Consequence, stated honestly:** a component that crashes more slowly than `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS` always starts its consecutive count from 0, so only the rolling window bounds it, and a crash cadence slower than `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_SECONDS` divided by `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX` (360 s with the defaults) is never degraded: the component is restarted indefinitely, each time with a critical log and an updated `last_failure` (SUP-6). The default maximum 5 is the value of every example in this document; a test that wants fewer restarts uses a test-only override of the constant.

- **SUP-6 DEGRADED: triggers, effects and exposure.** A component becomes DEGRADED when (i) the consecutive-failure budget is exceeded, (ii) the rolling-window budget is exceeded, (iii) a fatal configuration error is found when the supervisor reads a restart constant (CG-1: the value is invalid, so no delay can be computed) or (iv) the supervisor itself ends abnormally (SUP-10, the unit `supervisor`). The supervisor then stops restarting **that component only** (no whole-Runner restart, the other components continue, the lifecycle stays `RUNNING`), registers no waiter and keeps `last_failure`. **Effect on new CLI work, decided per component:** a degraded `sweeper` does **not** block new work (it only reconciles old rows and leaves them unresolved, so the project stays `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED`, which is conservative; blocking dispatch would repair nothing); a degraded `risk-worker` does **not** block new work (operator risk requests wait and the existing cancel path still works, §7.5 item 13); a degraded `capability` updater lets the TTL expire into `STATUS_UNKNOWN`, which refuses Test-Run requests (§6.2) but no workflow Task; a degraded **`supervisor` blocks new work** (SUP-10). **Exposure:** the fixed code `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` in the top-level `/health.warnings` and in the report `warnings`; the boolean `runner.background_degraded` of the runtime snapshot and of `/health` (true while any component or the supervisor is DEGRADED, always present); the list of component detail items (component, reason code, `since`, `restart_exhausted` and `display_state`; field plan in §14.2): the items with `display_state` `DEGRADED` are carried by the diagnostics `RUNNER_STATE` cause `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` (WARN and `blocks_execution = false`, except the supervisor case of SUP-10; it replaces the earlier code `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_FAILED`), and the derived units of SUP-17 (BACKOFF_ORPHANED, EXITED_UNSUPERVISED and BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED) by the separate cause `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` (WARN, `blocks_execution = false`, display only; §14.1). `ready`, `runner_active` and `blockers` are unchanged by a component other than the supervisor. There is **no automatic un-degrade**: the budgets are reset only by a **new Runner generation** (SUP-11), that is a `stop()` followed by a `start()` of the same object, or a new process.

- **SUP-7 Settlement and reporting (rewritten in r29, SUP-23 and SUP-24).** `stop()` and `_settle_failed_start` cancel and await every component task **and every restart waiter** and the supervisor under one common deadline (the registry is the source, not the supervisor, so a dead supervisor does not stop the settlement); one that cannot be settled is listed in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` with its canonical id (SUP-24) and keeps its reference; no run id is invented; a repeated `stop()` retries the remaining entries, and DEGRADED components are settled like the others. Stale references are cleared at fixed points: the task reference and its cancel reason when the task has settled after its exit; the waiter reference when the waiter deregisters (it created a component, its re-check failed, or it was cancelled and awaited); everything for a component when a new generation starts (SUP-11) after the settling record of SUP-22 is empty. A component that ends abnormally while the lifecycle is `STOPPING` or `STOP_INCOMPLETE` starts no restart and counts against no budget (SUP-T T9 and T10). **`STOP_INCOMPLETE` does not self-heal (revision 32, W1):** the supervisor is already cancelled and, once it has ended, nobody consumes exit events; **a supervisor that ignores the cancellation and is still alive** (listed in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components`) may still consume queued events, but SUP-T T10, T29 and T30 only record them (no restart, no budget, no state change; revision 33, D33-12, F4), so in both cases only a repeated `stop()` through the registry settles the remaining entries. 

- **SUP-8 Interaction with the sweeper state.** An abnormal exit and a restart never touch the sweeper stall record or the persistent configuration-invalid state (§7.4 rows 20 and 27, CI-4); they belong to the Runner, not to the task, and only the cursors are lost. A pass that ends with a fixed `SWEEP_*` code is a normal return for the supervisor (SUP-5).

- **SUP-9 Supervisor execution model (creation, exit detection, no lost and no double notification).** *Creation (revision 30, D30-3):* `start()` creates the supervisor task in the creation section of SUP-19 step 3 (one synchronous section under the lifecycle lock) **after** the lock connection, the self-test and the capability upsert and **before** the required components, which the same section creates; it is not created in the entry critical section that sets `STARTING` and bumps `_generation` (`runner.py:240-248`), so that no task exists in an incarnation that does not own the lock; the Runner owns the single reference `_supervisor_task` and the component registry, and a second creation for the same generation is refused (the slot is occupied). The success boundary (`STARTING` to `RUNNING`, `runner.py:258-260`) is the atomic check of SUP-14, which replaces the r27 requirement that 'the supervisor task is alive and its queue exists'. *Exit detection:* every component task and every restart waiter gets a **done-callback registered in the same synchronous section that creates the task**, so no exit can precede it; the callback does nothing but put a typed exit event `(event_id, generation, unit_id, task_identity)` into a **per-generation `asyncio.Queue`** (it reads no cause; the one exception is the done-callback of the supervisor itself, SUP-13); since revision 28 the event also carries `exit_time` (`loop.time()`: the stamp of the task wrapper's `finally` first and the callback's own stamp as the fallback, SUP-27), the `ready_seen` and `stable_since` registered on that task identity at that moment and the cancelled-by-normal-settlement flag (SUP-15), and the cause is read from the carried task reference **once per exit** (revision 35, D35-2; a decision of the user's revision-35 instruction): whichever of the supervisor and `start()` (table SUP-LF row 8 and the hand-off of SUP-19 step 6) reaches the finished task first reads the exception or the cancellation and stores the result in the exit-cause slot keyed by (generation, unit, internal task identity), and the other reuses the stored value and never reads again (the slot lives as table SUP-C says, final decision Q2-3: it is discarded once a normal settlement, a cleanup event or an event of a previous generation has been processed and no `last_failure` record carries that identity, and it is kept with the identity for the lifetime of a record of that identity, so that a late observer neither re-reads the exception nor rewrites the record; a finished Task object need not be retained); **one** supervisor loop consumes the queue, so the supervisor processes each event once. *Stop-cancel versus unexpected exit:* the cancel reason (`STOP` or `FAILED_START`) is recorded **before** the cancel is requested (§7.4 'Explicit cancel reason') and the supervisor applies SUP-2, so a stop-cancel is never taken for an unexpected exit and no recorded reason means abnormal. *No lost notification:* an exit that happens while the lifecycle is `STARTING` or while the supervisor is busy stays in the queue and is handled when the supervisor reads it (during `STARTING` it never settles anything: it sets `start_failed`, SUP-T T6 and SUP-13); the queue is drained before the supervisor ends normally, and a generation change discards only the events of the old generation, after its tasks have settled. *No double processing:* each event has a unique `event_id` and each task identity is handled once (a `handled` mark on its registry entry is set before any budget is touched), so one exit is never counted twice; a restart that cannot create its task is a **new** exit with its own event id.

- **SUP-10 The supervisor ending unexpectedly.** The supervisor cannot restart itself and nothing restarts it (a second supervisor would be a second owner of the budgets). When the supervisor task ends without the stop signal (an exception, an unexpected cancellation or a return), its done-callback sets the Runner-side flag `supervisor_degraded` synchronously (no `await`) and the unit `supervisor` is DEGRADED at once (reason code `SUPERVISOR_EXITED`; `restart_exhausted` is false because no restart is defined). The consequences are all immediate: the dispatch loop `_loop` claims **no new work** while the flag is set (a Task that is already running continues and finishes; recovery and the existing cancel path keep working); no component restart is scheduled or performed any more (a waiter that is already running finds the flag in its re-check and creates nothing); `runtime_snapshot` adds the blocker `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED` (a new value of `RunnerBlocker`, `runtime_status.py:25-33`), so `ready` is false; the lifecycle stays `RUNNING` and is **not** moved to STOP_INCOMPLETE (that value says that a stop or a failed start could not confirm its resources, `runner.py:122-125`, and nothing was stopped here). `/health.warnings` carries `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, `runner.background_degraded` is true and the diagnostics `RUNNER_STATE` item is FAIL with `blocks_execution = true` (the Runner accepts no new work; this is the one Runner-wide effect of a degraded unit). `stop()` still works: it records `STOP`, cancels and awaits the remaining tasks and waiters through the registry (not through the dead supervisor) and settles them as in SUP-7, so a later `start()` of the same object is possible (SUP-11). **Revision 28:** the live component tasks are **not** claimed dead, but their automatic restart and observation are no longer guaranteed, so the whole background subsystem is shown as DEGRADED (SUP-17).

- **SUP-11 Stop then start of the same Runner object is a new generation.** `runner.py` allows `STOPPED` to `STARTING` on the same object and bumps `_generation` in `start()` (`runner.py:247`) and in `stop()` (`runner.py:347`), so this contract does not rely on 'a new `Runner` object'. **Reset when the new generation starts** (after the previous stop has settled, before the success boundary): the previous task references, the restart-waiter and backoff references, the cancel reasons, `consecutive_failure_count`, `rolling_restart_timestamps`, the DEGRADED state of every unit and the flag `supervisor_degraded`, `stable_since` and `ready_seen`, a pending configuration wake-up (CI-7), every undelivered exit event of the old generation and the `start_failed` signal of the old generation (it is invalidated and never completed by an event of another generation, SUP-13). **Preserved** because they are not supervisor budgets: (1) the sweeper stall record and the persistent configuration-invalid state (the Runner-owned `SweeperStallState`, in memory), so a state with `config_invalid_active` and no stall record (**CI-only**) must be recognized by the start and recovery paths; (2) the recorded `config_invalid_next_retry_at` and `next_retry_at` values (audit values: the new sweeper task does not wait for them, its first pass starts after `startup_mutation_done`, CI-7 and R31-4); (3) every database-stored workspace and process-safety state (rows, lineage, risk requests), which a Runner restart never erases. The committed and the scan cursor belong to the task and start at the first page again (§7.4 'Sweeper continuation and restart'). **Last-failure audit information** (`last_failure`: code, time, unit, generation) is kept until the new generation crosses its **successful start boundary** and is cleared there by that explicit rule (table SUP-LF, which fixes owner, generation, update, preserve and clear points): a start that fails leaves the records of the earlier generation unchanged and labelled with their own generation, and the failure of that start is the raised start error plus an updated record only for a unit whose own exit or READY timeout caused it (the examples are in table SUP-LF); a successful start shows a clean list. **Principle:** supervisor budgets are per generation and in memory; a replaced process or a new `Runner` object starts with every in-memory record empty (§7.4 row 21); the persistent configuration-invalid state clears only when the configuration is valid **and** the recorded position has been passed (CI-5).

- **SUP-12 Public names and ownership (decision D27-2).** The public names are the warning code `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, the health field `runner.background_degraded` (boolean) and the diagnostics DTO `SweeperConfigInvalidOut`. **Direction of dependency:** the Runner side owns the source state (the supervisor and the component state live in the new module `app/services/background_supervisor.py`, one instance owned by `Runner`; `SweeperStallState`, the frozen `SweeperStallSnapshot` and the frozen `SweeperConfigInvalidSnapshot` live in `app/services/sweeper_stall.py`; the runtime-status layer `app/services/runtime_status.py` holds the frozen `RuntimeSnapshot` and the frozen `BackgroundComponentStatus`); the API schema layer (`app/schemas/api.py`, `app/schemas/reports.py`) defines the DTOs; `DiagnosticsService` returns frozen dataclasses (internal view models) whose attribute names equal the DTO field names, `ReportService` returns the plain dictionary that it returns today (`report_service.py:325-329`) and the `/health` body builder (`RuntimeSnapshot.as_dict()`) stays a plain dictionary; the **routers and the FastAPI `response_model`** (`from_attributes`, `_Out` of `app/schemas/api.py:11-12`) convert them to the public shape, which supersedes the r27 wording 'services convert'; **no service imports `app.schemas`** (the existing rule `tests/architecture/test_rules.py:114` already covers every service; the architecture test of §13 extends it with the Runner-specific checks) and the Runner imports no API DTO. The field plan of every snapshot and DTO is the single table of §14.2; no other place lists fields.

**Table SUP-C: the state of one component (the one field list of the supervisor; `N` = `BACKGROUND_MAX_RESTARTS`).**

| Field | Meaning | At a new generation (SUP-11) |
|---|---|---|
| `state` | IDLE, RUNNING, BACKOFF, DEGRADED or STOPPED (table SUP-T) | reset to IDLE |
| `task_ref` and its cancel reason | the current task and the reason bound to its identity (§7.4) | cleared |
| `restart_waiter` | at most one reference | cleared |
| `consecutive_failure_count` | the consecutive-failure budget, SUP-5 (1) | reset to 0 |
| `rolling_restart_timestamps` | the bounded record of the rolling-window budget, SUP-5 (2) | emptied |
| `ready_seen`, `stable_since`, `task_identity` | the READY signal of the **current task identity** and its monotonic time (`loop.time()`), SUP-5 and SUP-15; reset when a task is registered or replaced and detached when its exit has been processed, **except** the exit-cause slot and the task identity of the `last_failure` record (revision 35, D35-2; final decision Q2-3): the slot is keyed by (generation, unit, internal task identity) and is filled by the first reader of the exit (SUP-9). **Lifetime of the slot:** (a) after a normal settlement, a cleanup event or an event of a previous generation has been processed and **no `last_failure` record carries the same identity**, the slot is discarded; (b) when a record with the same identity exists, the identity and the collected result stay for the lifetime of that record (until it is replaced or cleared, table SUP-LF), so a late observer neither reads the exception again nor writes the record again; the finished Task object itself need not be retained in either case | cleared |
| `degraded`, `degraded_reason` | the flag behind the state DEGRADED and its reason code | cleared |
| `last_failure` | code, time, unit, generation and internal task identity of the failed task of the last abnormal exit or READY timeout of this component (audit only; table SUP-LF) | **kept** until the successful start boundary of the new generation, then cleared |
| `generation` | the lifecycle generation under which the current task was created | replaced |
| `start_failed` (one per generation, owned by `Runner`) | the single completion signal that holds the first start failure (SUP-13); not a component field | invalidated, a new one is created by `start()` |
