**Table SUP-LF: the `last_failure` record of a component (revision 33, D33-5; the one rule set for owner, generation, update, preserve and clear points; SUP-11, SUP-T T6, T23 and T36 and table SUP-R refer here and do not restate it).** There is one record per component unit (`sweeper`, `risk-worker`, `capability`); the `supervisor` has none (it is not a component, table SUP-R). **Owner:** the component registry entry that the supervisor module owns (table SUP-C). A record holds the code, the time, the unit and **the generation of the failed task**, the field that tells a preserved record of an earlier generation from a failure of the current start (the field `generation` of the record is an **authoring choice, not user-approved**, §12 A33-1). Since revision 35 (D35-2; a decision of the user's revision-35 instruction) the record also holds **the internal task identity of the failed task**: it is the dedup key of rows 2, 8 and 9 (one exit = generation + unit + task identity), it is never exposed (not in the log line and not in an API field), and it is the only thing that lets `start()` tell whether an exit was already recorded after table SUP-C has detached the per-task data. **Two separate questions:** (a) which ONE failure becomes `start_failed` and the raised error, the *first failure* (the group priority and the tie order of SUP-21, unchanged), and (b) which `last_failure` records are written, the record of EACH failed component unit whatever (a) chose; (a) never suppresses (b). **'First failure' in one sentence:** the failure that is first recorded in `start_failed` or, while none is recorded yet, the failure first observed at one observation point in the order of SUP-21; it names the representative start failure of (a) only and never decides (b). **Exposure (audit only):** the critical log line written at each update and the internal registry accessor that tests read; no API field carries it (§14.2).

| Row | Point | Writer | Generation of the record | Effect on the record of that unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | abnormal exit of a component task while `RUNNING` (SUP-T T3 to T5; a waiter's own exception counted by SUP-T T32 and T15) | the supervisor, when it processes the exit event | the generation of the failed task (the current one) | **update**: the record of that unit is replaced; DEGRADED keeps it (SUP-6) |
| 2 | abnormal exit of a component task in `STARTING`, READY reached or not (SUP-T T6; a later failure after `start_failed`, SUP-T T36) | the supervisor, when it processes the exit event (it never settles), unless row 8 has already recorded the same task identity | the current generation | **update** of the failing unit only; each failing component writes its own record and only the first failure becomes `start_failed` (SUP-T T36) |
| 3 | READY timeout of a component (SUP-20, B6) | `start()`, when it observes the timeout | the current generation | **update** of the unit that missed READY only; table SUP-R only supports this cause and is not the writer rule; a READY timeout of the supervisor writes no record |
| 4 | a failure that is neither a component's own exit nor its READY timeout: the lock (`RunnerAlreadyActive`), the capability self-test, the startup recovery, a caller cancellation, B1, B2 or B8 (revision 35, final decision Q1-2: this row applies to **these reasons themselves**; a required unit that had **abnormally exited** when the hand-off ran is a separately observed exit and is covered by rows 8 and 9) | none for the reason itself | not applicable | **preserve** every record unchanged, each with its own generation, **except the units covered by rows 8 and 9** (each of them gets one record per generation + unit + task identity, and an existing record is reused); the reason itself is never recorded as a `last_failure`; the raised start error is the failure, and the audit record written by rows 8 and 9 changes neither the main exception delivered to the caller, nor the first start failure of SUP-21, nor any restart budget |
| 5 | a normal-settlement end or a cleanup event (SUP-T T17; table SUP-G priorities 0 and 1), a `stop()`, a failed-start settlement (SUP-T T24) | none | not applicable | **preserve**: nothing is written and nothing is cleared |
| 6 | a new generation begins (`start()` entry, SUP-11) | none | the records of earlier generations stay as they are | **preserve** until row 7 clears them or row 1, 2, 3 or 8 replaces one |
| 7 | the successful start boundary (SUP-T T23) | `start()`, in the same critical section that publishes `RUNNING` | every record, whatever its generation | **clear** the records of every unit |
| 8 | `start()` observes `task.done()` of a required component task (B5, SUP-21 group 4) before the supervisor has processed its exit event; a required supervisor that ended (B4) writes no record, because the supervisor has none | `start()`, only when the record of that unit does not already carry this task identity | the current generation (the generation of the failed task) | **update** of the failing unit, once: one exit is identified by (generation, unit, internal task identity) and the record carries that identity (table SUP-C), so `start()` and the supervisor record the same exit exactly once in either order: whoever comes second finds the identity already in the record and writes nothing; **the exit cause is collected once per exit** (SUP-9): the first reader fetches the exception or the cancellation from the task and stores it in the exit-cause slot of that key, the second reuses the stored value, so both writers use one code and one time (the `exit_time` of SUP-27, the stamp of the task wrapper first) and no code derivation exists twice; this table introduces no new code name (the code is the one the supervisor derives for an abnormal exit of that unit; **the one place for the signal-less return (revision 35, D35-2; user-fixed policy):** two separate judgements. (1) Termination judgement: a required component that must keep running and ends with no stop or settlement signal is an abnormal exit (SUP-2 (c) and the last sentence of SUP-2). (2) Code judgement: if that component returned by itself without an exception, then regardless of the return value `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN` (the **planned** B2 code of SUP-2 (c)) is recorded exactly once; if it ended by an uncaught exception or an unexpected top-level cancellation, it is treated as an abnormal exit per SUP-2 (c); an expected settlement cancellation (a recorded `STOP` or `FAILED_START`, SUP-2 (a)) and a normal stop are excluded from the failure records; no code under `app/` uses that name today, so the current supervisor does not already use it); a late writer never replaces the record of a **newer** generation and never replaces the first record of this exit; the table holds the failure although the exit event is still unprocessed |
| 9 | the hand-off of SUP-19 step 6 (any failure path of `start()`) at which `start()` checks the result of each required component task that is `done()`; only a task that **abnormally exited** and whose task identity no `last_failure` record carries yet is recorded (revision 35, D35-2; user-fixed policy) | `start()`, in the synchronous section of the hand-off (the same section that sets `_start_aborting` and writes the settling record, before `_fail_start` is called) | the current generation (the generation of the failed task) | **update** of **each** such abnormally exited unit, exactly once per generation + unit + task identity, by the rule of row 8 (an already collected result is reused: the stored exit cause when the supervisor already fetched it); an expected settlement cancellation (a recorded `STOP` or `FAILED_START`) and a normal stop create **no** new failure record; the representative failure of the start is still only the one of SUP-21, and the record is an audit record only: it changes neither the main exception delivered to the caller (a caller cancellation stays final), nor the first start failure, nor any restart budget, and it is written also when the reason of the hand-off is a caller cancellation, B1, B2 or B8 (row 4 preserves records for those reasons themselves and never suppresses this row; final decision Q1-2): even when the caller's `start()` was cancelled, the audit record of a unit (for example the `capability`) that had abnormally exited separately before that is kept; after the marker the supervisor treats the exit as a cleanup event (table SUP-G priority 0) and writes nothing, so the hand-off is the last point at which the record can be written; the record is **preserved** by the failed-start settlement and by `STOPPED` (rows 4 to 6) and is cleared only by row 7 of a later successful start |

**Examples (what is exposed when a preserved record of an earlier generation and a failure of the current start coexist):** (a) generation 1: the `sweeper` exits abnormally with code X1 (row 1) and the Runner stops; generation 2 starts and fails in the startup recovery (row 4): the `sweeper` record is still {X1, generation 1}, there is no generation-2 record and the raised error is the startup recovery failure; the record is a diagnostic of an earlier generation and is **not** the cause of this start, because its generation differs from the current one. (b) The same, but in generation 2 the `capability` exits abnormally before READY (row 2, code X2): `capability` holds {X2, generation 2}, which is also the first failure of `start_failed` and the raised error, and the `sweeper` still holds {X1, generation 1}; both records exist and a reader separates them by the stored generation; if `start()` observes the `done()` task of the `capability` first (row 8, before the supervisor processed the exit event), `start()` writes {X2, generation 2}, the supervisor that later processes the same exit event finds the same task identity and writes nothing, and the record and the raised error are the same in either order; a late processing of an event of generation 1 (SUP-T T34) never replaces {X2, generation 2}. (c) The same, but the `sweeper` itself exits abnormally in generation 2 (code X3): its record is replaced by {X3, generation 2} and X1 is gone, because there is one record per unit. (d) Generation 2 starts successfully (row 7): every record is cleared at the boundary and the start shows a clean list; a later abnormal exit in generation 2 starts a new record (row 1). (e) (revision 35, D35-2) Generation 2 starts, the `capability` and the `risk-worker` both end abnormally before the boundary and `start()` observes both `done()` tasks at the hand-off with no event processed: the `capability` is the representative failure that `start_failed` and the raised error carry (the tie order of SUP-21), and **both** units receive a record {code, generation 2} written by the hand-off (row 9); the supervisor, which treats the later events as cleanup events (priority 0), writes nothing, and both records survive the settlement.

**Table SUP-T: the state machine of the supervisor (transition table of the supervisor contract, SUP-1 to SUP-32; `N` = `BACKGROUND_MAX_RESTARTS`, `W` = `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX`; 'unit' is a component or the supervisor).**

| T33 | `RUNNING` | component, BACKOFF | a status read (or any snapshot of the registry) finds the unit of the current generation in BACKOFF with neither a registered component task nor a registered restart waiter (revision 33, D33-1: the derivation of BACKOFF_ORPHANED is defined once in SUP-17) | a lookup only: the same rule whether the supervisor is alive or dead; the earlier 'detected when the supervisor processes any event' is removed, because no processing is needed for a display | none: display only (SUP-17, SUP-26): **no state write, no SUP-T T15 failure count, no restart-budget consumption, no waiter creation and no automatic recovery**, so repeated lookups leave the registry, the budgets and the state identical; the existing handling of a **real** waiter failure event is preserved (SUP-T T32, counted as SUP-T T15 by that event) and an observation never counts the same failure again; a done waiter is counted only by its own event (SUP-T T32); the earlier 'handled as SUP-T T32' is removed; the state is legitimately reachable (revision 32, M2; supersedes 'reachable only through a defect'): when the supervisor dies while the lifecycle is `RUNNING` and a unit is in BACKOFF, the waiter's later re-check is refused by reason (3) of SUP-T T14 and the waiter deregisters (SUP-3), so the unit stays BACKOFF without task or waiter in that generation, shown as derived BACKOFF_ORPHANED, with budgets unchanged and no self-heal because the supervisor is dead; with a live supervisor it is not expected to arise, because a failed `RESTART` is a new exit event and not a BACKOFF unit without a waiter (R31-1), and if the state is present anyway (a defect, or a snapshot built by fault injection) the lookup rule above is unchanged: it is displayed as BACKOFF_ORPHANED and nothing is written, and with no other fault and a live supervisor the output is the derived-only shape of case A2 of SUP-17 (`background_degraded` false, `RUNNER_STATE` WARN, one cause `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED`), a reachability remark never invalidating that output rule (revision 35, final decision Q1-1); `stop()` settles only the resources that exist (SUP-T T12) | BACKOFF unchanged; display value BACKOFF_ORPHANED (read-only) | unchanged | the component detail item with `display_state` BACKOFF_ORPHANED (§14.2) | none |
| T34 | any | any unit | an exit event of a **previous generation** | the event's generation differs from the current one and no settling record contains the identity of the event's task, waiter or startup task (table SUP-G priorities 0 and 1 are evaluated first; branch 3 of table SUP-X) | no state change, no budget, no restart, no effect on `start_failed`; one audit record (a log line with the unit id, the generation and the event id) | unchanged | unchanged | none | none |
| T35 | `RUNNING` | component | a status read finds a task reference whose `task.done()` is true while its exit event is not yet processed (the supervisor is dead or lagging) | a task reference exists and the registry entry is not marked handled (the existing unsupervised-exit condition, SUP-17); a unit without a task reference never matches | the read shows the component as `EXITED_UNSUPERVISED` (a derived read-only value; nothing is written, no SUP-T T15 failure is counted and no budget is consumed, the same lookup rule as SUP-T T33); never as RUNNING | derived EXITED_UNSUPERVISED | unchanged | the component detail item with `display_state` EXITED_UNSUPERVISED (§14.2); with a dead supervisor SUP-17 applies | none |
| T36 | `STARTING` | component or supervisor | a second failure after `start_failed` is completed | `start_failed` is already completed and `_start_aborting` is false (afterwards SUP-G priority 0) | recorded as a note on the first failure; never overwrites it; each failing component still writes its own `last_failure` (table SUP-LF, row 2), and only the first failure becomes `start_failed` and falls under the note rules (revision 32, C5) | unchanged | `STARTING` until `start()` settles (SUP-T T24) | none | none (not counted) |
| T37 | `RUNNING` | restart waiter | a status read finds a unit in BACKOFF without a component task whose registered restart waiter is `done()` with its exit event not processed, while the supervisor is dead (revision 34, A4) | the unit is of the current generation, the waiter entry is not marked handled and `supervisor_degraded` is true in the same snapshot; with a live supervisor this is the normal window of SUP-T T32 and the row never matches | the read shows the unit as `BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED` (a derived read-only value; nothing is written, no SUP-T T15 failure is counted, no budget is consumed and no waiter or recovery is created: the lookup rule of SUP-T T33); never as RUNNING | derived BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED | unchanged | the component detail item with `display_state` BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED (§14.2); SUP-17 applies | none |

**Supervisor start, stability and waiter contract (revision 28; rules SUP-13 to SUP-18, decisions D28-1 to D28-3, §12; design only: nothing here is implemented or verified).** These rules supersede, where they name it, the wording of SUP-4, SUP-9, SUP-10 and of the SUP-T T3, T6, T7 and T14 of table SUP-T ('superseded in r28'; the rows carry the r28 text, and SUP-T T14 and T33 are superseded again in r29, SUP-26); the row numbers SUP-T T22 to T36 are the rows of table SUP-T and are never the rows of the §7.4 transition table (a reference to the other table always says '§7.4 row N').

- **SUP-13 Failed-start delivery: `start()` is the only settler (D28-1; rewritten in r29 on the ten steps of SUP-19).** The supervisor and the required components are registered in the startup registry and every failure path of `start()` runs the steps 6 to 10 of SUP-19. **Who sets `start_failed` (one statement, revision 30, C9):** the supervisor completes it from its event processing when a **component** ends abnormally while the lifecycle is `STARTING` (SUP-T T6); the done-callback of the **supervisor itself** completes it when the supervisor ends abnormally (SUP-T T7: nothing else can; the callback checks `task.cancelled()` first and reads `task.exception()` exactly once; an unrequested cancellation becomes a `RuntimeError` start error with the `CancelledError` as `__cause__`); the done-callback of a component or of a waiter never completes `start_failed` and reads no cause (SUP-9); the exit cause of a component is read once per exit, by the supervisor or by `start()`, whichever reaches the finished task first, and the other reuses the stored value (SUP-9, table SUP-LF row 8); a task cancelled before its first step never enters its `finally` and is observed only through its done-callback (SUP-27); **only the first failure is set** (guarded with `done()`), a later failure is added as a note and never overwrites it (SUP-T T36). A restart waiter does not exist in `STARTING` (waiters exist only in `RUNNING`). The supervisor **never** calls `_settle_failed_start` or `_fail_start`, never cancels or awaits itself and does not cancel the task that runs `start()`. `start()` waits for every startup step together with `start_failed` (SUP-19 step 5); when a failure wins, `start()` does only the synchronous hand-off of step 6 and `_fail_start` runs the cancellation, the wait and the settlement (steps 7 to 9) inside its one shielded settle task (D30-1; `runner.py:265-294`, SUP-T T24); a success candidate passes the boundary of SUP-21 (SUP-T T23). **Original exception:** the value of `start_failed` is the original exception of the first failure and is the `original` that `_fail_start` receives; the priority rules of `_fail_start` are unchanged (an original start error stays the main error, cleanup problems become notes; a caller cancellation stays final, SUP-19). **Stop racing a start failure:** `stop()` while `STARTING` raises `RuntimeError` and changes nothing today (`runner.py:344-345`, SUP-T T25); the failed start settles itself and a repeated `stop()` follows SUP-T T11 or T10. **Done-callback and the marker (r31):** the done-callback of the supervisor reads `_start_aborting` first: once the marker is set it records nothing in `start_failed` (the exit is a cleanup event of priority 0, table SUP-G), and a READY signal (SUP-T T22) that arrives after the marker is set is ignored. **Cleanup of the signal:** SUP-21. 

- **SUP-14 The `RUNNING` publication boundary (D28-2; rewritten in r29, the full rule is SUP-21).** Right before `RUNNING` is published, `start()` takes the lifecycle lock and checks **atomically** (no `await` inside the critical section) every item of table SUP-B; only when all hold is `_state` set to `RUNNING` in the same critical section (SUP-T T23), otherwise `start()` enters `_fail_start` (SUP-T T24). **Liveness is never decided from done-callbacks or from the supervisor queue alone:** a task whose `task.done()` is true while its exit event is not yet queued is a start failure, and an empty queue proves nothing. The READY boundary of every required component is the uniform rule of SUP-20 (superseded in r29: the revision-28 interpretation that the sweeper passes 'by READY **or** by the end of the bounded startup wait'); a task that is done is never accepted at any boundary. 

**Table SUP-B: the atomic boundary check of SUP-14 (all items hold under the lifecycle lock, or the start fails).**

| Item | Condition | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | the lifecycle is still `STARTING` | SUP-T T24 (a changed lifecycle is a defect and fails closed) |
| B2 | the generation equals the generation that `start()` captured | SUP-T T24 |
| B3 | `start_failed` is not completed | SUP-T T24 with the recorded first failure |
| B4 | the supervisor task exists and `not done()` | SUP-T T24 (a supervisor that has already ended is a STARTING exit, SUP-T T7) |
| B5 | every required component task exists and `not done()` (read from the registry, not from the queue) | SUP-T T24 |
| B6 | every required component has passed its READY boundary (SUP-20: the initial entry point sets `ready_seen`) for **that task identity and generation** | SUP-T T24 |
| B7 | no stop request exists and `_start_aborting` is false, which also means that no failed-start settlement has begun (SUP-21); r31: the 'no stop request' part is always true because `stop()` raises in `STARTING` (`runner.py:344-345`), and the marker part is the same value as B9, which stays a separate row only because SUP-19 names it | SUP-T T24 |
| B8 | the lock connection `_lock_conn` is held and valid and the start resources are valid (`_recovery_clean()`; a synchronous check, not liveness, SUP-21) | SUP-T T24 |
| B9 | `_start_aborting` is false (SUP-19) | SUP-T T24 |
| B10 | the startup recovery task is done without error (SUP-19, step 4) | SUP-T T24 |

- **SUP-15 Stability judgement per task (D28-3).** The exit event carries: the component identity, the task identity, the generation, the **real exit time** `exit_time` (`loop.time()`: the stamp of the task wrapper's `finally` takes precedence and the stamp of the done-callback is the fallback, SUP-27; it is **not** the time at which the supervisor reads the event), `ready_seen` and `stable_since` as registered on that task identity at that moment, the task reference (the cause is read from it once per exit, by the supervisor or by `start()`, whichever comes first, SUP-9) and the flag 'cancelled by a normal settlement'. **An exit is stable if and only if** `ready_seen` is true **and** `stable_since` is set on this task **and** `exit_time - stable_since >= BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS`. **Per-task state:** registering or replacing a task (SUP-T T1) resets `ready_seen`, `stable_since`, the previous task identity and the per-task exit information, so a restarted task never inherits a stale `stable_since`; a READY signal (SUP-T T2, T22) sets `ready_seen` and `stable_since` only when the task identity **and** the generation of the signal equal the registered ones; when the exit of a task has been processed both are detached from the registry entry. The rolling-window timestamps use `exit_time` too. A late processing of an event therefore never changes the verdict, and an exit before READY is never stable (SUP-T T3 requires `ready_seen`): repeated failures before READY cannot bypass the consecutive count (it rises at every exit) and the growing delay of SUP-3, and each of them also consumes the rolling window. The model scenarios of §13 are: A, a task that is READY, lives long and then exits (stable); B, a task that exits before READY with a stale `stable_since` of its predecessor (not stable); and exits just before, exactly at and just after the stability boundary.

- **SUP-16 Restart waiter lifecycle.** The states of a waiter are those of table SUP-W. A waiter is created in the same synchronous section that registers it with its done-callback (SUP-T T4), there is at most one waiter per component (SUP-T T20) and a waiter of a component without a task and without a waiter never exists silently: **no waiter and no task is never shown as RUNNING** (it is the derived BACKOFF_ORPHANED of SUP-T T33; EXITED_UNSUPERVISED of SUP-T T35 needs a task reference, SUP-17). A stop or a generation change cancels the waiter and no restart follows (SUP-T T12, T28, T30). A normal end of the delay re-verifies the lifecycle, the generation, the stop signal, `supervisor_degraded`, the slot, a duplicate waiter and the budget (SUP-T T13 or T14; the budget check cannot fail while the unit is BACKOFF, because budgets change only on that component's own exit, and the slot and duplicate-waiter checks cannot fail without a defect, revision 33, D33-15) and only then starts the component through the guarded start (state COMPLETED_AND_STARTED_COMPONENT); a start failure of the component is a failure of the component budget (SUP-T T15). **The waiter's own exception** is handled by the supervisor as an abnormal exit of the same component (SUP-T T32), so the component cannot stick in BACKOFF; repeated waiter failures count against the **same** component budgets (the consecutive count and the rolling window, SUP-5), so they end in DEGRADED and never in an endless loop. The waiter reference is removed atomically when the waiter ends (in the same synchronous section that handles its exit event); a waiter of a previous generation is STALE and changes nothing (SUP-T T34).

**Table SUP-W: the states of a restart waiter (`<id>:restart-waiter`).**

| State | Meaning | Next state and rule |
|---|---|---|
| CREATED | registered with its done-callback (SUP-T T4) | BACKOFF when its task starts to wait |
| BACKOFF | waiting for the delay of SUP-3 (a cancellable wait) | the delay ends (SUP-T T13, T14), or CANCELLED_BY_STOP, CANCELLED_BY_GENERATION_CHANGE or FAILED |
| CANCELLED_BY_STOP | the stop signal cancelled it | terminal; no restart (SUP-T T12, T28, T30) |
| CANCELLED_BY_GENERATION_CHANGE | the generation changed | terminal; no restart (SUP-T T34) |
| COMPLETED_AND_STARTED_COMPONENT | the delay ended, the re-check passed and the guarded start created the task | terminal; the reference is removed (SUP-T T13) |
| FAILED | the waiter's own exception | terminal; the supervisor handles it as an abnormal exit of the same component (SUP-T T32) |
| STALE | an event or a waiter of a previous generation | terminal; no state change, one audit record (SUP-T T34) |

- **SUP-17 Supervisor death and the status read (refines SUP-10; D28 follow-up).** The supervisor is a required lifecycle component. When it ends unexpectedly the background subsystem is DEGRADED **at once and independently of any backoff** (`BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, `runner.background_degraded` true); new CLI work is blocked (the blocker `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED`, the lifecycle stays `RUNNING`); the status snapshot shows the absence of the supervisor; the live component tasks are **not** claimed dead, but because their automatic restart and observation are no longer guaranteed the whole background subsystem is shown as degraded; `stop()` settles the remaining tasks and waiters directly through the registry; the supervisor is never restarted by itself and a recovery exists only in a new Runner generation (SUP-11). A **status read derives three display values from one registry snapshot** (revision 33, D33-1, extended in revision 34, A4; this is the only definition and every other section refers to it; the one decision table is table SUP-DS below; `DEGRADED` of `display_state` is the real state and not a derived value): **EXITED_UNSUPERVISED** is derived when a task reference exists for the unit, `task.done()` is true and the existing unsupervised-exit condition holds (its exit event is not yet processed and the registry entry is not marked handled, SUP-T T35); a unit without a task reference is **not** EXITED_UNSUPERVISED. **BACKOFF_ORPHANED** is derived from a snapshot in which the unit of the current generation is BACKOFF and has neither a registered component task nor a registered restart waiter (SUP-T T33; whether the supervisor is alive or dead, revision 35, final decision Q1-1). **BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED** is derived from a snapshot in which the unit of the current generation is BACKOFF, has no registered component task, its registered restart waiter is `done()` with its exit event not yet processed (the registry entry is not marked handled) **and the supervisor is dead in the same snapshot** (`supervisor_degraded`, SUP-10; SUP-T T37): nobody is left to process that exit event. A registered restart waiter that is done with its event not yet processed while the supervisor is **alive** is the normal short window in which the supervisor processes the event (SUP-T T32): it is none of the three derived values, the unit stays shown as BACKOFF (an **authoring choice, not user-approved**, §12 A33-1) and that waiter is counted only by its own event; a supervisor that is alive but lagging cannot be told apart in a snapshot and is shown the same way. None of the three values is ever shown as a stale RUNNING. **Derived display exists only in the lifecycle `RUNNING` (revision 35, D35-1; a decision of the user's revision-35 instruction):** the status read takes the lifecycle from the same snapshot as the registry, and in `STARTING`, `STOPPING`, `STOP_INCOMPLETE` and `STOPPED` it derives **no** value (rows 2 to 4 of table SUP-DS hold only in `RUNNING`, row 6 covers every other lifecycle), so a normal stop, in which `stop()` itself settles done tasks and waiters (SUP-T T12, T17, T27 to T30), produces no derived item, no `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` cause and no warning. **Exactly two cases, with no other abnormality, are the oracle of every example and test; §13, table SUP-DS, table DIAG-BG and §14 reference these same two:** *Case A* (lifecycle `RUNNING`, the supervisor alive, no other fault; case A1: a component task is `done()` and the live supervisor has not yet processed its exit event; case A2, revision 35, final decision Q1-1: a unit of the current generation is in BACKOFF with neither a component task nor a registered restart waiter): `display_state` of that unit `EXITED_UNSUPERVISED` (A1) or `BACKOFF_ORPHANED` (A2); `/health` and the runtime snapshot: `runner.background_degraded` **false**, no `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` warning, `ready` and `blockers` unchanged; diagnostics: **one** cause, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` (WARN, `blocks_execution` false), and `RUNNER_STATE` WARN. *Case B* (lifecycle `RUNNING`; the death of the supervisor is reflected as DEGRADED; a unit is in BACKOFF without a component task and its registered restart waiter is `done()` with its event not processed): `display_state` of that unit `BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED` and of the `supervisor` `DEGRADED`; `/health`: `runner.background_degraded` **true**, the warning `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, the blocker `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED` (`ready` false); diagnostics: **two** causes, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` (the supervisor item, FAIL, `blocks_execution` true) and `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` (the derived item, WARN), and `RUNNER_STATE` FAIL. **`BACKOFF_ORPHANED` is derived by one rule whatever the supervisor state (SUP-T T33; revision 35, final decision Q1-1):** with a live supervisor and no other fault it is the derived-only shape of case A2 (`runner.background_degraded` false, `RUNNER_STATE` WARN, exactly one cause `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED`); with the death of the supervisor reflected as DEGRADED it follows the existing FAIL contract of case B (the supervisor DEGRADED plus the derived item: FAIL, two causes), as does a component task that is `done()` while the supervisor is dead. How the state is reached is a reachability remark and never invalidates the output rule: SUP-T T14 (3) reaches it legitimately after the supervisor died, and with a live supervisor it is not expected to arise (SUP-26); a test of the live-supervisor shape that can only be built by fault injection is labelled an 'output test on a synthetic snapshot'. The values are tested by their own SUP-T rows (T33, T35, T37) inside the shapes of case A and case B and are not a third case. A lookup never changes a budget, the queue, a restart or a dispatch, and the diagnostics cache key contains the set of derived values computed from the same snapshot (§14.3), so a change inside the TTL is visible at the next read. **All three are display only, under the same lookup rule (reading the supervisor state held in the snapshot is a read, never a write):** the lookup writes no state, counts no failure (no SUP-T T15), consumes no restart budget, creates no waiter and starts no automatic recovery, so repeated lookups change nothing. A real waiter failure event keeps its existing handling (SUP-T T32, counted once as SUP-T T15 by that event), and an observation and a real event never count the same failure twice. For every derived item `reason_code` and `since` are `null`: a derived item has no real failure record, and the time of the lookup is never shown as a failure time (§14.2). The transported field, the value set and the units that a response includes are fixed in §14.2. **The operator action that exists today:** a new Runner generation (`stop()` followed by `start()` of the same object, or a new process, SUP-11); nothing else clears the display.

**Table SUP-DS: the derived display values of a status read (revision 34, A4; one decision table; every row is display only, D33-1: a lookup never changes state, failure counts, budgets or dispatch; revision 35, D35-1: rows 2 to 4 hold only in the lifecycle `RUNNING` and row 6 covers every other lifecycle; the two oracle cases of SUP-17 are case A = row 3 (A1) or row 2 (A2) with a live supervisor and case B = a derived row (row 4, or row 2 or 3 with a dead supervisor) together with the DEGRADED supervisor; final decision Q1-1).**

| Row | Unit state, component task, registered restart waiter and supervisor in the snapshot | `display_state` of the item | `reason_code` and `since` | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | BACKOFF; no component task; the registered waiter is not `done()` (it is really waiting to restart); the supervisor is alive or dead | none: no derived item, the unit is shown as BACKOFF | no item | the normal backoff (SUP-T T4); when the supervisor is dead the waiter's later re-check is refused and it deregisters (SUP-T T14 (3)), after which row 2 applies |
| 2 | lifecycle `RUNNING`; BACKOFF; no component task; no registered waiter (reached legitimately after the supervisor died, SUP-T T14 (3); with a live supervisor it is not expected to arise, SUP-26, and if the state is present it is derived all the same) | `BACKOFF_ORPHANED` | `null`, `null` | SUP-T T33; one rule for a live and a dead supervisor (final decision Q1-1): a live supervisor with no other fault is case A2 of SUP-17, a dead supervisor is case B |
| 3 | lifecycle `RUNNING`; a task reference exists, `task.done()` is true, its exit event is not processed and the registry entry is not marked handled | `EXITED_UNSUPERVISED` | `null`, `null` | SUP-T T35; a unit without a task reference never matches; with a live supervisor this is case A1 of SUP-17 |
| 4 | lifecycle `RUNNING`; BACKOFF; no component task; the registered waiter is `done()` with its event not processed; the supervisor is dead (`supervisor_degraded`) | `BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED` | `null`, `null` | SUP-T T37; together with the DEGRADED supervisor this is case B of SUP-17 |
| 5 | as row 4 but the supervisor is alive (the normal short window; a lagging supervisor looks the same) | none: shown as BACKOFF | no item | the supervisor processes the event and counts it once (SUP-T T32) |
| 6 | any state of rows 2 to 4 but the lifecycle is `STARTING`, `STOPPING`, `STOP_INCOMPLETE` or `STOPPED` (revision 35, D35-1) | none: no derived item | no item | a normal stop makes no derived warning: `stop()` settles the tasks and waiters that exist (SUP-T T12, T17, T27 to T30); aligned with SUP-T T33, T35 and T37, which hold only in `RUNNING` |

- **SUP-18 Default rules for every lifecycle and event combination.** Table SUP-E lists the combination of every lifecycle value with every event kind and names the row that applies. A combination without its own row follows these default rules: **R1** an event of a previous generation changes no state and leaves an audit record only (SUP-T T34); **R2** a normal-settlement event (a cancel with `STOP` or `FAILED_START` recorded before the cancel) never creates a restart and is never a failure (SUP-T T17); **R3** an unknown abnormal event of the current generation (an unknown unit or an unknown cause) is recorded **fail-closed** as diagnostic state (the unit, if known, follows SUP-T T3 to T5; an unknown unit makes `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` visible and restarts nothing); **R4** a RUNNING component is never lowered to IDLE without evidence: only an exit event (SUP-T T3 to T5) or a stop settlement changes it, never a failed re-check, a lost waiter or a status read; **R5** in `STOPPING` and `STOP_INCOMPLETE` no automatic restart is scheduled and no waiter is created; **R6** any other event that matches no row and is not abnormal is ignored with no state change.

**Table SUP-E: lifecycle and event (the entry names the table SUP-T row or the default rule of SUP-18; 'refused' is a `RuntimeError` or a no-op that changes nothing).**

| Event | `STOPPED` | `STARTING` | `RUNNING` | `STOPPING` | `STOP_INCOMPLETE` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| READY signal | R1 (no task exists) | SUP-T T22 (ignored after `_start_aborting`: SUP-G priority 0) | SUP-T T2 | R6 | R6 |
| component abnormal exit | R1 | SUP-T T6, T36 (after `_start_aborting`: SUP-T T9, SUP-G priority 0) | SUP-T T3 to T5 | SUP-T T9 | SUP-T T10 |
| component normal-settlement end | R2 | SUP-T T17 | SUP-T T17 | SUP-T T17 | SUP-T T17 |
| supervisor exit | R1 | SUP-T T7, T36 (after `_start_aborting`: SUP-T T27, SUP-G priority 0) | SUP-T T8 | SUP-T T27 | SUP-T T29 |
| restart waiter ends | R1 | R3 (a waiter exists only while `RUNNING`) | SUP-T T13, T14, T32, T33 | SUP-T T28 | SUP-T T30 |
| `stop()` | SUP-T T11 | SUP-T T25 (refused) | SUP-T T12, T31 and the settlement | SUP-T T26 (refused) | SUP-7 (a repeated stop retries) |
| `start()` | SUP-T T19 | refused (`runner.py:241-242`) | refused | refused | refused |
| configuration recheck (CI-7) | SUP-30 (`STALE_GENERATION` first, otherwise `NOT_RUNNING`) | SUP-30 (`STALE_GENERATION` first, otherwise `NOT_RUNNING`) | SUP-30 (`STALE_GENERATION`, `STILL_INVALID`, `NO_SWEEPER_TASK`, `NO_INVALID_STATE`, `ALREADY_PENDING`, `WAKE_SCHEDULED` in this order) | SUP-30 (`STALE_GENERATION` first, otherwise `NOT_RUNNING`) | SUP-30 (`STALE_GENERATION` first, otherwise `NOT_RUNNING`) |
| exit event of a previous generation | SUP-G | SUP-G | SUP-G | SUP-G | SUP-G |

**Revision 29 contract (decisions D29-1 to D29-5; rules SUP-19 to SUP-30; design only: nothing here is implemented or verified).** These rules supersede, where they name it, SUP-4 (first sentence), SUP-7, SUP-13 and SUP-14, table SUP-B, items 2, 4 and 5 of this section and the SUP-T T14 and T33 of table SUP-T ('superseded in r29'). A row of table SUP-T is always written with the prefix 'SUP-T' (for example 'SUP-T T14') and a row of the §7.4 table as '§7.4 row 28'; the two numberings are never mixed. **Terms:** the *startup registry* is the per-generation set of tasks that `start()` must reap (SUP-19); a *settling record* is the set of identities (tasks, waiters, startup tasks) that `stop()` or a failed start is settling, matched by identity and not by generation number (SUP-22, revision 30); `_start_aborting` is the per-generation marker of SUP-19 (a plain bool, set in the same synchronous step as the settling record, revision 30).

- **SUP-19 Startup flow with a startup task registry (D29-3; supersedes the step list of SUP-13 and item 2 of this section where they differ).** *Real code today:* `start()` awaits `recover(startup=True)` inline (`runner.py:257`), takes the lifecycle lock only to enter `STARTING` (`:238-248`) and to publish `RUNNING` (`:258-260`), and the 'startup sweeper wait' does not exist yet. B2 **restructures `start()`**: a `create_task` for the startup recovery, one `asyncio.wait` over the registered tasks, an explicit cancel and an explicit await (revision 30, D30-1: the explicit cancel and the explicit await run inside the one shielded settle task of `_fail_start`, not in `start()` itself). **Owner:** the `Runner` owns the startup registry (`_startup_tasks`, canonical id to task; the ids are those of SUP-24); the supervisor never owns or edits it. **Lock boundaries:** an entry is added in the same synchronous section (no `await`) that creates the task, under the lifecycle lock, and only while `_start_aborting` is false and the generation matches; an entry is removed under the lifecycle lock only after its task is confirmed done, never earlier. **Startup tasks versus RUNNING tasks:** the supervisor and the required components are *component tasks*: they are also in the component registry and continue into `RUNNING` (the startup registry holds an additional reference only for the reaping of a failed start and drops it when the boundary passes, SUP-21); `startup-recovery` and the READY waits are *startup-only tasks* and never survive the boundary. **Previous generation:** a generation changes only at the entry of `start()` (which needs `STOPPED` and an empty Runner, `runner.py:241-245`) and of `stop()`; the references of a previous generation stay in the settling record (SUP-22) until their termination is confirmed, and an event of such a task never changes the state of the new generation. **The ten steps (revision 30, D30-1 and D30-3; steps 7 to 9 run inside the shielded settle task):** (1) the entry critical section under the lifecycle lock (`runner.py:240-248`): `STARTING`, the new generation, `_start_aborting` = false, the per-generation `start_failed` Future and the per-generation event `startup_mutation_done` (SUP-31); (2) `engine.connect()` and `pg_try_advisory_lock` (`:251-256`), then, in this order, the capability `UNKNOWN` upsert (mandatory, fail closed), the self-test and the result upsert (§6.2, R31-11): a failure here, `RunnerAlreadyActive` included, is a failed start with an **empty** registry, because nothing has been created yet; (3) **one synchronous section** (under the lifecycle lock, no `await` inside; it checks that the lifecycle is `STARTING`, the generation matches and `_start_aborting` is false) that creates the supervisor, registers the startup registry and creates the required component tasks with the origin `START` (SUP-31), each with its done-callback; (4) the startup recovery as the explicit task `startup-recovery`, which calls `self.recover(startup=True)` **through the instance attribute** (the existing tests replace `r.recover` with a `recover(*, startup=False)` double and assert `calls == [(True, True, L.STARTING)]`, `tests/integration_pg/test_runner_lifecycle.py` about `:350`); (5) observe the READY waits, the startup recovery, `start_failed` and caller cancellation together (`asyncio.wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`; `asyncio.wait` never cancels what it waits for, so a cancelled `start()` does **not** cancel those tasks by itself and they would be orphaned: step 7 is explicit); when the startup recovery has failed, `start()` re-raises **the same exception object** that `task.exception()` returned (the tests assert `info.value is error`); (6) on **any** failure path (a READY timeout, an ended task, the failure of the startup recovery, `start_failed`, any exception, caller cancellation) the hand-off, **synchronous with no `await`**: set `_start_aborting` = true, write the settling record (SUP-22) in the same section, **check the result of every required component task that is `done()` and write the `last_failure` record only of those that abnormally exited and whose task identity no record carries yet, exactly once per generation + unit + task identity, reusing an already collected result and creating no new failure record for an expected settlement cancellation or a normal stop (table SUP-LF row 9; the writer is `start()`; this is the last point at which such a record can be written, because the supervisor treats an exit after the marker as a cleanup event; revision 35, D35-2; final decision Q1-2: this holds on every failure path, a caller cancellation, B1, B2 and B8 included, because table SUP-LF row 4 preserves records for those reasons themselves and gives way to rows 8 and 9 for a unit that had abnormally exited, which gets one audit record per generation + unit + task identity, an existing record being reused and kept even when the caller's `start()` was cancelled, and this record changes neither the main exception delivered to the caller nor the first start failure nor any restart budget)** and call `_fail_start`; (7) inside the settle task: cancel every startup task that is not done; (8) inside the same settle task: await all of them (under the common deadline of SUP-23 for the components, the restart waiters and the supervisor, and under the own bounded wait of SUP-32 for `startup-recovery`); (9) inside the same settle task: the existing `_settle_failed_start` (`:296-328`), which closes the lock connection only when the registry is empty; (10) a task that did not settle stays in the registry and in the component list and is listed in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` (SUP-24) and attached as a structured note to the original start error, which stays the raised error (R31-5; the r30 wording that put it into the start-failure error is **superseded in r31**). **Why steps 7 to 9 are inside the shield (the blocker of r29, closed in r30):** in the r29 text `start()` itself set the marker, cancelled and awaited outside the shield of `_fail_start`, so a second cancellation of `start()` during the bounded wait of step 8 would have ended `start()` with the lifecycle still `STARTING` and the startup tasks neither confirmed nor reported. Now everything after the hand-off belongs to the one settle task that `_fail_start` awaits through `_wait_shielded`: a further caller cancellation only adds a note, it never aborts the settlement, and the lifecycle always ends in `STOPPED` or `STOP_INCOMPLETE`. **While `_start_aborting` is true** `_ensure_background_tasks` and every guarded creation refuse to create a task, and the success boundary checks the marker and the generation (SUP-21), so a component that a recovery creates during the settlement does not survive; a task created before the marker was set is in the registry and is settled in step 8. **Priority of causes:** when a caller `CancelledError` and an internal failure are observed together the caller cancellation stays the final error (the rule of `_fail_start`, `runner.py:265-294`) and the internal failure becomes its `__cause__`. **Original exception:** the first non-cancellation failure is the original; a `CancelledError` that comes from the settlement of a child (a task that **step 7 cancelled**) is never the original and is swallowed after the task is retrieved; a cancellation that nobody requested (no caller cancel, no stop, no step 7) is converted into a start error (`RuntimeError` with the `CancelledError` as `__cause__`) so that `start()` does not end with an unexplained `CancelledError`. The result or exception of every startup task is retrieved exactly once (no 'exception was never retrieved'). **`CancelReason`:** a caller that cancels `start()` reaches the startup recovery as the cancellation of its own task, which `_drive_recovery` sees as `CALLER_CANCEL` (`runner.py:726`); the normal stop settlement uses `SHUTDOWN`; a recovery operation that is still live after a failed start is settled by `_settle_recovery_for_stop` (called from `_settle_failed_start`, `runner.py:305`, and from `_shutdown_resources`, `:408`; it assigns `SHUTDOWN`, `:773`), so the existing reasons are used and no member is added to `CancelReason`: the reason is `SHUTDOWN` only while no reason was recorded before, and the first recorded reason stays (R31-5; the r30 wording that gave a complete rule is **superseded in r31**); the sweeper task is cancelled with the recorded reason `FAILED_START` (§7.4).

- **SUP-20 Bounded READY for every required component (D29-3 follow-up; supersedes the READY interpretation of SUP-14 and the special case of the sweeper).** **READY means:** the event loop and the task registration are normal and the task has reached its **initial entry point** (the first statement of the coroutine runs and sets its READY event); it does **not** mean that the first sweep, any database work or the first tick has completed. **One uniform rule:** every required task is READY when its READY event for **this task identity and generation** is set, within `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (default 5.0 s, §9.2, §9.4) counted from its creation; all deadlines run concurrently, so the whole READY phase is bounded by one timeout and not by their sum. The revision-28 rule that the sweeper passes the boundary 'by READY **or** by the bounded startup wait with the task alive' and its special case are **removed**: `ready_seen` becomes true at the entry point for every component, and the first-pass event of the sweeper is no longer READY. `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS` **stays** with its other meaning: the startup recovery's bounded wait for the first sweeper pass before `reconcile()` (§7.4, item 2 of this section); its expiry neither passes nor fails the READY boundary and never fails the start. A task that ends right after READY is caught by the `task.done()` checks of the boundary (SUP-21), not by READY. Capability updater and risk worker: READY does not depend on when their first loop iteration runs (immediately at creation or after the idle or refresh interval); only the entry point counts. **Table SUP-R: READY contract per required component** (the reason code is `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT` with the canonical id of the task as detail).

| Component | Task identity | READY event | Timeout | Where the timeout is recorded | Delivery |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| orphan sweeper | `sweeper` and its generation | set by the first statement of `_sweeper_task`, before the first page query | `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | the `last_failure` of the `sweeper` component and, as the first failure, `start_failed` | the original start error stays the raised error; unsettled tasks are in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` and in a note on it (R31-5) |
| capability updater | `capability` and its generation | set by the first statement of `_capability_task`, before the first refresh | `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | the `last_failure` of `capability` and `start_failed` | same as the sweeper row |
| risk worker | `risk-worker` and its generation | set by the first statement of `_risk_task`, before the first claim iteration | `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | the `last_failure` of `risk-worker` and `start_failed` | same as the sweeper row |
| supervisor | `supervisor` and its generation | set by the first statement of the supervisor coroutine, before it reads its queue (its own boundary) | `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `start_failed` (the supervisor is not a component and has no `last_failure`) | same as the sweeper row |

Each timeout is attributed to the exact task identity that missed it and writes only that component's record (the writer, the generation and the clearing of the record are fixed by table SUP-LF, not by this table): one component's timeout never overwrites another's (the first one is also the `start_failed` value, a later one is added as a note, SUP-T T36). **Consequence for stability (D28-3):** `stable_since` is stamped at the READY of the current task, which is now the entry point, so stability is judged from the alive time of the task and no longer from its first pass; a task that dies after READY and before `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS` is an unstable exit.

- **SUP-21 The STARTING success boundary (replaces SUP-14; table SUP-B is amended).** Right before `RUNNING` is published, `start()` takes the lifecycle lock and checks **synchronously (no `await`)** every item: the lifecycle is `STARTING`; the generation equals the captured one; `_start_aborting` is false; `start_failed` is not completed; the supervisor task exists and is not `done()`; every required component task exists and is not `done()`; every required READY event is set for this task identity and generation; the startup recovery has completed without error; no stop request exists; the required lock connection is valid, which a synchronous check can state only as `_lock_conn is not None`, not closed (`getattr(_lock_conn, "closed", False)` is false, because the `ConnProxy` test double of `tests/integration_pg/test_runner_lifecycle.py` (about `:120`) has no `closed` attribute unless it is given one; in the project's SQLAlchemy 2.1.6, read in the project virtual environment without a database, `AsyncConnection.closed` is a property that proxies `Connection.closed`; it reports only the local closed flag and not the state of the server, and `invalidated` is a separate property) and `_recovery_clean()` (`runner.py:602`), **not** that the server is alive. Only when all hold are the startup registry entries of the component tasks dropped and `_state` set to `RUNNING` in the same critical section (SUP-T T23); otherwise `start()` enters `_fail_start` (SUP-T T24). **An empty done-callback queue is never treated as liveness**; `task.done()` is read from the registry. **Priority when several completions or failed items are observed together (revision 33, D33-3; every item B1 to B10 of table SUP-B is in exactly one group, the lowest group number decides the one reported failure and the others become notes, R31-5):** (1) caller cancellation or a stop request (B7, the 'no stop request' part; it is always false in `STARTING` because `stop()` raises there, `runner.py:344-345`); (2) the **already recorded first failure**, which a later failure or a failure of a lower-priority group (a higher group number) never replaces: B3 (`start_failed` is completed) and B9 (`_start_aborting` is true, which is also the marker part of B7: a settlement has begun, so a first failure or a cancellation is already recorded); (3) a defect of the state, failing closed: B1 (the lifecycle is not `STARTING`) and B2 (the generation differs), which raise a defect error only when no failure is recorded yet and are notes otherwise; (4) a required task that ended: B4 (the supervisor) and B5 (a component); (5) a READY timeout: B6; (6) a startup recovery that failed or is not done: B10; (7) the lock connection or the start resources invalid: B8; (8) a success candidate (B1 to B10 all hold). **Tie order:** when several failures of one group are first observed at the same observation point (several tasks `done()` with no queued event, several READY timeouts at the same deadline), the first failure is that of the supervisor and then those of the components in the order of `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_IDS`, which is the creation order of SUP-19 step 3 (this replaces the r32 C6 wording 'registry creation order'). 'First failure' is defined once, in table SUP-LF: the failure first recorded in `start_failed` or, while none is recorded, the failure first observed at one observation point; it selects only the representative start failure and never the `last_failure` records (revision 35, D35-2). A caller cancellation observed together with an internal failure stays the final error and the failure becomes its `__cause__` (SUP-19, 'Priority of causes'), and the preserved original start error of R31-5 is unchanged by this grouping. **The `start_failed` Future:** its result or exception is consumed on every path (retrieved exactly once, so no 'Future exception was never retrieved'); `set_exception` is guarded with `done()` so a second completion cannot raise `InvalidStateError`; 'discard' means retrieve and then drop the reference and **never** `cancel()` a Future that the supervisor may still complete. The supervisor's done-callback of a supervisor that died during `STARTING` sets only `start_failed` (SUP-25).

**Table SUP-21X: the order of the reported failure and the propagation of a caller cancellation (revision 34, A7; the group priority of revision 33 is unchanged; the order inside a group is an authoring choice, §12 A33-1).**

| Group | Items | Reported failure when it is the lowest group observed | The same observation together with a caller cancellation | Order inside the group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | B7 (caller cancellation, stop request) | the caller cancellation | it is the cancellation itself and stays the final error | not applicable |
| 2 | B3, B9 | the already recorded first failure, **preserved**: a later failure or a failure of a lower group never replaces it | the caller cancellation is the final error and the preserved first failure is its `__cause__` (SUP-19 'Priority of causes'; the rule of `_fail_start`, `runner.py:265-294`) | the order in which the failures were recorded |
| 3 | B1, B2 | a defect error only when no failure is recorded yet, otherwise a note | as group 2 | not applicable |
| 4 | B4, B5 | the first ended required task | as group 2 | the supervisor first, then the components in the order of `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_IDS` (the creation order of SUP-19 step 3), when first observed at the same observation point |
| 5 | B6 | the first READY timeout | as group 2 | as group 4 |
| 6 | B10 | the failed or unfinished startup recovery | as group 2 | not applicable |
| 7 | B8 | the invalid lock connection or start resources | as group 2 | not applicable |
| 8 | B1 to B10 all hold | none: the start succeeds | not applicable | not applicable |

- **SUP-22 Generation kinds and the event priority (replaces SUP-T T34 as a blanket rule).** Three kinds: the **current active generation** (the generation of the live tasks while the lifecycle is `STARTING` or `RUNNING`), a **settling identity** (an identity listed in a settling record, whatever generation number its event carries) and an **unrelated stale generation** (any other). The *settling record* is written in the **same synchronous step** that sets `_start_aborting` (a failed start; its generation is not bumped) and by `stop()` under the lifecycle lock **before** it bumps `_generation` (`runner.py:347`). It holds **identities, not a generation number**: the task identities, the restart-waiter identities and the startup-task identities that are being settled, and an event is matched **by identity**. The reason: `stop()` bumps `_generation` on **every** entry, retries from `STOP_INCOMPLETE` included (`runner.py:347`), so a record keyed by 'the settling generation id' would turn the exit of a still unsettled generation-1 task into an 'unrelated stale' event (SUP-T T34, an audit record only) after the second or third retry. A retry adds the identities that still exist, **every record is retained until all of its identities are confirmed ended**, and an identity is removed only after its termination is confirmed, so an unsettled one stays (`STOP_INCOMPLETE`). **Table SUP-G: the priority table** (evaluated top to bottom; the first match decides, so the cleanup rows and SUP-T T34 never apply together).

| Priority | Condition of the event | Kind | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | the lifecycle is `STARTING` (revision 33, D33-2: stated explicitly), `_start_aborting` is set and the event's generation equals `_generation` (checked first) | failed-start cleanup | the cleanup rules (SUP-T T9, T17 and T27, branch 2 of table SUP-X, for `STARTING` with `_start_aborting`; SUP-T T10 and T28 to T30 never apply to `STARTING`, R31-6): no restart, no budget, no `start_failed`, no degraded flag and no effect of a READY signal (SUP-13), even for the events that the settlement itself produces (the cancelled children and the cancelled supervisor); the reference is removed after confirmed termination |
| 1 | a settling record contains the identity of the event's task, waiter or startup task (any lifecycle, whatever generation number the event carries: a `stop()` retry bumps the generation) | settling identity | the cleanup rules by the event's lifecycle (SUP-T T9, T17, T27, T28 in `STOPPING`; SUP-T T10, T17, T29, T30 in `STOP_INCOMPLETE`; SUP-T T9, T17, T27 in `STARTING`): no restart, no budget; the task or waiter reference is removed after confirmed termination |
| 2 | the event's generation equals `_generation`, `_start_aborting` is false, no settling record contains its identity, and the lifecycle is `STARTING` or `RUNNING` | current active generation | the normal transition rules (SUP-T T1 to T8, T13 to T16, T18, T20 to T24, T32, T33, T35, T36) |
| 3 | any other event, including an event whose generation equals `_generation` while the lifecycle is `STOPPED`, `STOPPING` or `STOP_INCOMPLETE` and no record contains its identity (a defect, recorded as such) | unrelated stale generation | SUP-T T34: no state change, an audit record only |

An event of an old generation never changes the state of the new generation. SUP-T T36 (a second failure after `start_failed`) applies only until `_start_aborting` is set; afterwards the failure is a cleanup event of priority 0 (and of priority 1 once a record holds its identity). The cell of table SUP-E for an exit event of a previous generation is this table. **Priority 0 and the other lifecycles (revision 32, C2 and C3; derived form in revision 33, D33-2):** priority 0 requires the lifecycle `STARTING`, so it never matches in the other four. In `STOP_INCOMPLETE` (also when a failed start left `_start_aborting` true) an event whose identity a record holds is priority 1 (branch 5 of table SUP-X: SUP-T T10, T17, T29, T30), and an event of the current generation whose identity is in no record is priority 3 (an audit record only, a defect); the same two outcomes hold in `STOPPING` (branch 4: SUP-T T9, T17, T27, T28) and, for an identity in a record or in none, in `STOPPED`. At `RUNNING` the marker is false (the success boundary re-checks it, SUP-21), so a current-generation event is priority 2. Each cell of the lifecycles `STOPPED`, `RUNNING`, `STOPPING` and `STOP_INCOMPLETE` therefore has exactly one rule.

- **SUP-23 Bounded settlement with one common deadline (D29-1, D29-2; rewrites items 4 and 5 of this section and SUP-7).** *Real code today:* `_shutdown_resources` (`runner.py:393-426`) cancels the loop task and awaits it with an unbounded `asyncio.gather` (`:402-406`), then runs `_settle_recovery_for_stop` (`:408`), `_drain` (`:472-495`, bounded by `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` for in-flight request tasks) and the lock release; the component tasks of B2 do not exist yet. **Flow:** (1) take one snapshot of the settle targets (the loop task `_loop_task`, the supervisor, the restart waiters, the component tasks and, in a failed start, the startup tasks); (2) request cancellation of all of them, the supervisor first so that it cannot create a restart; (3) start **one** common deadline of `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (`loop.time()` plus the copy of the constant, see 'The validated copy' of this rule) for the component set (the components, the restart waiters and the supervisor) and, concurrently, the own deadline of the loop task and of `startup-recovery` (SUP-32); (4) await all targets concurrently with one `asyncio.wait(targets, timeout=remaining)` (never one timeout per component and never sequential waits, so the total settle time is bounded by **one** timeout and not by N times it); (5) classify the finished tasks (retrieve each result or exception once); (6) keep the references of the unfinished ones in their registries; (7) record their canonical ids in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` (SUP-24); (8) continue all other resource cleanup (the recovery settlement, the drain and, only when the registry is empty and the recovery is clean, the lock release); (9) the final lifecycle is `STOP_INCOMPLETE`; (10) a later `stop()` retries the remaining settlement with a fresh common deadline for the remaining set. **Order inside `_shutdown_resources`:** wake, then the settlement of this rule (one snapshot that includes the loop task; the supervisor, the waiters, the components and the loop task are cancelled together), **then** `_settle_recovery_for_stop` (`:408`), then the drain, then the lock release; cancelling the components first means a recovery that is still settling cannot rely on them, and the generation guard (SUP-19) refuses a creation in any case. **Effect of the timeout (D29-2):** an unsettled component is not cleared as if it had succeeded, its registry reference stays, and ownership and workspace safety are not declared settled: the advisory-lock connection stays held (the existing rule at `:417-420` is extended by 'and the registry is empty'; `clean` at `:376-377` and the 'still holds resources' check at `:243-245` (the state check is `:241-242`) include the registry). A task that ignores cancellation is never awaited forever; it stays alive and is reported. **The loop task and `startup-recovery` (revision 30, D30-5):** they are settled with their **own** bounded wait (SUP-32), and the unbounded `asyncio.gather(loop_task, ...)` at `:402-406` is replaced by that bounded wait (a loop task that ignores cancellation would otherwise make `stop()` wait forever, which D29-2 forbids); a loop task that has not ended at its deadline keeps `_loop_task` set, is listed with the canonical id `runner-loop` and keeps the lifecycle `STOP_INCOMPLETE` (`clean` already requires `_loop_task is None`, `:376-377`). **What the common deadline bounds (stated plainly):** the one common deadline bounds **only** the component set (the components, the restart waiters and the supervisor, the D29-1 set); it does **not** bound the total duration of `stop()` or of a failed start: `_drain` has its own wait of up to three times the grace (`:472-495`, R31-8), the close of the lock connection is documented as unbounded and the recovery settlement has its own bound (SUP-32). **The validated copy (revision 30, C4; amended by R31-9):** the `Runner` constructor builds a validated copy of `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (and of the margin of SUP-32) through the validation entry of R31-9 (the r30 wording that `start()` captures it is **superseded in r31**) and every settle path (`stop()`, the failed-start settlement and the startup settlement) uses the copy, never the module constant. Including the loop task is this document's reading of D29-1 and D29-2 and its own deadline is a design choice made in r30; neither is user-approved. **Separation from the shutdown grace (D28-5, D29-1):** `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` keeps bounding the in-flight request tasks of `_drain` and takes part in no B2 relation; the settle timeout is a separate B2 constant. The same mechanism settles the startup tasks in a failed start, inside the shielded settle task (SUP-19, steps 7 and 8).

- **SUP-24 `RunnerStopIncomplete` contract (one shape; class at `runner.py:50-61`).** Fields: `run_ids: tuple[str, ...]`; `recovery: str | None` (today's meaning, unchanged); `components: tuple[str, ...]` of canonical component ids. **The id format is defined here once:** `sweeper`, `risk-worker`, `capability`, `supervisor`, `runner-loop`, `<id>:restart-waiter` (for example `sweeper:restart-waiter`) and `startup-recovery`; no run id is invented for them. **Compatibility:** today's constructor is `(run_ids: list[str], recovery: str | None = None)`; it is built with lists in `_settle_stop` (`:388`) and `_drain` (`:495`) and in `tests/unit/test_lifespan_shutdown.py` (`RunnerStopIncomplete(["r"])`); the B2 constructor is `(run_ids=(), recovery=None, *, components=())`, accepts any sequence and **stores tuples**, so the attribute `run_ids` changes from a list to a tuple (a search of `app` and `tests` finds no use of `.run_ids` other than the assignment at `:60`). **Merge rules:** the components merge **into the single** `RunnerStopIncomplete` together with the run ids and the recovery description (today `_combine`, `:150-152` and `:425-426`, raises one error as itself and several as a `BaseExceptionGroup`; B2 does **not** turn this combination into a group); other cleanup failures (for example a connection close error) are attached to an **existing** `RunnerStopIncomplete` as structured detail (a `cleanup_errors` tuple and `add_note` text) and the incomplete error stays the primary error; **when the close of the advisory-lock connection is the only failure** (nothing else is unsettled) there is no `RunnerStopIncomplete` to attach to, because it is never constructed for an empty failure set, so the cleanup-attachment path is not reached: `stop()` re-raises the **original close exception** (a caller cancellation keeps the existing outcome rule below), keeps the reference `_lock_conn` and the lifecycle `STOP_INCOMPLETE`, and the next `stop()` retries the close of the same connection (`_release_lock_connection` already leaves the reference in place when the close fails or is cancelled, `runner.py:435-444`; revision 35, D35-4); a caller cancellation keeps the existing outcome rule of `stop()` (`CancelledError` from the error, `:353-360`). **Where the single exception is built (revision 30, C10):** `_drain` raises a bare `RunnerStopIncomplete(run_ids)` with no recovery description (`:495`), and the recovery text is added by `_settle_stop` only when `error` is `None` (`:387-389`); B2 therefore makes `_shutdown_resources` find the `RunnerStopIncomplete` that the drain raised and **rebuild** it with the components and the recovery description (one exception, never a `BaseExceptionGroup` of run, component and recovery errors; `_combine`, `:150-152`, is unchanged for stops with only non-incomplete errors). The recovery message keeps the word 'unsettled' (`tests/integration_pg/test_runner_recovery_bounded.py:513-516` checks `"unsettled" in str`). **`clean` and the registry:** `clean` (`:376-377`), `closed = owned is None` (`:302`), the `_recovery_clean()` gate (`:308`), the final transition of `_settle_failed_start` (`:319-327`) and the check at `:243-245` include the component, waiter and startup registries; the lock-release gate of `_shutdown_resources` (`:417-420`) keeps the advisory lock held while the registry is non-empty; a `stop()` retry after a failed start has the startup registry among its targets. **Messages:** run ids only, components only, recovery only and every combination each name what is unsettled. **Never constructed for an empty failure set:** the B2 intent is that it is never built when run ids, recovery and components are all empty; today's generic fallback message (`:59`) stays only for compatibility. A `stop()` from `STOPPED` is an idempotent success (`runner.py:342-343`, SUP-T T11).

- **SUP-25 Dispatch guard and the reset of the DEGRADED state.** *Real new-work start points:* `Runner._dispatch` (`runner.py:896-911`): the loop condition at `:899`, `claim_next` at `:900-902` and `_launch` at `:909`; `_loop` calls it at `:943`. `runtime_snapshot` `ready` and `blockers` are **informational today and are not read by dispatch** (they are read by `/health`, `main.py:107`, by `DiagnosticsService`, by `ReportService._runtime` and `_next_actions` and by `Container.runner_active`). The B2 plan adds one internal guard, a private Runner predicate (a name that does not start with `recover`) that reads **only** the `supervisor_degraded` flag (a degraded sweeper, risk worker or capability updater never blocks dispatch; **amended in r31**, R31-2), with the checks named in R31-2 inside `_dispatch` (§14): in the loop condition, **before** `claim_next` **and after** the claim transaction committed and **before** `_launch`. The post-claim check **breaks out of the `while` loop** of `_dispatch` (`:899`) and never uses `continue` (revision 32, W3: `continue` would also leave exactly one CLAIMED row, because the `while` condition, guard point (1), reads the flag again and ends the loop; `break` stays the specified form because it does not depend on that re-read; the earlier statement that `continue` piles up CLAIMED rows is corrected). `_dispatch` returns the number started and the next iteration of `_loop` re-evaluates the pre-claim check. A request that was claimed while the flag was set is **not launched**: it stays `CLAIMED` without a lease and the existing stale-claim recovery requeues it after `claim_timeout_seconds` (default 300 s, `config.py`), which adds no new database write; the delay of up to that grace is the stated cost, approved in revision 31 (D31-2; the retention rule is stated once in R31-3). Recovery (`recover(startup=False)`, `_loop` `:937`) keeps running while the flag is set. Tasks that already run are not cancelled by the flag (SUP-6). **Reset rule (generation based):** `background_degraded` and `supervisor_degraded` belong to the generation that set them; the done-callback of the supervisor that ends while the lifecycle is `STARTING` writes **only** `start_failed` (a component's exit is recorded by the supervisor's event processing, SUP-13) and never sets a degraded flag; the flags are reset when `start()` enters a new generation and when a failed-start settlement reaches `STOPPED`, so a `STARTING` failure followed by `STOPPED` leaves no stale `background_degraded` or `supervisor_degraded`.

- **SUP-26 Transition-table cleanups (supersede SUP-T T14 and T33; SUP-T T17, T34 and SUP-E as amended).** **SUP-T T33 is display only:** it writes no state; a status read derives BACKOFF_ORPHANED, EXITED_UNSUPERVISED and BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED from the registry (defined once in SUP-17, table SUP-DS) and changes nothing (consistent with SUP-17 and the status rule R4). A lost restart waiter is **proven impossible while the supervisor loop runs** (the one loop that consumes the per-generation queue, SUP-9; revision 33, D33-15): the waiter is created and its done-callback is registered in one synchronous section, so a done waiter always delivers its event; a waiter that is done with its event still queued stays registered, so the unit is shown as BACKOFF while the supervisor is alive (none of the derived values, SUP-17; with a dead supervisor it is BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED, table SUP-DS row 4) and the waiter is counted by the normal processing of that event (SUP-T T32), never by a second mechanism. **SUP-T T14 is split by the real state of task, waiter and budget:** (a) a live task or a second live waiter: **cannot occur for a BACKOFF unit** (a unit with a task is RUNNING and a second waiter is refused, SUP-T T20) and is dropped (revision 32, M2; revision 33, D33-15); (b) no task and exactly one registered waiter, the normal BACKOFF: wait for the waiter, no action; (c) no task, no waiter and a restart allowed: **is not expected while the supervisor is alive** (the guarded start either creates the task or fails, and that real failure event is counted as SUP-T T15); it arises after the supervisor died (SUP-T T33, revision 32 M2; the refusal precedence of SUP-T T14 applies). **In every case (revision 33, D33-1) it is the derived display value BACKOFF_ORPHANED under the same lookup rule whether the supervisor is alive or dead:** no state write, no SUP-T T15 count, no budget consumption, no waiter and no automatic recovery, so no re-registration loop of any kind exists; the output is the one of SUP-17 (a live supervisor with no other fault: case A2, `background_degraded` false, `RUNNER_STATE` WARN, exactly one cause `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED`; the supervisor DEGRADED: case B, FAIL; revision 35, final decision Q1-1); the earlier sentence that a live supervisor reaching it counts it as SUP-T T15 is removed, because a failure is counted only by its own real event. **Revision 31 (supersedes the r30 sentence that the helper refuses a unit in BACKOFF or DEGRADED whatever the origin):** creation is decided by table SUP-O: `START` and `RECOVERY` refuse a BACKOFF or DEGRADED unit, `RESTART` re-creates a BACKOFF unit only for its registered current waiter and DEGRADED refuses every origin, so a periodic recovery cannot realise case (c) (R31-1; a failed RESTART counts once and a refusal never counts). **Rows that remain by rule:** the own exit of a waiter and of the supervisor in `STARTING`, `STOPPING` and `STOP_INCOMPLETE` are SUP-T T7, T27 to T30 and T36 through table SUP-E; a stop of an unstarted unit (`STOPPED`, idempotent) is SUP-T T11; a late event is classified by table SUP-G. **SUP-T T17** (the normal end after a stop signal) applies in `STARTING`, `RUNNING`, `STOPPING` and `STOP_INCOMPLETE` as table SUP-E already uses it, not only in `RUNNING`. **SUP-4:** its first sentence 'routes into the failed-start settlement' is superseded: the supervisor never settles (SUP-13); an exit during `STARTING` is recorded in `start_failed` and only `start()` settles. `stop()` in `STARTING` raises `RuntimeError` today (`runner.py:344-345`) and keeps doing so.

- **SUP-27 Stability time base and liveness limits (refines SUP-15).** **exit_time** is the monotonic time at the closest point where the termination of the task can be observed: when the task wrapper can record the time itself, a `try/finally` around the coroutine stamps `loop.time()` and that is the source; the done-callback stamps `loop.time()` as a **fallback**. Honest limit: a blocked event loop delays the done-callback stamp and the bias is toward 'stable' unless the wrapper recorded the end. A task that is cancelled before its first step never enters its coroutine and so never reaches the `finally`: its `exit_time` is always the done-callback stamp (revision 30, C9). The processing delay of the supervisor never extends or shortens stability. A new task registration starts with `ready_seen` false and `stable_since` null; READY (the entry point, SUP-20) sets `stable_since` of the **current** task; a replacement drops the previous values. After stability a repeated crash still consumes the rolling-window budget (stabilization resets the consecutive count and never deletes a window entry; this is the one reading of D27-3 and D27-4). **Tests use a fake clock with dyadic values** because the real `loop.time()` gives `(s + 300.0) - s >= 300.0` false for some floats. **Known liveness limits for persistent state:** when the sweeper is restarted before every pass finishes (a cadence slower than `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_SECONDS` / `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX` (360 s with the defaults, the one formula of SUP-5) never degrades it), each same-object restart restarts the cursor at the first page, so the records that need a pass beyond the first ~12 passes of batch rows (the stall record, the configuration-invalid state and the decode-error rows) may be cleared late or never; the bound is: a record is reached only if its keyset position lies within the rows that one pass scans before the next restart.
