- **SUP-28 Policy snapshot validated at pass entry (replaces 'the guard runs at the END of every pass', RV-2).** At the **entry** of every pass the sweeper builds **one** policy snapshot of every constant that the pass body or its failure handling consumes (**membership, revision 35, final decision Q2-2: the members of the pass snapshot are the constants that §9.3 validates as sweeper pass inputs and whose validation failure it maps to `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`**; §9.3 is the single membership reference and CG-1 refers to it; this rule lists no constant again, so a name added to or removed from §9.3 changes the membership with no edit here; the decision rule is the §9.3 vocabulary paragraph, by which a member constant that is also used on another path as a construction copy stays a member; the configuration-invalid fallback `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` and the separate supervisor-only and READY inputs and the relation inputs are **not** members just because they appear in the same error text, in the same validator call or in a relation) and checks every type, range and relation; sleep, arithmetic, comparison, range and timeout use **only snapshot values**, so no unvalidated constant is consumed first. **Validator order:** reject a bool; accept a supported type only (`int` or `float`; a `Decimal` is **rejected as unsupported**); compare against the range with exact int comparison (safe for huge ints); convert to float only when needed; `math.isfinite` only on a safely converted float; then minimum, maximum and relations; normalise `ArithmeticError`, `OverflowError`, `TypeError` and `ValueError` into the one settings-validation error envelope. NaN is rejected explicitly (`v < lo or v > hi` passes NaN). `None`, a `str`, a bool, NaN, infinity and `10**400` all become a validation error. **Verdict:** an invalid snapshot constant means no pass runs and the state is `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` for **every** snapshot constant, including the stall threshold and the log throttle (the failure handler reads the validated copy) and the batch, page and scan row limits (the revision-28 verdict 'top-level exception handled by the supervisor' for them is superseded in r29); a corrupted **fallback** value itself (`ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS`; it cannot be used to wait) is a supervisor failure: an abnormal exit with the bounded restart, never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` (R31-10 (e)). **Three cases of the fallback, each judged in its own place (revision 34, A8; consistent with CG-1, CG-2, R31-10 (e) and the table of §9.3):** (1) *snapshot validation failure*: a snapshot constant is invalid; it is judged at the pass entry, in `_recheck_sweeper_configuration` and at `start()`, and the state is `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`; (2) *valid fallback use*: after such an entry failure the failure path of the pass waits `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS`, computed first as `now + ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` (§7.4 rows 22, 23 and 30); the value is exactly 86400.0 and is used without a snapshot; (3) *the fallback itself corrupted*: it is judged where it is used and by the validator of the Runner construction (R31-9, §9.3); on a live process it is the abnormal exit of §7.4 row 28 with the bounded restart and never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`. **The three owners of constant values and the consumption time of each (revision 35, D35-4; a decision of the user's revision-35 instruction):** (1) the *pass snapshot* is built, owned and discarded by the sweeper pass: it is built at the entry of every pass from the live values of the members defined by §9.3 (membership, above), consumed only inside that pass and by the evaluations of SUP-30 and of `start()`, and never reused by the next pass; (2) the *READY copy and the other construction copies* are built once by the `Runner` constructor in the one validation entry (R31-9: the READY timeout, the settle timeout, the margin, the restart and interval constants), are owned by the `Runner` object and are consumed by `start()` (the READY wait), by the settle paths and by the supervisor for the whole life of that object; they are never rebuilt per pass (a constant that is a member by §9.3 and also has a construction copy here stays a member: the copy is another path, not an exclusion), and a copy that is unusable when it is read is SUP-6 (iii) or a refusal at construction and never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`; (3) the *separate fallback* `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` is a code literal that belongs to neither (1) nor (2): the Runner validator only refuses a corrupted value at construction, and the value is consumed only at the instant at which the failure path of a pass computes `now + fallback`. **Membership, validation rule and snapshot lifetime are three different things (revision 35, final decision Q2-2):** *membership* is the one sentence above, decided by §9.3 alone; the *validation rule* is the validator order and the verdict of this rule, which the `Runner` factory applies to the same inputs at construction (R31-9, a refusal), the sweeper applies at the entry of every pass (`SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`), and `start()` and `_recheck_sweeper_configuration` (SUP-30) apply to the inputs as they are at each call time; the *snapshot lifetime* is one pass: the sweeper captures and validates the values that pass will use at its entry and discards them with the pass (owner (1)), while the construction copies live as long as the `Runner` (owner (2)). No second constant list and no hot-reload path is added. **Outcomes for the fallback (one rule each):** a **valid** fallback whose sum with `now` overflows the datetime range stores `datetime.max` in UTC as `next_retry_at`, the record is written as usual and nothing is raised (§7.4 item (7), row 28 and R31-10 (f) say the same); a **corrupted** fallback itself writes nothing (all or nothing) and the pass ends as an abnormal exit (§7.4 row 28). *The link per value (revision 33, D33-8):* `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` has the consumer **the failure path of the pass itself** (the wait after a `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` entry failure), is **not** a snapshot constant and is checked where it is used (the validator of the Runner construction refuses a corrupted value, R31-9; on a live process a corrupted value is the abnormal exit above); every other constant of this list has the consumer **the sweeper pass**, is validated at the entry of the pass, in `_recheck_sweeper_configuration` and at `start()`, and its corruption gives `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`. No end-of-pass check remains, because no value is read after the entry. **Evaluation timing (config validity):** the evaluation happens at pass entry, in `_recheck_sweeper_configuration` (SUP-30) and at `start()`. **Consumers (revision 30, C4 and C5; one verdict per constant and consumer):** the snapshot covers **only** the constants that the sweeper consumes. `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_RECOVERY_SETTLE_MARGIN_SECONDS` are consumed by the Runner's settle paths: they are validated by the single validation entry of R31-9 (refused at the construction of the Runner) and copied there, and the copy is used afterwards (SUP-23, SUP-32); they are not snapshot constants, and an invalid value never produces `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`. `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` is consumed by `start()` for the READY wait of each required component (SUP-20) through the READY copy that the `Runner` constructor validated and built (R31-9), not through the pass snapshot, and it too is never a sweeper snapshot constant. The supervisor-only constants (`BACKGROUND_MAX_RESTARTS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_CAP_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP`, `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_RESTART_WINDOW_MAX`) are validated by the entry of R31-9 and copied into the supervisor's own state; a value of that copy that cannot be used when the supervisor reads it degrades that component (SUP-6 (iii)) and is never a sweeper state. `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` is validated where it is consumed (the snapshot for the sweeper's debounce and retry delays, the supervisor copy for its restart base and cap).

- **SUP-29 Configuration validity fields (output timing).** `config_currently_valid: bool | None`, `config_evaluated_at: datetime | None`, `config_invalid_active: bool` and `clearance_pending: bool`. `None` means **never evaluated** (no bound of 'too old' exists: the value is `None` only before the first evaluation; afterwards the reader judges age from `config_evaluated_at`). A configuration that is valid now while the clearing trigger has not passed is `config_currently_valid` true, `config_invalid_active` true, `clearance_pending` true; the output never claims 'currently invalid' for a valid configuration and its wording separates a **current configuration error** from a **past error that is not cleared yet**. The cause text and the recommendation of `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` are conditional on `config_currently_valid`: when true the text says that the earlier error is not cleared yet and no correction is needed; when false (or `None`) it says that the configuration is invalid and has to be corrected.

- **SUP-30 The `_recheck_sweeper_configuration(generation, policy)` contract (RV-3).** Owned by `Runner`; `ConfigWakeResult` is defined in `app/services/runner.py` beside `RunnerLifecycle` and `CancelReason` (a Runner-side module, **not** `app.schemas`, and not imported by any schema). There is still no production automatic caller, no `Settings` hot reload, no endpoint and no `validate_*` name. **Naming rule for new Runner and service methods and modules (corrected in revision 30, C11):** the architecture test `tests/architecture/test_project_rules.py` (`_attribute_calls`, `:171-178`, used by the test at `:185-186`) walks **all of `app/`** and fails when an attribute **call** whose name **starts with** `recover` (`node.func.attr.startswith(name_prefix)`; `recovery_x` starts with `recover` too) occurs outside `services/runner.py`; the earlier statement 'only the exact name `recover`' was wrong. A property read is not a call and is not matched. So outside `services/runner.py` nothing may **call** a method whose name starts with `recover`, and a new method of another module is therefore never named `recover*` or `recovery*`; inside `services/runner.py` any name is allowed. The snapshot builder of SUP-28 lives in `app/validation` (any name) or, in a service, under a name that does not start with `validate_` (the test at `tests/architecture/test_rules.py:165-174` rejects a `validate_*` definition outside `app/validation`, except in the single allow-listed file `app/services/artifacts.py`, `ALLOWED_VALIDATE_OUTSIDE` at `:162`, which validates agent output; revision 33, D33-13); a service may import `app.validation` (`LAYER_RULES`, `test_rules.py:110-116`; the services line is `:114`). **Inputs and the result precedence (revision 30, C3; the first match decides):** the inputs are the passed `generation`, the lifecycle, the validity of the policy snapshot of SUP-28, `config_invalid_active` (the persistent configuration-invalid state, SUP-29), whether a **live** sweeper task exists (a task that is `done()` while its exit event is not yet processed does **not** count as present) and `wake_pending`. The validity input is judged by the verdict rule of SUP-28 on the pass inputs (the members defined by §9.3) as they are **at the time of the call**; the call keeps no snapshot between calls and no hot-reload path exists (final decision Q2-2). 1 `STALE_GENERATION` (the passed generation differs from `_generation`, in **every** lifecycle, `STOPPED` included); 2 `NOT_RUNNING` (the lifecycle is not `RUNNING`: `STOPPED`, `STARTING`, `STOPPING`, `STOP_INCOMPLETE`); 3 `STILL_INVALID` (the policy snapshot of SUP-28 is invalid); 4 `NO_SWEEPER_TASK` (no live sweeper task exists; `wake_pending` is never set when no task exists and is cleared when a task is created); 5 `NO_INVALID_STATE` (the configuration is valid and `config_invalid_active` is false: there is nothing to wake, and an ordinary failure backoff must not end early, because CI-7 allows a wake-up only for an active invalid-to-valid transition); 6 `ALREADY_PENDING`; 7 `WAKE_SCHEDULED` (a valid configuration, `config_invalid_active` true, a live sweeper task and no pending wake). `NOOP` no longer exists and `WAKE_SCHEDULED` is never returned without a live sweeper task or without `config_invalid_active`. **Unique answer per combination:** a stale generation gives `STALE_GENERATION` whatever the other inputs; a matching generation and `STOPPED`, `STARTING`, `STOPPING` or `STOP_INCOMPLETE` gives `NOT_RUNNING`; a matching generation and `RUNNING` gives the first of `STILL_INVALID`, `NO_SWEEPER_TASK`, `NO_INVALID_STATE`, `ALREADY_PENDING`, `WAKE_SCHEDULED` that matches; this is the same for the table SUP-E row 'configuration recheck'. `ConfigWakeResult` is owned by `app/services/runner.py`, not by `app.schemas`.

**Revision 30 contract (decisions D30-1 to D30-5; rules SUP-31 and SUP-32 and the amendments named in each rule; design only: nothing here is implemented or verified).** D30-1 (the failed-start settlement runs inside the one shielded settle task) is SUP-19 and item 4 of this section; D30-2 (the settling record by identity, priority 0 of table SUP-G) is SUP-22; D30-3 (one start order) is SUP-19 and SUP-31; D30-4 (the origin of `_ensure_background_tasks`) is SUP-31; D30-5 (the own wait of the loop task and `startup-recovery`) is SUP-32 and **is a design choice made in r30 that the user approved in revision 31 (D31-1)**; D30-1 to D30-4 are applied as decided by the revision-30 instruction and are not user-approved (D30-4 is amended by R31-1 and the lock wording of D30-1 to D30-3 by D31-3). A row of table SUP-T is still always written with the prefix 'SUP-T' and a row of the §7.4 table as '§7.4 row N'.

- **SUP-31 Component creation: origins, the first creation and the startup mutation gate (D30-3 and D30-4; revision 30).** *Where components are created:* by `start()` in SUP-19 step 3 (origin `START`), after the lock connection, the self-test and the capability upsert, so a start that fails at the lock (`RunnerAlreadyActive`) leaves no task behind; `_recover_rest` no longer creates the components of a first generation (items 1 and 2 of this section are read that way). *The sweeper versus the startup mutation:* the components exist while the startup recovery runs, so the sweeper's first pass is **held** until the startup mutation is done: the sweeper task sets its READY event first (the entry point, SUP-20) and then awaits the per-generation event `startup_mutation_done` (a cancellable `await`), which `_finish_mutation` sets for `startup=True` at the set point of R31-4, under its common set condition (current generation, valid `STARTING`, `_start_aborting` false; D35-3) (after the raising branches, `RecoveryUnsettled` at `runner.py:792-793` included, and after the guard `:800-803`, immediately before the `_recover_rest` call `:804`; the commit is confirmed by then; the check of `_start_aborting` right before the set is behaviour that B2 adds, the current guard `:800-803` does not read the flag, so the flag alone never skips `_recover_rest` (final decision Q2-1), and the refusal below to create or register a background task while `_start_aborting` is true is unchanged). The startup requeue of **all** CLAIMED rows (`_recovery_body`, `runner.py:811-815`) therefore cannot race a sweeper pass, and, **except in the case (iv-b) of table R31-4X (revision 35, user-fixed policy)**, the event is set before the wait of `_recover_rest` for the first sweeper pass (`ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS`), so the two waits cannot deadlock (the guarantee 'the event is set before the wait' does not cover (iv-b): there the current generation is `STARTING` with `_start_aborting` true and neither setter newly sets the event; if the event is unset and the real wait is entered, the wait ends by whichever comes first, the cancellation by the settlement or the expiry of `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS`, so it is never unbounded and the aborting `start()` never publishes `RUNNING`); if the startup recovery fails the start fails and the settlement cancels the sweeper; a sweeper restarted in `RUNNING` finds the event already set. READY (SUP-20) and the boundary items B5, B6 and B10 are unchanged (READY is the entry point; B10 requires the startup recovery to be done without error). *Origins:* `_ensure_background_tasks(generation, origin)` has three. `START` (only `start()`, step 3). `RECOVERY` (the caller `_recover_rest`, which `recover(startup=False)` reaches in every iteration of `_loop`, `runner.py:937`, at most `_poll` = 0.5 s apart (a wake-up can shorten it and the tests use a long poll), `:945`): it may create a component **only** if the unit has never been created in this generation (state IDLE, no task, no waiter, the supervisor is not degraded). `RESTART` (only the restart waiter after its delay and re-check, SUP-3). **Refusals common to every origin:** `_start_aborting` is set; the lifecycle is not `STARTING` or `RUNNING`; the generation differs; the slot is occupied (**a task that is `done()` while its exit event is not yet processed still occupies the slot**; the processed event frees it); the unit is DEGRADED or `supervisor_degraded` is set, and a unit in BACKOFF is refused for `START` and `RECOVERY` and re-created only by the registered current waiter of `RESTART` (**superseded in r31:** the r30 wording 'BACKOFF (a waiter is registered) or DEGRADED refused for every origin' is replaced by table SUP-O, R31-1). So a periodic recovery creates no task during BACKOFF and a DEGRADED component stays DEGRADED across periodic recoveries (SUP-T T14, T21). *The loop task:* `_loop_task = create_task(self._loop())` stays in the `RUNNING` publication critical section (`runner.py:259`); no loop task exists in `STARTING`, and `_settle_failed_start` sets `_loop_task = None` unconditionally (`:320`). **Revision 31:** the origin verdict is table SUP-O (R31-1) and the second setter of `startup_mutation_done` is R31-4.

- **SUP-32 The loop task and `startup-recovery` have their own bounded wait (D30-5; revision 30; a design choice made in r30 and approved by the user in revision 31, D31-1).** *Why not the common deadline:* cancelling the loop task cancels the `recover(startup=False)` that it runs inside `_drive_recovery`, which delivers `CALLER_CANCEL` (`runner.py:726`) and runs the shielded `_settle_recovery`; that settlement waits up to the recovery shutdown wait (`DEFAULT_RUNNER_RECOVERY_SHUTDOWN_WAIT_SECONDS` = 5.0 s, `policies.py:87`; the `Settings` field `runner_recovery_shutdown_wait_seconds` accepts any finite value above 0, `config.py:37`, checked by `validate_recovery_timeouts`, `config.py:55-58`, `runner.py:176`) plus lock waits. `startup-recovery` runs the same recovery code. A bound of 15.0 s for them would turn a working configuration (a recovery shutdown wait of 20 s) into a permanent false `STOP_INCOMPLETE`. *The deadline:* the loop task (id `runner-loop`) and `startup-recovery` are awaited concurrently with the component set and under their **own** deadline `recovery_shutdown_wait_seconds + BACKGROUND_RECOVERY_SETTLE_MARGIN_SECONDS`; the first term is the validated copy that `Runner.__init__` keeps, the second is a new code constant of `policies.py` (default 5.0 s, fixed bounds 0.5 to 60.0, no environment variable; rows in §9.2, §9.3 and §9.4). With the defaults the own deadline is 10.0 s. The `Runner` constructor builds validated copies of both settle constants and the margin (R31-9; **superseded in r31**: the r30 text had `start()` capture them), and every settle path uses the copies (SUP-23). *Why a constant and not a relation:* a relation 'common settle deadline > recovery shutdown wait + margin' would be checked where `validate_recovery_timeouts` is called and would refuse the construction of the Runner for a runtime setting that works today, and the two deadlines bound different task sets, so no relation between them is needed; `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` stays out of B2. *Outcome:* a loop task or `startup-recovery` that has not ended at its deadline keeps its reference (`_loop_task` stays set; `clean` already requires `_loop_task is None`, `runner.py:376-377`), is listed as `runner-loop` or `startup-recovery` in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` and keeps the lifecycle `STOP_INCOMPLETE`; the reference of `startup-recovery` is dropped only after its termination is confirmed (SUP-19). *What the deadlines bound:* the common deadline bounds only the component set (the components, the restart waiters and the supervisor); neither deadline bounds the total duration of `stop()` or of a failed start, because `_drain` has its own wait of up to three times the grace (R31-8; `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` = 30.0 s, `policies.py:82`, `runner.py:472-495`), the close of the lock connection is documented as unbounded and the recovery settlement has its own bound.

**Revision 31 contract (decisions D31-1 to D31-3, approved by the user in the revision-31 instruction; amendments R31-1 to R31-12; design only: nothing here is implemented or verified).** An amendment supersedes the statements that it names; every older statement that differs is marked 'superseded in r31' where it stands, and the amendment is the implementation basis. A row of table SUP-T is still written with the prefix 'SUP-T'. Where the instruction of revision 31 and the real code differed the code was followed: the real `_dispatch` has the loop condition at `:899`, the claim transaction at `:900-905` and the call of `_launch` at `:909` (R31-2).

- **R31-1 Creation by origin (supersedes the refusal list of SUP-31, the last sentence of SUP-26, the origin sentence of SUP-3 and the D30-4 row; D30-4 amended).** **Table SUP-O** gives the verdict per origin. Every condition of the column is read in **one synchronous section** (no `await`) together with the registration, so no other task can change a condition in between. A refused creation returns a verdict and nothing else.

**Table SUP-O: creation of a component task by origin (all conditions of a column must hold; otherwise the creation is refused).**

| Condition | `START` | `RECOVERY` | `RESTART` |
|---|---|---|---|
| lifecycle | `STARTING` | `STARTING` or `RUNNING` | `RUNNING` |
| the generation equals the generation of the caller | required | required | required |
| no stop signal and `_start_aborting` is false | required | required | required |
| unit state | IDLE | IDLE | BACKOFF |
| no component task is registered (a task that is `done()` while its exit event is not processed still counts as registered) | required | required | required |
| restart waiter | none registered | none registered | the caller is the registered CURRENT waiter of the unit (the waiter identity equals the registry identity exactly), not cancelled and not stale |
| restart budget | not applicable | not applicable | remains (SUP-5) |
| unit not DEGRADED and `supervisor_degraded` false | required | required | required |

- *Registration of a RESTART* (the same synchronous section): the component task object is created first (the only step that can raise); then, with nothing that can raise left, the waiter reference is consumed (the registry entry is cleared), the task is registered and the unit state becomes RUNNING (SUP-T T13). A second RESTART of the same waiter is therefore impossible: its reference is gone and the state is no longer BACKOFF. If the creation raises, nothing was consumed: the waiter ends with that exception, which is **one** abnormal exit of the component (SUP-T T32, counted as SUP-T T15), so a failed RESTART consumes the budget **exactly once**.

- *Refusals:* a refusal is **never** an exit and consumes no budget; a waiter whose check fails deregisters (SUP-3), so there is no refusal loop and no refusal is counted twice. DEGRADED refuses **every** origin (`START`, `RECOVERY`, `RESTART`, an internal re-check and the RV-3 wake-up); only a new Runner generation recovers it (the reset rules of SUP-11). BACKOFF without a registered waiter is refused for every origin and has **no path out inside its generation** (revision 33, D33-1; the earlier 'the supervisor's own consistency check counts it once as SUP-T T15' is removed): it is only displayed as BACKOFF_ORPHANED (SUP-17, SUP-T T33) and the operator action is a new Runner generation (SUP-17). So while the supervisor is alive SUP-26 (c) is not expected to arise: a unit in BACKOFF holds its waiter until the RESTART of that same waiter consumes it, and a failed RESTART is a new exit event and not a BACKOFF unit without a waiter. After the supervisor died it legitimately arises (revision 32, M2; supersedes 'unreachable by construction'): the waiter's re-check is refused by the ordered precedence of SUP-T T14 (stale generation, lifecycle not `RUNNING`, supervisor dead, no component-level reason because an exhausted budget cannot occur in BACKOFF), the waiter deregisters, and the unit stays BACKOFF without task or waiter, shown as derived BACKOFF_ORPHANED (SUP-17) with budgets unchanged and no self-heal.

- *The `RECOVERY` origin is effectively dead code:* `start()` creates every unit with the origin `START` before the first `_recover_rest` (SUP-31), so a RECOVERY creation meets an occupied slot, a BACKOFF unit or a DEGRADED unit and is refused; it stays only as a defensive path for a unit that is IDLE and was never created in this generation (revision 32, C1: the `STARTING` entry in the RECOVERY column of table SUP-O is likewise defensive only, kept for that path and effectively never taken, so the table and this bullet say the same).

- **R31-2 Dispatch predicate (amends SUP-25).** Dispatch is blocked **only** by `supervisor_degraded`, in addition to the existing conditions (the Runner lifecycle is not `RUNNING`, a stop, the claim, lease and fencing conditions and the loss of ownership). A degraded `sweeper`, `risk-worker` or `capability` updater **never** blocks global dispatch: their DEGRADED state is exposed in the health warnings, in the diagnostics and in the component detail only, and `ready` and `blockers` stay informational (dispatch does not read them). The private Runner predicate (a name that does not start with `recover`) reads exactly this one flag. *Guard points* (`runner.py`): (1) the `while` condition at `:899`, a cheap check without database access; (2) inside the claim transaction **immediately before** `claim_next` (`:900-902`): a set flag leaves the transaction without a claim and `break`s (whether `Database.transaction()` yields to the event loop before the first statement was not verified, because the ORM session begins lazily, so this check costs nothing and closes the window only if there is a yield; the test injects the flip); (3) after the claim transaction **commits** and **before** `_launch` (`:909`): the commit awaits, so the flag can flip between (2) and (3); a set flag `break`s (not `continue`: `continue` would also leave exactly one CLAIMED row because guard (1) is evaluated again, SUP-25, revision 32, W3; guard (2) is effective only when the transaction yields), the claimed row stays `CLAIMED` without a lease (the retention rule of R31-3) and `_dispatch` returns the number started. *No third check before the CLI spawn:* `_launch` (`:913-917`) has no `await`: it creates the request task and registers the in-flight entry in one synchronous step, and the spawn happens later inside `process()` in that task; the request is admitted at (3), so the post-claim check is the last point of admission. A flip after (3) admits **at most that one request**, the one already admitted at (3): the next evaluation of guard point (1) reads the flag and ends the loop, so one flip never admits more than one request (revision 33, D33-15, F11; the earlier wording 'at most the free slots, one claim per iteration' is removed). *In-flight work:* a task that already runs continues; the death of the supervisor **never** cancels a running task and `stop()` settles it (SUP-6, SUP-10). The next iteration of `_loop` evaluates the guard again, and recovery (`recover(startup=False)`) keeps running while the flag is set.

- **R31-3 Retention of a claim and the floor of the risk backoff (decision D31-2, approved in revision 31; the single statement of the CLAIMED-retention rule, referenced by SUP-25, §9.4 and §13.1).** (a) `PROCESS_RISK_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS` and `PROCESS_RISK_BACKOFF_CAP_SECONDS` have the fixed positive floor of `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (§9.2, §9.3). (b) **CLAIMED-retention rule:** when the termination of a process is not confirmed, or when a settlement is incomplete, the execution or request stays `CLAIMED`; a timeout, a cancellation or a failed observation **alone never** releases a claim; there is no automatic re-run; the next state follows only a termination proof or an explicit recovery decision. A claimed row that was not launched (R31-2) stays `CLAIMED` until the existing stale-claim recovery, which is the explicit recovery decision (no process was started, so there is nothing to prove), requeues it after `claim_timeout_seconds` (default 300, `config.py:20`); this adds no database write and the delay of up to that grace is the stated and approved cost.

- **R31-4 `startup_mutation_done` (amends SUP-31; the first sweeper pass of a generation).** The per-generation event has exactly two setters, and each has its own set condition (revision 34, A1). **One common set condition (revision 35, D35-3; a decision of the user's revision-35 instruction):** `_finish_mutation` and the startup-recovery wrapper set the event **only** when (a) the generation is the current generation, (b) the lifecycle is a valid `STARTING` and (c) `_start_aborting` is false; the marker `rest_skipped` alone never decides whether the event is set; an event that was already set before a failure of `_recover_rest` stays set; and a start is judged successful only at the existing success boundary of SUP-21. The checks (b) and (c) are **behaviour that B2 adds** at the set statement, immediately before the set; the current behaviour is only the guard `runner.py:800-803`, which admits `STARTING` and `RUNNING` and does **not** read `_start_aborting`, so today the flag neither skips `_recover_rest` nor writes `rest_skipped`, and B2 keeps it so (final decision Q2-1, option A). **With the current generation, `STARTING` and `_start_aborting` true, neither setter newly sets the event and an already-set value is kept; the flag alone never skips `_recover_rest` and never writes `rest_skipped`; what runs afterwards is decided by the existing generation and lifecycle guards and by the real cancellation of the settlement (SUP-19 steps 6 to 9), not by the flag.** The refusal of SUP-31 to create or register a new background task while `_start_aborting` is true stays. **Setter 1:** `_finish_mutation` sets the event of the generation `ctx.generation` after it has passed the common set condition above and **all** guards of the set point below (the branch that raises `RecoveryUnsettled` for an unreleased connection, `runner.py:792-793`, and the generation and lifecycle guard, `:800-803`), immediately before it calls `return await self._recover_rest(summary)` (`:804`) (SUP-31, `runner.py:784-804`). **Setter 2:** the startup-recovery wrapper (the task `startup-recovery` of SUP-19 step 4) sets the same event idempotently when `self.recover(startup=True)` **returns normally** for that generation, which includes a normal return of a test double that replaces `recover` (a **test-double case**: a real `recover(startup=True)` never returns early and normally, `runner.py:630`; of the existing monkeypatches in `tests/integration_pg/test_runner_lifecycle.py`, `:343` wraps the real `recover` and calls it, and `:377`, `:526` and `:831` raise; a double that returns early and normally does not exist yet and is a **new test of this plan**); the wrapper writes only the event of its own generation, only under the common set condition (that generation is the current one, the lifecycle is `STARTING` and `_start_aborting` is false). **This event alone never decides whether a start succeeded,** and once it is set for a generation it is **never reset** by a later failure. The marker `rest_skipped` (written at `runner.py:802`) is **never a sole judging condition**: neither setter reads it, and both setters decide by the common set condition (table R31-4X, note A34-1). **Set point of `_finish_mutation` (revision 33, D33-4; verified against `runner.py`):** the event is set **after** the branch that raises `RecoveryUnsettled` for an unreleased connection (`:792-793`; the earlier raising branches are `:786-791` and the rollback `RuntimeError` at `:794-795`) **and after** the generation and lifecycle guard (`:800-803`), **immediately before** the call `return await self._recover_rest(summary)` (`:804`). It is **never** set after a failure of the mutation, a cancellation or a change of generation, and a holder of an older generation never sets the event of the current one. **Three cases are distinguished (ordering, revision 32, C4, restated):** (1) **a failure before the guard** (`UNCERTAIN`, a failure before commit, an unreleased connection, a rollback after a cancellation, or the guard of `:800-803` that skips `_recover_rest` because the generation or the lifecycle changed): the event is **not** set; **sub-case (1b, option A of final decision Q2-1):** with the current generation, `STARTING` and `_start_aborting` true the guard of `:800-803` is passed, the check that B2 adds right before the set finds the flag and the event is not newly set, and `_recover_rest` is **not** skipped by the flag (it is still called, and what runs afterwards is decided by the existing generation and lifecycle guards and by the real cancellation of the settlement, SUP-19 steps 6 to 9); an event set earlier stays set; **if the event is unset and `_recover_rest` has entered its real wait for the first sweeper pass, that wait ends by whichever happens first, the cancellation by the settlement or the expiry of `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS` (user-fixed policy; SUP-31 excludes (iv-b) from 'the event is set before the wait'); it is never unbounded and the aborting `start()` never publishes `RUNNING`;** (2) **the event is set and then `_recover_rest` fails:** the event stays set, the start fails and takes the settlement path of SUP-T T24, and the sweeper that the event released may be cancelled in the middle of its pass with the reason `FAILED_START`; this is bounded and harmless, because that sweeper is settled under the common deadline and consumes no budget; (3) **a normal start:** the event is set and `_recover_rest` returns. **A start is never judged successful by the event alone:** it is set before `_recover_rest` and in case (2) it is set in a failed start; only the success boundary of SUP-21 (B1 to B10, in particular B10) decides. Before it is set **no sweeper mutation pass runs** (the sweeper waits after its READY event, SUP-31). A failed start settles a held sweeper with the recorded reason `FAILED_START`, which is **not** a component failure and consumes no budget (SUP-2 (a)). **The five cases of table R31-4X (revision 34, A2) refine these three:** (i) is the failure part of case (1), (iv) is its guard part, (ii) is case (2), (iii) is the wrapper path of case (3) and (v) is the edge in which the event is already set. **Note A34-1 (the conflict is resolved by the user's revision-35 decision D35-3):** revision 33 stated that a return carrying `rest_skipped` never sets the event; the revision-34 instruction stated that the wrapper sets the event on every normal return of `recover(startup=True)` for its generation and that `rest_skipped` is never a sole judging condition; the two statements collided for the one return that is normal and carries `rest_skipped` for the **same** generation (the lifecycle left `STARTING` while the startup recovery finished its commit, `:800-803`; reachable only in the B2 design, in which the startup recovery is its own task). **The user's revision-35 instruction decides it:** both setters set the event only under the common set condition (current generation, valid `STARTING`, `_start_aborting` false); `rest_skipped` alone never decides; so a same-generation return with `_start_aborting` true sets nothing new and is not skipped by the flag, an event already set stays set (it is never reset) and the start is judged only at the success boundary of SUP-21. The conflict is closed, and the rule is a decision of the user and not an authoring choice. Statements that the first pass of a new generation starts 'at once' or 'immediately' (CI-6, RV-1, §7.4 row 31, SUP-11) mean: after `startup_mutation_done`.

**Table R31-4X: the five cases of `startup_mutation_done` (revision 34, A2; the reachable paths are read from `runner.py`, nothing was run).**

| Case | Real reachable path (read from `runner.py`) | Setter | Event at the end | Start success |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (i) a failure before the set guard, and the wrapper did not return normally | `_finish_mutation` raises before the set point: `UNCERTAIN` (`:786-787`), a failure before commit (`:788-791`), an unreleased connection (`:792-793`, `RecoveryUnsettled`) or a rollback after a cancellation (`:794-795`); `recover(startup=True)` then raises and does not return | none: the guard was not passed and the wrapper has nothing to set | not set | no: the start fails and takes SUP-T T24 |
| (ii) the set point was passed, then `_recover_rest` fails | `_finish_mutation` has passed `:792-793` and `:800-803` and called `_recover_rest` (`:804`, defined at `:842`), and that call raises | `_finish_mutation` (setter 1), immediately before `:804` | set, and it stays set (never reset) | no: the start fails and takes SUP-T T24; the sweeper that the event released is settled with `FAILED_START` (SUP-31), no budget |
| (iii) a valid startup recovery returns early and normally, so no set point of `_finish_mutation` is reached | not reachable in the real `recover(startup=True)` today (a registered recovery makes a startup call raise `RuntimeError`, `runner.py:630`; every real return of a mutation goes through `_finish_mutation`); a **test-double case**: reachable only with a double that replaces `recover` and returns early and normally; no existing test does that (in `tests/integration_pg/test_runner_lifecycle.py`, `:343` wraps the real `recover` and calls it, and `:377`, `:526` and `:831` raise), so it is a **new test of this plan** | the wrapper (setter 2), idempotently and only under the common set condition (D35-3); on the normal path of case (3) setter 1 has already set the event and the wrapper's set changes nothing | set | not by the event: yes only when every item B1 to B10 of SUP-21 holds |
| (iv) the event is not newly set although the mutation did not fail: **(iv-a)** `rest_skipped`, the marker of a return that skipped `_recover_rest` because the generation changed (`ctx.generation != self._generation`) or the lifecycle left `STARTING` and `RUNNING` (`:800-803`); it cannot write the event of the current generation; **(iv-b)** the current generation, lifecycle `STARTING` and `_start_aborting` true (option A of final decision Q2-1; the flag is not `rest_skipped` and does not skip `_recover_rest`) | **(iv-a)** the guard at `:800-803` returns the summary with `rest_skipped` (`:802`) **before** the set point; for the same generation it is reached when the failed-start settlement ends the lifecycle while the startup recovery finishes its commit (SUP-19 steps 6 to 9; possible only in the B2 design with its own startup-recovery task, not in today's inline `start()`); for a previous generation it is reached by a periodic recovery that `stop()` overtook (`stop()` raises the generation, `runner.py:346-347`); no existing test sets or asserts `rest_skipped` (read-only search of `tests/`); **(iv-b)** the guard `:800-803` is passed because it does not read `_start_aborting` (current behaviour); the check that B2 adds immediately before the set finds the flag and the event is not newly set, and `_recover_rest` (`:804`) is still called: the flag alone never skips `_recover_rest` and never writes `rest_skipped`, and the existing generation and lifecycle guards and the real cancellation of the settlement decide what runs afterwards; **(iv-b) wait (user-fixed policy):** the guarantee of SUP-31 'the event is set before the wait' excludes this case, and with the event unset and the real wait of `_recover_rest` entered the wait ends by whichever happens first, the cancellation by the settlement or the expiry of `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS`, never unbounded | **(iv-a)** none: setter 1 is not reached, and setter 2 does not set unless the common set condition holds (the generation is current, the lifecycle is `STARTING` and `_start_aborting` is false; resolved by D35-3, note A34-1); **(iv-b)** setter 1 reaches the added check and sets nothing, and setter 2 sets nothing because the common set condition fails on `_start_aborting` | the event of the current generation is unchanged: a return of a previous generation never sets it, and an aborting start (iv-b) newly sets nothing (an unset event stays unset and an already-set event stays set) | no: an aborting start fails (SUP-T T24); - **R31-5 `CancelReason` and the preserved start error (replaces 'no new reason; SHUTDOWN' in SUP-19; amends SUP-19 step 10 and SUP-24).** *Facts of the code:* cancelling the startup-recovery task makes `_drive_recovery` record `CALLER_CANCEL` (`runner.py:719-726`); `_settle_recovery` sets `ctx.reason` only while it is `NONE` (`:754`), so the later `_settle_recovery_for_stop` (`:773`, `SHUTDOWN`) never overwrites a recorded reason; no precedence rule between reasons exists in the code, the **first recorded reason stays**. *Reasons by cause:* the caller cancels `start()`: `CALLER_CANCEL`; a normal `stop()`: `SHUTDOWN`; the internal cleanup of a failed start that is not a caller cancellation: `SHUTDOWN` through `_settle_failed_start` (`:305`); an already recorded reason is never overwritten. *The raised error:* the original startup error stays the raised error and the **same exception object is re-raised**, as `_fail_start` does today (`runner.py:265-294`); information about components that did not settle is attached as a structured note on it (`add_note`) and, only where `_fail_start` already links causes (a cancellation that arrives while cleaning up), through `__cause__`; the cleanup error **never replaces** the raised error and no `BaseExceptionGroup` is built unconditionally. Only an **unexpected** result of a child task (not a caller cancellation and not the original startup exception) is converted to the stated `RuntimeError`; the existing test `test_an_original_start_cancellation_stays_final_and_extra_cancels_are_only_noted` (about `:464`), which injects a bare `CancelledError` and asserts `info.value is original`, keeps passing.

- **R31-6 `STARTING` with `_start_aborting`: one rule per branch and the lock-free marker (decision D31-3, approved in revision 31; supersedes the lock wording of D29-3 and the transition cells SUP-T T9, T10 and T27 to T30 for `STARTING`).** **Table SUP-X** gives exactly one rule per branch; every combination of the enumerated inputs (the lifecycles `STARTING`, `STOPPING` and `STOP_INCOMPLETE`, the marker, the generation kind and whether a settling record holds the identity; revision 33, D33-2: the claim is scoped to these inputs, and the lifecycles `STOPPED` and `RUNNING` are cells of table SUP-G priorities 1 to 3, not branches of this table) falls in one branch, and the branch is the consequence of the priority of table SUP-G that decides first (branch 2: priority 0, or priority 1 for a record identity; branch 1: priority 2; branches 4 and 5: priority 1; branch 3: priority 3), so no two branches apply to one cell; SUP-T T10, T29 and T30 **never** apply to `STARTING` (that lifecycle becomes `STOP_INCOMPLETE` only through the final transition of `_settle_failed_start`, `runner.py:318-327`), and a restart waiter exists only while the lifecycle is `RUNNING`, so 'a waiter in `STARTING`' is unreachable (table SUP-E) and priority 0 of table SUP-G never gives SUP-T T28 or T30 for a waiter. The guard 'the stop signal is set' of SUP-T T9 and T27 means for `STARTING`: `_start_aborting` is true for the event's own generation, and for `STOPPING`: the stop request.

**Table SUP-X: the five branches (the state change never concerns the lifecycle except where a cell says so).**

| Branch | Lifecycle, marker, generation kind | Rule | State change | Reference removal | Budget and restart | `STOP_INCOMPLETE` condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `STARTING`, `_start_aborting` false, current generation | SUP-T T6, T7, T36 | none by the supervisor; the first failure goes to `start_failed` | not before the settlement | no budget, no restart (SUP-4) | none; only `start()` settles |
| 2 | `STARTING`, `_start_aborting` true, current generation, identity in the settling record or not (table SUP-G priority 0 and 1; priority 0 alone covers an identity that is not in the record, revision 32, C3) | SUP-T T9, T17, T27 | none; an audit record | only after the identity is confirmed ended | no budget, no restart | only the final transition of `_settle_failed_start`, when an identity is unsettled |
| 3 | `STARTING`, unrelated stale generation | SUP-T T34 | none | not allowed | no budget, no restart | none |
| 4 | `STOPPING`, identity in a settling record (a current-generation event without a record is SUP-G priority 3, revision 32, C3) | SUP-T T9, T17, T27, T28 | none; the result is recorded | after confirmed termination | no budget, no restart | an identity is unsettled at the end of `stop()` |
| 5 | `STOP_INCOMPLETE`, identity in a settling record (also when `_start_aborting` was left true, revision 32, C2 and C3) | SUP-T T10, T17, T29, T30 | none; a repeated `stop()` settles | after confirmed termination | no budget, no restart | stays until a repeated `stop()` has settled every identity |

- *The marker without a lock (D31-3):* `_start_aborting` is set **without** the lifecycle lock under all of these conditions: there is a single asyncio event loop; it is set to true in a synchronous section without `await`; it is set as the **first action** of the cancellation cleanup and **before** any other startup task is cancelled or awaited; it is owned by a per-generation `StartContext` (or an equivalent object) that is never shared with another generation; it is never mutated from another thread or another event loop; the `RUNNING` success boundary re-checks the value of the **same generation** under the lifecycle lock (SUP-21). If any implementation path breaks one of these conditions the design reverts to a marker that is guarded by the lifecycle lock. `_start_aborting`, `start_failed`, `startup_mutation_done` and the startup registry belong to this per-generation context.

- **R31-7 The startup registry at the success boundary.** At the success boundary (B10) and after it the completed startup-only entries are dropped: the startup-recovery task, the READY waits, the startup helper tasks, the consumed `start_failed` Future and the temporary waiters; the component and supervisor tasks stay in the component registry. `stop()` also prunes entries that are done. So `stop()` followed by `start()` on the same object is not refused with 'STOPPED but still holds resources' (`runner.py:243-245`); after a failed start only the unsettled references stay, and a start is allowed once they have settled.

- **R31-8 The two settle deadlines and the phases of `stop()` (decision D31-1, approved in revision 31; supersedes the 'not user-approved' wording of SUP-32 and D30-5, and the wording of D29-1 that puts every startup task under the common deadline).** `BACKGROUND_RECOVERY_SETTLE_MARGIN_SECONDS` (`policies.py`; a finite positive code constant, no environment variable, default 5.0, bounds 0.5 to 60.0; the code facts require no other value) is **approved**. *Recovery deadline:* `runner_recovery_shutdown_wait_seconds` (the validated copy that `Runner.__init__` keeps) plus the margin, **one** common deadline for the whole recovery settlement phase and never one per recovery task: 5.0 + 5.0 = 10.0 s with the defaults. *Component deadline:* `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, default 15.0 s. *Partition (each id belongs to exactly one deadline):* the recovery deadline covers `runner-loop` (the loop task), `startup-recovery` (the startup-recovery task) and the recovery operation task that either of them drives; the component deadline covers every other id of the settle set: `sweeper`, `risk-worker`, `capability`, every `<id>:restart-waiter`, `supervisor` and the remaining startup helper tasks (the READY waits). Both deadlines start at the same moment and run concurrently, so both phases together take at most the larger one, 15.0 s with the defaults. *Not covered by `recovery_shutdown_wait`:* a cancellation delivered inside `_recover_rest` (the awaits of `reconcile` and `_cancel_idle_tasks`, `runner.py:842-848`, which run in the task of the caller and not in the recovery operation task): `_drive_recovery` has already returned, so the wait does not apply there; only the recovery deadline bounds the **wait of the Runner**, and a task that has not ended by then is listed (`runner-loop` or `startup-recovery`) and keeps `STOP_INCOMPLETE`. *Maximum wait of each phase of `stop()` with the defaults:* (1) the settle phase of the two deadlines, 15.0 s; (2) `_settle_recovery_for_stop` (`runner.py:764-782`): one `_settle_recovery` for a live recovery (the call at `:773`, up to the recovery shutdown wait of 5.0 s) plus up to two attempts of the loop at `:776-782`, each a `_drive_recovery` of at most the recovery operation timeout plus the shutdown wait (20.0 + 5.0 = 25.0 s with the defaults), that is 5.0 + 2 x 25.0 = 55.0 s, **a conservative upper bound for these settings and for this phase only, not a guarantee for `stop()` as a whole**, plus waits for the lifecycle lock (acquisitions in `_register_recovery`, `runner.py:622`, in `_drive_recovery`, `:723`, and in `_settle_recovery`, `:752` and `:760`; these waits are in no sum of this document). *Derivation of about 50 s along the path on which a `RecoveryTimeout` leaves `_settle_recovery_for_stop` (revision 33, D33-6; premises: the defaults 20.0 s and 5.0 s, no cancellation of the caller, no wait for the lifecycle lock, the reaping steps take no time):* a `RecoveryTimeout` raised by `_drive_recovery` propagates out of the loop at `:782` at once, so the second attempt runs only if the first one **returned**, and a first attempt that returns has ended inside the operation timeout, that is in less than 20.0 s; the longest such path is 5.0 s (the live recovery settled at `:773`) + just under 20.0 s (a first attempt that returns with evidence still unsettled) + 25.0 s (the second attempt: 20.0 s of waiting, one cancel, 5.0 s of shutdown wait, then the `RecoveryTimeout`) = about 50 s, and the finite phases then add up to 15.0 + 50 + 90 = about 155 s; the 55.0 s and 160.0 s of this paragraph are the conservative bounds above these figures; (3) `_drain`, up to three `asyncio.wait` calls of the shutdown grace each (`runner.py:478`, `:485`, `:490`; `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` = 30.0 s), that is up to 90.0 s, so 'grace-bounded' means up to three times the grace; (4) the close of the lock connection (`_release_lock_connection`), which is **unbounded**; when this close is the only failure, `stop()` re-raises the original close exception (no `RunnerStopIncomplete` is built for an empty failure set), keeps the connection reference and the lifecycle `STOP_INCOMPLETE`, and the next `stop()` retries (SUP-24; revision 35, D35-4). The bounded phases add up to 15.0 + 55.0 + 90.0 = 160.0 s with the defaults (a conservative upper bound for these settings and these phases; about 155 s along the path derived above), plus the lifecycle-lock waits (revision 32 correction: revision 31 counted phase (2) as 5.0 s and gave 110.0 s, which was wrong). Because phase (4) is unbounded, **`stop()` and a failed start as a whole are not bounded**, and this document never claims that they are.

- **R31-9 One validation entry for the constant snapshots (supersedes every statement that `start()` captures or validates the settle, margin, READY, restart or interval constants: SUP-23, SUP-28, SUP-32 and the rows of §9.3 and §9.4).** The **owner is the `Runner` constructor**, which calls one explicit policy factory of `app/validation` (a private function; it holds no second copy of any rule) right after the existing `validate_recovery_timeouts(...)` call (`runner.py:176`). The factory validates and builds the **immutable snapshots**: the settle timeout, the recovery settle margin together with the validated copy of `recovery_shutdown_wait_seconds`, the READY timeout, the restart, backoff, stability and window constants, `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (as a construction copy: its membership of the pass snapshot is unaffected, by the decision rule of the §9.3 vocabulary paragraph) and the tracked-age live sum; for the sweeper pass inputs (the members defined by §9.3, SUP-28) the factory **validates** the inputs at construction, so that an invalid one is refused, but it builds no pass snapshot: the sweeper captures and validates the values that pass will use at the entry of every pass (SUP-28); the factory also calls the other validators of the linked set (`validate_process_input_constants()` and `validate_process_risk_limits()`), so every validator of §9.3 and §9.4 refuses at construction. `Runner.start()` **only consumes** the construction snapshots and applies the same verdict rule of SUP-28 to the sweeper pass inputs as they are at the time of its call, as `_recheck_sweeper_configuration` does (SUP-30), so a refusal at construction happens **before** the entry critical section of `start()` (`runner.py:240-248`) and a refused configuration changes no lifecycle; a Runner that a test constructs directly, without `create_app()`, takes the same path. `create_app()` keeps calling `validate_process_timing_limits()` early, as a **thin wrapper of the same factory function** and not as a second validator: it only makes the refusal appear at the construction of the application. `validate_recovery_timeouts` stays what it is today (`validators.py:21-33`, called by `Settings` and by the constructor) and is not extended: it checks the three recovery values (finite, positive, statement below operation, millisecond range; a bool is accepted, `None` and a string raise `TypeError`, `10**400` raises `OverflowError`), and the factory only copies the validated shutdown wait. The tables of §9.2, §9.3 and §9.4, the judgement rows and the tests say 'refused at construction' for this verdict (the vocabulary of §9.3); the verdict itself is unchanged. **Three notions are kept apart (revision 35, final decision Q2-2):** membership of the pass snapshot is §9.3 alone; the validation rule is one verdict rule (SUP-28) applied by the factory at construction, by the sweeper at every pass entry and by `start()` and SUP-30 at each call; the snapshot lifetime is the life of the `Runner` for the construction copies and one pass for the pass snapshot; no hot-reload path exists.

- **R31-10 Numeric verdicts and the configuration-invalid side effects (amends §9.2, §9.3 and §9.4; the §7.4 rows 22, 23, 28 and 30 and CI-1 to CI-3 state the rules of (f) directly in their own cells and do not rely on this item; wording of these places that differs is superseded in r31).** (a) `BACKGROUND_DB_CONCURRENCY` has the fixed code-policy upper bound **8** (an integer from 1 to 8, not a bool): only the three components of `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_IDS` share the semaphore, so no value above 3 limits anything, 8 is compared with the pool sizes below (revision 33, D33-9; `effective_db_pool_size` is `db_pool_size` when set and otherwise `4 * max_concurrent_tasks + 6`, `config.py:44-45`): **14** for the `Settings` default `max_concurrent_tasks` = 2 (`config.py:22`; 4 x 2 + 6; premise: `DB_POOL_SIZE` unset), **10** for a `Runner` built directly with the default `DEFAULT_MAX_CONCURRENT_TASKS` = 1 (`policies.py:80`; 4 x 1 + 6; premise: the engine was sized with that value, the `Runner` does not size the pool itself), and the **minimum pool 2** that `config.py:49` allows (pool plus overflow below 2 is refused; premise of §9.1 item 7: the advisory-lock connection occupies one of them); 8 is below 14 and 10 but **exceeds the minimum pool of 2**, so this table claims **no real concurrent checkout of 8 connections**: the bound only limits the accepted value, at most three components use the semaphore at once, and with a small pool the waiting is bounded by `pool_timeout` (§9.1 item 7), and `10**400` is refused consistently. (b) `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS` has the fixed finite upper bound 86400.0 (the ceiling of the sweeper intervals; a pass longer than a day is not a pass), so `1e300` and 86400.5 are refused consistently and its label is 'code-policy upper bound'. (c) *One verdict per consumer of `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS`:* the sweeper snapshot (debounce and retry delays) validates it at each pass entry and an invalid value is `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`; the supervisor copy (restart base and cap), the risk worker (idle interval and backoff) and the capability refresh use the copy built at construction (R31-9), where an invalid value is refused; a copy that is unusable when the supervisor reads it can arise only through a corrupted copy and degrades that component (SUP-6 (iii)), which is the only way SUP-T T16 is reached. (d) *Restart constants:* the supervisor uses the copy built at construction and never reads the module constants again (the wording 'read again by the supervisor when it uses it' is **superseded in r31**). (e) `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` is **not** a snapshot constant: it is the wait of the failure path itself, so every value other than exactly 86400.0, a usable number such as 86400.5 included, is the abnormal exit of row 28 and never `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`; when the ceiling `ORPHAN_SWEEP_MAX_INTERVAL_SECONDS` is changed alone, the verdict follows the changed constant: the fallback relation fails. (f) *Side effects of the rows 22, 23, 28 and 30 (a design choice of r31, not user-approved):* four fields are distinguished in the text, in the snapshots and in §14.2: the ordinary latest failure code (`last_failure_code`), the original failure code that triggered the configuration-invalid state (`config_invalid_trigger_failure_code`), the public representative code and the current validation result (`config_currently_valid`); a repeated detection keeps the stored trigger code: it takes the code of the record only when that code is not `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` and otherwise keeps the stored one, so `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` itself is never taken as the trigger; every detection computes `now + ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` **first**, before any mutation, so a corrupted fallback together with a failing snapshot ends in the abnormal exit of row 28 with the record and the count unchanged; a **valid** fallback whose sum overflows the datetime range stores `datetime.max` in UTC and writes the record as usual (revision 35, D35-4; §7.4 item (7)); the pass count rises exactly once for a failed pass and the `config_invalid_*` context is replaced in one step as before (row 30).

- **R31-11 Capability and self-test order (amends §6.2 'Persistence and write order', item 3 (c) of this section and SUP-19 (2)).** After the lock the canonical order of `start()` is: (1) the advisory lock; (2) the `UNKNOWN` upsert of the capability row of the current incarnation; (3) the self-test; (4) the result upsert (`SUPPORTED` or `UNAVAILABLE` with the reason code); (5) only then the READY and success candidate, that is the creation of the components (SUP-19 step 3). It is written everywhere as 'UNKNOWN upsert, self-test, result upsert'. A failure of the `UNKNOWN` upsert fails the start closed (`_settle_failed_start`, an empty registry); a failing self-test stores the state that §6.2 defines for it (`UNAVAILABLE` on Windows) and does not by itself fail the start; a failed result upsert leaves `UNKNOWN` and follows the refresh rule of §6.2 (a failed write is retried on the next tick); a row of a stale incarnation is never trusted (the trust rule of §6.2 and the `incarnation_id` condition of the upsert).

- **R31-12 Test doubles of the Runner lifecycle tests (§14 plan).** In `tests/integration_pg/test_runner_lifecycle.py` the `ProxyDb` (`:160`) offers only `engine.connect()` and `transaction()`, and its `ConnProxy` (`:120`) has `execution_options`, `execute` and `close` but no `closed`, `invalidated` or `scalar`. The new code of `start()` (the self-test, the capability upsert and the boundary item B8) therefore uses only `db.transaction()`, `_lock_conn.execute` and `getattr(conn, 'closed', False)`; production code gets **no** test-only branch; the minimal surface that the doubles need is added to the doubles themselves and no existing lifecycle test is weakened. The tests that monkeypatch `r.recover` (R31-4) and the wrapper `count_rest` (`test_runner_recovery_bounded.py:156-164`, which patches `r._recover_rest`) keep working because the startup-recovery task calls `self.recover(startup=True)` through the instance attribute.

### 9.2 Timing constants: inventory, relations and validation (W-3)

All values live in `app/validation/policies.py`. The existing constants that this section reuses directly are `PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS` (`policies.py:93`) and `MAX_PG_TIMEOUT_MS` (`policies.py:89`), which have rows in the table of this section, and `MAX_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (`policies.py:65`), and `PROOF_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (`policies.py:70`), which have no row of their own here (the first of them appears in the relation of `TRACKED_EXECUTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`); `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` (`policies.py:82`) and `DEFAULT_RUNNER_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (`policies.py:86`) take part in no B2 relation and are therefore not constants of this design (revision 28, decision D28-5; §9.4 'Existing external settings'); the list of every constant with owner, type and validator is §9.4, which also lists `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MAX_LENGTH` (`policies.py:28`), `TRACKED_ONLY_KEYS` and the canonical SQL constants of §7.4; **every default of this table that is not marked 'existing' is a design default proposed here and not verified on any real host** (conservative values chosen so that the stated relations hold). "Real-OS verified" is **no** for every row: the only OS observations are the probes of §2.1. A second central validator, `validate_process_timing_limits()` (`validators.py`; since r31 the thin wrapper of the one policy factory that the Runner constructor calls, R31-9, and that `create_app()` calls early; refused on any violation), enforces every relation of the table that is marked "yes"; `validate_process_risk_limits()` keeps the rules (i)–(vii) of §7.5 item 5 and the recheck rule of item 8; the non-timing constants have their own validator in §9.3. The constants of `validate_process_timing_limits()` include the constants of r30 (`BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_RECOVERY_SETTLE_MARGIN_SECONDS`) besides the restart, stability and window constants.

**Relation to the recovery operation timeout (W-c, settled from code).** `_recover_rest` runs **after** the recovery operation and outside it: `Runner._recover` drives the operation with `_drive_recovery`, which waits for the operation task for at most `recovery_timeout_seconds` (`DEFAULT_RUNNER_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` = 20, `policies.py:86`; `runner.py:719`) and returns; only then does `_recover` call `_finish_mutation` (`runner.py:534-536`), whose last statement is today `_recover_rest(summary)` (`runner.py:804`; B2 passes `generation` and `startup` too, §9.1 item 1), documented as running outside the lifecycle lock (`runner.py:842-844`). So the sweeper's startup wait, the process-risk worker and the capability task are **not** inside the recovery operation timeout, there is **no containment relation** between `DEFAULT_RUNNER_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and any constant of this table (the 10 s startup wait is not a part of the 20 s), and `validate_process_timing_limits()` contains no rule that relates them. Each background task is bounded by its own timeout, pass budget or claim timeout (sweeper: `ORPHAN_SWEEP_PASS_SECONDS`; worker: the row, request, pass and claim timeouts of §7.5 item 5; capability: `CAPABILITY_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`). The only overall-time statement concerns the Runner lifecycle and is separate: `start()` has no single overall timeout in the code today (`runner.py:237-263`) and awaits `recover(startup=True)`; with B2 the start is bounded piece by piece: the READY phase by `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (5.0 s, all deadlines concurrent), the startup recovery by the recovery operation (at most 20 s plus its shutdown wait) followed by `_recover_rest`, which B2 extends by at most `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS`, and a failed start by the settle deadlines (`BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` for the component set, the own deadline of §9.1 SUP-32 for `startup-recovery`); no sum of these is stated as a bound; `stop()` settles the component tasks, the restart waiters and the supervisor inside `_shutdown_resources` (`runner.py:393`) under the common deadline and the loop task under the own deadline of SUP-32, shielded, and reports a task that did not settle in `RunnerStopIncomplete.components` (§9.1 item 5).

**Derivation of the tracked-age threshold and the lease TTL (revision 29, decision D29-4; supersedes 'Derivation of the lease TTL relation' of revision 28).** **The revision-28 relation is withdrawn.** The claim that `lease_ttl_seconds` > `TRACKED_IDENTITY_PERSIST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (10 s) is a B2 safety condition, with 11 as the smallest accepted value, was **not approved and does not hold**: every statement that `ttl > 10` guarantees safety is removed, and B2 adds **no** new `lease_ttl_seconds` validation. *Read from code:* `LeaseService.start_heartbeat` sleeps `max(ttl / 3, 0.05)` seconds between two beats (`lease_service.py:158-161`); `heartbeat()` renews the lease only while it has not expired (`lease_expires_at > now`, `task_repository.py:71-79`) and `verify()` renews it the same way (`lease_service.py:138-143`); a beat that **raises** sets `alive` to false and calls `on_lost` immediately (`:163-168`), so the revision-28 sentence 'survives the loss of two consecutive beats' is **superseded in r29**: only a *late* beat is tolerated, a failed beat is not. Worst remaining lease: a lease that was renewed at time t lasts until t + T and the next beat is due at t + T/3, so just before a beat the remaining time is 2T/3; with T = 11 that is about 7.3 s, which is **less** than the 10 s that the relation was meant to protect, so the relation does not even cover a 10 s stall (T = 16 would give 2T/3 of about 10.7 s). A safe bound would depend on the stall length that B2 does not bound, so B2 does not narrow the accepted range without a separate safety proof. **As a plain fact of today:** `LeaseService.ttl` is the `int` of `Settings.lease_ttl_seconds` (`config.py:19`, `container.py:93`), which no validator checks, so any `int` (5, 0, a negative value, a huge value) is accepted and starts the application; this is unchanged by B2. The identity write of `on_started` is protected by its fence (§5.1 step 5), not by the TTL. No test at 9, 10 and 11 exists any more; a test 'no narrowing: the existing accepted range is unchanged' replaces it (§13). **Tracked-age threshold (re-derived).** `TRACKED_EXECUTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS` is the age after which an open tracked row is no longer 'normal running'. A normal execution ends at the latest after the command timeout (`MAX_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` 3600 s, `policies.py:65`), the bounded identity persistence (`TRACKED_IDENTITY_PERSIST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` 10 s), the kill grace (`PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS` 5 s, `policies.py:93`), the bounded drain (`PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS` 5 s) and the tree settle poll (`TREE_SETTLE_POLL_SECONDS` 1 s): 3600 + 10 + 5 + 5 + 1 = **3621 s**; the default **3660 s** is 3600 plus a fixed margin of 60 s, so it is 39 s above that computed bound (the margin covers scheduling and the closing write). The lease TTL is not part of it (a heartbeat keeps the lease alive as long as the run lives). **Where the code differs from the revision-29 instruction:** the instruction said that the executor slot wait is not part of the age because the `STARTING` row is written before the run; the code shows the opposite order for the agent-CLI path: the row is inserted first (`step_runner.py:151`, `_record_start` at `:198`) and the slot is acquired later inside the executor (`_acquire_slot`, `app/infra/command_executor.py:82-114`, called at `:143`), so a slot wait **is** inside the open age and is **not** bounded by B2 and not included in 3621. **Error direction:** a margin that is too small or an unbounded slot wait can only produce a **conservative false WARN** (`EXECUTION_TOO_OLD`), never a loss of safety. The relation is `TRACKED_EXECUTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS` >= the live sum `MAX_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` + `TRACKED_IDENTITY_PERSIST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` + `PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS` + `PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS` + `TREE_SETTLE_POLL_SECONDS` (3621 with the defaults), checked by `validate_process_timing_limits()` at construction from the live constants (revision 30, C14: the literal 3621 is not checked), so the live sum is a lower bound of the age and the age has no upper bound: `MAX_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `TRACKED_IDENTITY_PERSIST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS` get no upper bound from this relation (transitively unbounded), `PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS` and `TREE_SETTLE_POLL_SECONDS` are bounded by the settle relation of §9.2, and the effective minimum of the age is the live sum.

### 9.3 Non-timing constants and input validators (W4)

Every constant that this document names has a value, a range, one central validator and, for an input, one API error. All defaults are **design defaults proposed here**; none is verified on a real host. **Runtime-only** constants have no database constraint, so changing them needs no migration. **Schema-fixed** constants (`REQUESTED_BY_MAX_LENGTH`, `PROCESS_RISK_RATIONALE_MAX_LENGTH`, the text literals and numeric limits of the `risk_acceptance` schema, and the absolute `PROCESS_RISK_TARGETS_DB_LIMIT`) are written into migration `0005` (a CHECK or the frozen predicate of §7.4): their allowed range is exactly the fixed value, no environment variable and no setting can widen or narrow them, the writer validator and the migration SQL use the same value, and a change needs a new migration together with the validator change; they are never classified as runtime-only.

**Validator.** `validate_process_input_constants()` (`validators.py`, called by the policy factory at the construction of the `Runner` (R31-9) next to `validate_process_risk_limits()` and `validate_process_timing_limits()`; the construction is refused on any violation) checks the ranges of the table in this section, that `REQUESTED_BY_MAX_LENGTH` is 128 and `PROCESS_RISK_RATIONALE_MAX_LENGTH` is 2000 (no environment variable or setting reads them; that both equal the numbers frozen in migration `0005` and in the rendered SQL and regular expression is a **test**, a string and number equality test, and not a check at construction, because the file names under `migrations/versions` start with digits and cannot be imported; revision 30, C13), that `REQUESTED_BY_PATTERN` compiles and matches no space or control character, and that `RISK_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED_KEYS` has exactly 9 distinct keys and equals the required fields of `RISK_ACCEPTANCE_SCHEMA` (whose only optional field is `requested_by`), and that the regular-expression constants of the schema compile, and that `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STALL_THRESHOLD` is an integer in 1..1000 and not a bool and `ORPHAN_SWEEP_BACKOFF_EXPONENT_CAP` is an integer in 0..62 inclusive and not a bool (a value above 62, a negative value, a non-integer, NaN and infinity are rejected). There is **no** validator on `N_TOTAL`, on a Task's total row count or on a command-count cap: they are not database limits (§7.5 item 5). **Revision 27:** it also checks `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_IDS` (distinct non-empty ASCII ids without `:`, equal to the list of §9.1 SUP-1). The `BACKGROUND_*` constants (the restart delay base, cap and exponent cap, the consecutive budget, the stabilization time, the window length and maximum, the wake-up debounce) belong to `validate_process_timing_limits()`, which checks their types, ranges and relations (§9.2); the runtime guard of §7.4 (CG-1) validates the sweeper's shapes again at use time and never raises, and the supervisor uses the copy of its restart constants built at construction and does not read the module constants again (R31-10 (d); a copy that is unusable when it is read can arise only through corruption and degrades the component, SUP-T T16). The judgement table of this section states the verdict for the constants that its rows name, and its shape set S applies to every constant of that table; no sentence of this section claims that one shape list is rejected for every constant of the document.

**Validation judgement table (revision 27, completed in revision 28; the verdict for the constants that the rows name, design only; no validator exists yet; a constant without a row here is judged by its own row of §9.2 or §9.3 and by the shape rules of its validator).** Vocabulary: **refused at construction** means that the policy factory of `app/validation` raises when the `Runner` constructor calls it (R31-9) or when `create_app()` calls it early through the thin wrapper `validate_process_timing_limits()`: this happens before any Runner runs and before the entry critical section of `start()`, so no lifecycle changes (§9.4 error mapping); **SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID** means that the guard of §7.4 CG-1 (the entry snapshot of SUP-28) classifies the value at pass entry and raises nothing; **membership of the pass snapshot** is decided here and only here (revision 35, final decision Q2-2): the members of the pass snapshot are the constants that §9.3 validates as sweeper pass inputs and whose validation failure it maps to `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` (the rows of this table with that verdict). **Decision rule (revision 35, user-fixed policy):** a constant that this section explicitly names, validates as a sweeper pass input and whose validation failure on that path maps to `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` is a member of the pass snapshot; using the same constant on another path as a copy validated at construction does not remove its membership, so `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` and `CANDIDATE_MAX_SCANNED_ROWS` are members (each also has a construction copy). A constant that has no row here with that verdict and appears only as an operand of a relation (`PROCESS_RISK_ROW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `MAX_PG_TIMEOUT_MS`, `PROCESS_RISK_MAX_TARGETS`, `JOB_CLOSE_SETTLE_SECONDS` and `ORPHAN_SWEEP_STARTUP_WAIT_SECONDS`) is a **relation input**, not a member, and its relation validation is unchanged. A row with another verdict, such as the fallback, a supervisor-only copy or the READY copy, is not a member. This paragraph is the single place that names members: other sections refer to this rule and copy no list; **component DEGRADED** is SUP-T T16 of §9.1; **abnormal exit** is §7.4 row 28 (the supervisor path of CG-2). **Shape set S** is a bool, `None`, a string, NaN, +infinity and -infinity: it is rejected for **every** constant of the table (the counts also reject a float such as `5.0`); the columns list only what differs per constant. Boundary values are valid exactly where the 'Valid' column names them. **'Valid' means valid together with the related constants** satisfying the relations of §9.2: a value marked 'valid only when the related constants are raised' is valid only when the related constants are raised accordingly, and is refused when the others keep their defaults.
