**Order of the numeric checks and the error envelope (revision 28).** Every numeric validator of this document checks in this order, so that no check can raise before an earlier one has rejected the value: (1) reject a `bool` (a `bool` is an `int`); (2) check the supported type, `int` or `float` (a `Decimal`, a `Fraction`, a `str`, `bytes`, `None`, a list or a dict is an **unsupported type** and is rejected, `Decimal('1e10000')` included: B2 supports no `Decimal`); (3) compare the range **safely**: a comparison of a Python `int` of any size with a bound never raises, so `10**400` and `-(10**400)` are rejected by the range check without any conversion; (4) convert to `float` only when a float is needed (the `timedelta` or millisecond computation) and only after the range check, and apply `math.isfinite` only to a value that already is a `float` or was converted safely (`math.isfinite(10**400)` raises `OverflowError`: read-only check of the project interpreter, 'int too large to convert to float'); (5) every `ArithmeticError`, `OverflowError`, `ValueError` and `TypeError` raised anywhere in a validator is normalised into the **one settings-validation error envelope** that all validators of this document share (today a `ValueError`, as `validate_recovery_timeouts()` raises it, `validators.py:21-33`, and as the `Settings` model validators turn it into a pydantic validation error), so an `OverflowError` never leaves a validator. **Existing fact, unchanged by B2 (label (b)):** `validate_recovery_timeouts()` calls `math.isfinite(value)` first, so a direct call with `10**400` raises `OverflowError` today (a read-only call showed it); through `Settings` the float field rejects such an integer before the validator runs, and B2 does not change the function. Verdicts: `10**400` and `-(10**400)` refused (range); `Decimal('1e10000')` refused as an unsupported type; `1e300` refused by the upper bound of its constant; `5e-324` and `1e-9` refused by the lower bound `BACKGROUND_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` where the constant is an interval (they would be busy loops); NaN and plus or minus infinity refused; a bool refused; a `str` and `None` refused as unsupported types.

**Worst-case size of the fixed values (revision 15; arithmetic, not a PostgreSQL measurement).** In UTF-8 a `rationale` of 2000 code points of 4 bytes is 2000 × 4 = 8000 B; `requested_by` of 128 characters is 128 × 1 B (its alphabet is ASCII only; even a hypothetical 4-byte alphabet would give 128 × 4 = 512 B); all other keys, values and punctuation of the record together are 343 B. A throw-away script built the record with `ensure_ascii=False` and compact separators, which is the measure of `response_sanitizer.py:81`: the `risk_acceptance` worst case is **8471 B** (8855 B with a 4-byte `requested_by`), and the whole `detail` of a risk-accepted row with `tracked`, `v`, `disposition` and `reason_code` is 8590 B before its unrelated keys (`runner_process`, `checkpoint_step_key`, `lifecycle` …, well under 1 KiB more). Escaped as ASCII (12 B per 4-byte code point, as `json.dumps` does by default) the same record is 24471 B. Every figure is far below `SANITIZED_JSON_MAX_BYTES` = 64 KiB (65536 B, `policies.py:194`) and the 2000 characters are below the per-string cap of the sanitizer (`SANITIZE_MAX_STRING_CHARS` = 4000, `policies.py:182`), so a valid stored record is never truncated by a response view. **The sanitizer is never the authority for storage validity:** it only shapes a response (`response_sanitizer.py:95-103` redacts and truncates); the validator and the migration CHECK or predicate decide what may be stored. The `process_risk_requests.rationale` column and `ApprovalDecision.rationale` (`tables.py:318`) are `text` and hold at most 8000 B of it.

### 9.4 Constant inventory (one table)

This section owns the **list of every configuration and policy constant** of this design; it is the single place that answers 'which constants exist and who validates them', and no sentence of this document states how many there are (a count would go stale: the number of **reasons** in the options table of §7.5 item 2 is a different thing and is not touched). Values and relations are defined **once**, in the §9.2 and §9.3 tables, and this table points to them ('§9.2 row', '§9.3 row') instead of repeating them; the 'Default' column repeats only the value for lookup, and a text test compares it with its §9.2 or §9.3 row (a row whose Default cell is not a value, such as 'ten field specs', 'derived, 9 keys' or 'see §9.3', is excluded from that comparison). Every row has every column of the header (the canonical name, the owner module or class, the purpose, the default, the type, the bool rule, the finite check, the minimum and maximum, the relationships, the validator owner, the validation timing, the error mapping, the mutability, the runtime-configuration status, the test owner, the consuming component, the verification type and the approval status); the column 'Minimum / maximum' states **both** bounds in every row, and a bound that the constant does not have of its own says so and names what limits it; a value without a numeric validator says why and what protects it, and no cell is empty or says 'not specified'. **Constants that need no numeric validator** (strings, key sets, SQL text) name what protects them instead: an immutable code constant, a schema-architecture test, a golden SQL test, import-time construction, a PostgreSQL integration test or a consumer-side validator. **Decision D27-1 (confirmed by the user in revision 27):** every constant that is new in B2 is a literal of `policies.py` that no environment variable or settings object overrides; the 'Runtime configuration' column says yes only for an existing value that `app/config.py` `Settings` exposes today and then names the `Settings` field and the environment variable; the table 'Settings reality' states what validation exists for each such value and what B2 does. **Decision D28-5 (confirmed by the user in revision 28):** a value that takes part in **no** B2 relation is not a B2 constant: it is not a row of the table below, not an input of a B2 validator and not classified (I1) to (I5); `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS`, the recovery timeouts and the database pool timeout are described only in the table 'Existing external settings' that follows 'Settings reality', and `LEASE_TTL_SECONDS` is not listed there but only in the table 'Settings reality' (row 'Lease TTL': none by B2, because decision D29-4 superseded D28-4). **Numeric validators (one rule).** Every validator of this document that checks a time or a count accepts any **non-bool finite number** (an `int` **and** a `float`: `30` and `30.0` are both valid) and **rejects a bool explicitly**, because `bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python and `True` would otherwise pass as `1`; `NaN`, infinity, a string, `None` and an out-of-range number are rejected too, and an integer count must be an `int` (a non-integer float is rejected). The existing `validate_recovery_timeouts()` (`validators.py:21-33`) checks `math.isfinite(value)` and `value > 0` only and does **not** reject a bool (read from code; `math.isfinite(True)` is true and `True > 0` is true): it is reused unchanged, and B2 does not claim to have changed it. A validation failure refuses the construction of the Runner (R31-9; a `ValueError`-style failure, the existing convention of `validate_response_limits`; today `validate_recovery_timeouts`, `validators.py:21`, raises `ValueError` for a non-finite or non-positive number but `TypeError` for `None` or a `str` and `OverflowError` for `10**400`, because `math.isfinite` converts to float first, which is why the B2 validators normalise all of them); only the two request inputs have an API error (422 `VALIDATION_FAILED`). **Kinds.** 'design default, code-fixed' means no database constraint (no migration is needed to change it) and no environment or settings override, so it changes only by a code change. 'code-fixed policy constant' means a literal in `policies.py` that no environment variable or setting can change. 'schema-fixed' is defined in §9.3. 'existing, reused unchanged' constants exist today at the cited line and B2 adds no validator for them. **Revision 29 (D29-1, D29-4):** `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `BACKGROUND_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (and, since revision 30, `BACKGROUND_RECOVERY_SETTLE_MARGIN_SECONDS`) are rows of the table below; `DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` is still not a B2 constant and has no row (D28-5); the lease TTL has no B2 validator, no relation and no row in this table (D29-4); it is listed only in the table 'Settings reality' (row 'Lease TTL').

**Settings reality (revision 27, decision D27-1; read from `app/config.py` and `app/container.py`).** A value is **runtime-configurable** only when `Settings` (pydantic-settings, `.env` and environment variables, read once by `get_settings()` in `create_app`, `main.py:68`; there is no reload at run time) exposes it. The new B2 policy constants are **not** of that kind: they are code literals of `policies.py` with no `Settings` field and no environment variable, and the two kinds are never described as one. The table states, for each existing value that B2 touches, what validation exists today and what B2 does, using one of four labels: **(a)** a new validator in the B2 scope, **(b)** the existing validation reused unchanged, **(c)** a relation-only check added by B2 (**implementation scope, not existing**), **(d)** intentionally allowed (B2 adds nothing); since revision 28 this table holds the new B2 constants and the lease TTL, for which B2 adds nothing ('none by B2', decision D29-4), and the labels (b) and (d) are used by the table of existing external settings.

**The four upper-bound labels (revision 30, C14).** The 'upper bound' statement of every row of the table below is exactly one of four labels. *Truly unbounded above:* the constant appears in no relation of §9.2, §9.3 or the tracked-age sum that gives an upper bound, so an arbitrarily large value is accepted. *Bounded only by a relation:* a relation of §9.2 or §9.3 bounds the constant above (possibly through other constants), and the table states no fixed literal maximum of its own; the row says where the chain ends: '(chain ends at a fixed bound)' when the last constant has a fixed code-policy maximum, so the constant has a finite effective maximum, or '(transitively unbounded)' when the last constant is itself unbounded above, so the relation gives no finite maximum at all. *Code-policy upper bound:* a fixed literal maximum in `policies.py` or in the validator. *Type limit only:* B2 states no bound beyond the type or the form of the value (string, version, regular-expression, set and rendered-text values have no numeric maximum). **Tracked-age relation (revision 30, C14):** `TRACKED_EXECUTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS` must be at least the live sum `MAX_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` + `TRACKED_IDENTITY_PERSIST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` + `PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS` + `PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS` + `TREE_SETTLE_POLL_SECONDS`, computed at construction from the constants as they are (3621 s with the defaults) and validated by `validate_process_timing_limits()`; the sum is a lower bound of the age and the age has no upper bound, so `MAX_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `TRACKED_IDENTITY_PERSIST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS` have no upper bound through it (transitively unbounded), while `PROCESS_TERMINATE_GRACE_SECONDS` and `TREE_SETTLE_POLL_SECONDS` are bounded by the settle relation (chain ends at a fixed bound); the effective minimum of the age is the live sum. The label of every row was compared with the relations of §9.2 by a script (§13.1 r30); a label is a statement about the relations of this document and not about the host.

**Inclusion rule of this table (revision 27; it replaces the r26 sentence that every backticked token is a constant of the table, which did not hold).** **Included:** (I1) the new B2 production policy constants; (I2) existing production constants whose value or meaning B2 changes; (I3) constants that take part in a B2 validator relation; (I4) canonical SQL, schema and index constants that the B2 contract names; (I5) constants used directly as public API limits. **Excluded** (classified by the closed allow-list written in this paragraph, not by an external script; a token that matches no class and is not in the table is a defect of the document): state, lifecycle and enum values (`STARTING`, `RUNNING`, `DEGRADED`, `STOPPED`, ...); error, failure, warning and cause codes (`SWEEP_*`, `SWEEPER_*`, `VALIDATION_FAILED`, `PROCESS_TRACKING_*`, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_FAILED`, `SUPERVISOR_EXITED`, `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED`); proof, result and disposition values (`EXITED`, `TERMINATED`, `NEVER_RAN`, `OPERATOR_RISK_ACCEPTED` as a record value, ...); reason and refusal codes of §6.2 and §7.5 (`CAPABILITY_MISMATCH`, `RUNNER_MISMATCH`, `LEASE_EXPIRED`, `NO_OWNING_RUN`, `TASK_NOT_EXECUTING`, `TASK_TERMINAL_WITH_UNRESOLVED`, `CLOSED_UNPROVEN`, `FAIL_CLOSED`, `UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM`, ...); position kinds (`CANDIDATE`, `PAGE_AFTER`); names that an earlier revision removed (`BACKGROUND_RESTART_BACKOFF_SECONDS`, named only to say that it no longer exists); DTO and column names; rule IDs; local variables and explanatory symbols (`N`, `T`, `W`, `P`, `R`, `A`, `C`); **the retired names** `RISK_ACCEPTANCE_NUMBER_RE` and `RISK_ACCEPTANCE_CREATE_TIME_MAX` (named only to say that they no longer exist); **the existing external settings** of the table 'Existing external settings' (`DEFAULT_RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS`, `DEFAULT_RUNNER_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `DEFAULT_RECOVERY_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `DEFAULT_RUNNER_RECOVERY_SHUTDOWN_WAIT_SECONDS`, `DEFAULT_DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), which take part in no B2 relation (decision D28-5). **Test and architecture identifiers** (`LAYER_RULES`, the layer table of `tests/architecture/test_rules.py:110-116`, named in §9.1 SUP-30). **SQL keywords and clauses** written in upper case (`CASE`, `FROM`, `JOIN`, `OFFSET`, `EXPLAIN`, `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `ORDER`, `LIMIT`, `FOR UPDATE`); **environment variable names** (`RUNNER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS`, `DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `LEASE_TTL_SECONDS` and the like, as variable names of `Settings` fields); **operating-system API constants** (`JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`); **HTTP method and file-type words** written in upper case (`GET`, `POST`, `SQL`, `JSON`); and `LEASE_TTL_SECONDS` as the existing setting of D29-4 (its one row is in 'Settings reality', none in this table). **The allow-list is exactly these classes**: a token that belongs to none of them and is neither a row of the table below nor part of the allow-list is a defect. The check is two-sided: every constant that the prose names and that matches (I1) to (I5) is a row here, and every row here is named in the prose of §9.1 to §9.3 or §14 or has a stated reason in its purpose cell. A constant of this table is **runtime-configurable** only where its 'Runtime configuration' cell names a `Settings` field (§9.4 'Settings reality'); every other row is a code literal. **Exception list (revision 30, C15):** five rows are kept although they are not members of I1 to I5: `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MAX_LENGTH` (named in §9.3 as the coincidence with `REQUESTED_BY_MAX_LENGTH`, so that a reader finds its value), `PROOF_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (it bounds the retry loop that hosts the acquisition guard of §7.4), `DIAGNOSTICS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` (the unchanged constant that §14.3 names), `SANITIZED_JSON_MAX_BYTES` and `SANITIZE_MAX_STRING_CHARS` (existing public response limits that §9.3 uses only as comparison figures); none takes part in a B2 relation, and `DIAGNOSTICS_POLICY_VERSION` is a member by I2.

## 10. Scope: which commands get B2

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. all `CommandExecutor` commands | uniform proof; fixes provider CLI leaks too | provider CLIs (claude/codex) are `.cmd` shims on Windows, MCP/background helpers may legitimately outlive; larger regression surface; job-assignment fail-closed could stop all Tasks on restricted hosts |
| **B. tracked commands: orchestrator test commands and `collect_ids` (confirmed, H1)** | the smallest surface that covers every place the orchestrator runs project code | provider leaks remain a known gap (already tolerated by the takeover/RECOVERY model) |
| C. test commands + provider CLIs behind a setting | staged rollout | two code paths to keep correct |

Confirmed: **B, widened** — `TestPolicyService.run` **and** `TestPolicyService.collect_ids` are tracked (`python -m pytest --collect-only` imports conftest and runs project code, and must not outlive the write lock). `git clone` (`ProjectService`) and provider CLIs stay untracked and are follow-ups; the executor API (`TrackedRun`) is designed so they can adopt it later. Untracked commands only get the cancellation-safe settlement and the bounded drain of §9; they get no natural-exit sweep. On POSIX the tracked commands degrade to untracked (§5.2). **Approval boundary (proposed; nothing is approved):** tracking on Windows only; the untracked settlement hardening and the POSIX degrade and refusal contract are in scope; POSIX process tracking is not approved; POSIX real-execution verification has not been done; root process exit detected first by `returncode`; as a result the normal-exit outcome of untracked commands can differ from today's TIMEOUT or ALREADY_EXITED.

## 11. Regression risks (existing behaviour)

- Provider CLI path: untracked commands change only through the shielded settlement and the bounded pump drain (visible: a provider CLI that leaves background children no longer hangs `run()` forever; its output after the bound is not captured). Covered by the existing provider/executor tests plus new cancel-during-run and pipe-holding-survivor tests.
- Existing string-pinning tests (`TERMINATED`, `ALREADY_EXITED`, `KILLED_BY_HANDLE`, `STILL_ALIVE`) are protected by §4.1 and the golden test; `_settle`/`_acquire_slot` and their monkeypatching tests are untouched.
- Orchestrator test run inside a TESTER step: gains `run_key`, an `Execution` row with `STARTING` before spawn, a sticky cancel scope and tree proof. A test command that leaves a background process now ends with `survivors=true`, `termination=TERMINATED` and a warning instead of `SUCCESS` with a leaked process (H4). A run whose tree cannot be proven empty becomes `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED` → RECOVERY.
- **Build daemons (Gradle/Maven/mvnd), analysis only:** a daemon started inside the Job dies with it (the intended H4 outcome); each `gradle test` therefore reports `survivors=true` and pays a cold start. Because Gradle's daemon registry is user-wide, a daemon started under Job A that build B attaches to would be killed when A's Job ends (**unverified**). Mitigations are preset/policy choices (F scope, e.g. `--no-daemon`, isolated Gradle user home); B2 changes no preset. The per-policy switch of H4 only silences the warning; termination is never skipped.
- `LeaseService` takeover and `_finalize_cancel`/`_recovery_unsafe` filter executions by `role in STEP_ROLE.values()`: tracked rows use role `TESTER` and are included; a new role would not be.
- Hosts where Job creation/assignment is refused fail closed for tracked commands only (`SPAWN_FAILED`), reported by the self-test and diagnostics.
- **Visible behaviour changes for untracked commands:** a root that exits before the timeout is no longer reported as `TIMEOUT`/`ALREADY_EXITED` (it is a natural exit with the exit code's outcome); `run()` returns within `PUMP_DRAIN_SECONDS` of the root's exit instead of the descendant's lifetime; an `on_started` exception no longer leaks the process.
- **Abort/terminal behaviour (H7):** for Tasks with an open tracked execution a terminal transition now ends `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED` even when the fingerprint equals the baseline; the next Task of the project then needs the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate. Unchanged for untracked agent CLIs (H8).
- **API/diagnostics (H10):** Test-Run requests are refused with a stable reason code before any Task exists (§6.2); workflow Tasks and TESTER steps are unaffected on POSIX (degrade) and fail closed only on a Windows host whose self-test failed.
- **API differences (H9, MA-1, M1 of revision 10):** a stale gate of a **CLEAN** project behaves exactly as today (`continue` resumes); a stale gate of a **still-DIRTY** project offers only `refresh_gate` and `abort` (the other three options are omitted from `options` and `options_hidden`) instead of answering `continue` with `StaleProjectGate` (the options are recomputed on read); `ApprovalOut` gains `options`, `options_hidden`, `operator_request`; a gate whose Task/project link is broken returns `options = []` with `TASK_PROJECT_LINK_BROKEN` reasons instead of an abort that could not work (C-1).
- **API difference (H9, MA-1):** on a `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate a bogus option now returns `409 OPTION_NOT_AVAILABLE` instead of `422 ValidationFailed` (the effect validates against the recomputed list); every static gate keeps the 422 and its response and fingerprint.
- **API differences of the length and character rules (the single list; rules in §7.5 item 3, constants in §9.3):** (1) every `DecisionCreate.rationale`, for every decision type and not only the risk options, is bounded by `PROCESS_RISK_RATIONALE_MAX_LENGTH` code points (it was unbounded); (2) `requested_by` is bounded by `REQUESTED_BY_MAX_LENGTH` code points; (3) U+0000 is rejected in both fields; (4) lone surrogates U+D800–U+DFFF are rejected in both fields; (5) a violation is `422 VALIDATION_FAILED` and never a 500 from the database or the UTF-8 encoding; (6) the length unit is the Unicode code point in Python, in Pydantic and in PostgreSQL `char_length`; (7) the bounds apply in the API schema and in the service validators with the same constants; (8) validation runs before the idempotent replay lookup (`app/routers/approvals.py:19-23`, then `human_gate_service.py:107` and `147-150`), so a decision request whose `rationale` exceeded the bound and was accepted before this change, if resent identically after the upgrade, is answered `422` and not with the stored `200`; this is a deliberate difference, and the replay of a request within the bounds is unchanged; (9) backward compatibility: the existing callers and tests send a short `rationale` or none (`tests/api/test_api.py:135`, `tests/harness.py:128`, `tests/e2e_cli/test_real_cli.py:60`, `tests/e2e_cli/test_real_cli_projects.py:54`) and are unaffected within the checked range (read, not run).
- **Operator option (H9):** the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate shows a high-risk option, computed on read, only with unresolved tracked rows; nothing changes for projects without them. No existing Approval row is rewritten and the global lock order is unchanged (M1).
- **Visible behaviour change (C5):** a `CLEAN`, ownerless project with an old unresolved or anomalous tracked execution no longer lets the next Task acquire the write lock: the project becomes `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED` and the Task meets the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate (§7.4, acquisition guard).
- Migration: **`0005` adds two additive tables** (`runtime_capabilities`, §6.2, and `process_risk_requests`, §7.5) and three additive partial indexes (`ix_executions_tracked_unresolved`, `ix_executions_tracked_anomaly`, `uq_approvals_lineage_successor`); no column for execution facts (they stay in `detail`) and older rows keep today's semantics.

## 12. Decisions (confirmed by the user unless marked open; the rows D30-1 to D30-5 are applied but not user-approved, except where a D31 row says otherwise)

| ID | Decision | Confirmed choice |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | Scope (§10) | tracked commands = orchestrator test commands **and `collect_ids`**; `git clone` and provider CLIs are follow-ups |
| H2 | Persistence of group/termination facts | **`detail` (JSONB merge); no new column for execution facts** (qualifier: migration `0005` exists only for the tables `runtime_capabilities` and `process_risk_requests`, §6.2/§7.5, and three partial indexes); `process_group_id` dropped (redundant, POSIX unapproved) |
| H3 | After a Windows crash, accept "Job had `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`" | **conditional OS guarantee** (§8): previous Runner proven dead on the same host + root gone + best-effort sweep after a bounded settle wait → `ALREADY_EXITED` with `proof=JOB_KILL_ON_CLOSE_ASSUMED`; otherwise `TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED`; switchable off |
| H4 | Survivors after the root exits | terminate and report `TERMINATED` + warning; **fail only if the tree cannot be proven empty**; per-policy switch only silences the warning (daemon-centric presets) |
| H5 | Job assignment/creation failure | fail closed (`SPAWN_FAILED`, capability `PROCESS_TRACKING_UNAVAILABLE`), cause corrected (§5.1 step 3), startup self-test and a `PROCESS_TRACKING` diagnostics item |
| H6 | Resume mechanism | **`ResumeThread`** on the single primary thread (documented API); `NtResumeProcess`/`psutil.Process.resume()` not used |
| H7 | Abort with an open tracked execution or an unconfirmed termination | **never CLEAN: `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED`**; a user abort does not replace the termination proof; follow-up only through the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate; same rule reused by D4 test-only Task; existing abort path hardened inside B2 (§7.4, §14) |
| H8 | The same rule for **untracked** agent-CLI executions (today an abort can release CLEAN while a CLI is unterminated) | **open, not decided, not part of B2**; B2 leaves that behaviour unchanged |
| H9 | Exit when termination can be neither proven nor refuted | **explicit operator risk acceptance in the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate** (§7.5): separate high-risk option, never recorded as proof, `OPERATOR_RISK_ACCEPTED`, audited, Runner re-verification first through an approval-level request queue (`process_risk_requests`; live survivor → refused, then an explicit `recheck_processes` exit), project stays `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED` and must pass the existing baseline re-acceptance, no D4-specific bypass |
| H10 | POSIX/capability boundary for D4/E | Test-Run request refused before Task creation: `409 PROCESS_TRACKING_UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM` (POSIX); separate `PROCESS_TRACKING_UNAVAILABLE` (Windows self-test failed) and `PROCESS_TRACKING_STATUS_UNKNOWN` (capability unknown; no Task); workflow Tasks and TESTER steps keep the `UNTRACKED_PLATFORM` degrade, no STARTING row on POSIX; capability shared with API-only instances through a persisted, TTL- and advisory-lock-checked record (§6.2); HTTP status: 409 for the POSIX code is the user's; 409 for `PROCESS_TRACKING_UNAVAILABLE` and 503 + `Retry-After` for `PROCESS_TRACKING_STATUS_UNKNOWN` are **proposed**; capability row carries an incarnation id and the lock-holder backend pid so stale results of an earlier Runner are never trusted |
| H11 | Policy when an anomaly stays permanently stuck (new in revision 13; §7.4) | **open, not decided.** Options: (a) leave it: the project stays `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED`, diagnostics and the report show `may_be_permanently_stuck`, repair is a manual, audited correction of the row outside B2 (today's design); (b) an operator gate option that re-classifies an anomaly through the H9 procedure (rationale, request, worker, audit, original preserved), which would let the operator bless data written by a faulty writer and needs its own review; (c) a documented, audited offline repair procedure (an administrator script that moves the bad values to `detail.anomaly_original` as the sweeper does) without any new API. **Recommendation: (a) now, with (c) written as an operations note; (b) only if stuck anomalies occur in practice.** B2 implements (a) until this is decided |
| D27-1 | Constants and settings (§9.4, §9.2, §9.3) | **confirmed by the user in revision 27 (only this rule; the default values and bounds of the new constants are design proposals, not user-approved):** new B2 policy constants are code literals of `app/validation/policies.py` with no environment override; existing values exposed by `app/config.py` `Settings` are runtime-configurable and described with the validation that exists (labels (a) to (d) of §9.4 'Settings reality'); lease TTL gets no B2 check (the revision-28 relation-only check of the effective value was withdrawn in r29, D29-4) |
| D27-2 | Public names and ownership (§9.1 SUP-12, §14.2) | **confirmed:** warning `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, health field `runner.background_degraded` (boolean), DTO `SweeperConfigInvalidOut`; the Runner side owns the source state, the API schema layer owns the DTOs, the routers and the FastAPI `response_model` convert (the revision-27 wording 'services convert' is superseded in r28, §14.2), no service imports `app.schemas`; the component detail list is a separate list in the diagnostics |
| D27-3 | Stabilization (§9.1 SUP-5) | **confirmed:** the first normally returning pass is only a READY signal; the consecutive count resets only after the component stayed alive for `BACKGROUND_STABLE_SECONDS`; a task creation or one pass never resets it |
| D27-4 | Restart budgets (§9.1 SUP-3, SUP-5, SUP-6, SUP-11) | **confirmed:** two budgets per component (consecutive failures; a rolling window), bounded exponential restart delay, exceeding either degrades that component, only a new Runner generation resets the rolling window and both budgets, stabilization resets only the consecutive count and never deletes a window entry, a top-level crash always consumes the window |
| D27-5 | Configuration-fixed wake-up (§7.4 CI-7) | **confirmed:** an invalid-to-valid transition at an explicit revalidation boundary wakes the sweeper once (coalesced, debounced), does not clear the warning, deletes no audit value and starts no pass when it races a stop or a generation change |
| D28-1 | Owner of the STARTING failure settlement (§9.1 SUP-13) | **confirmed by the user in revision 28:** the supervisor never calls `_fail_start` or `_settle_failed_start` and never cancels or awaits itself; it records the first start failure of a generation in a per-generation `start_failed` signal and a later failure never overwrites it; only `start()` settles, through the existing `_fail_start` path |
| D28-2 | `RUNNING` publication boundary (§9.1 SUP-14) | **confirmed:** right before `RUNNING` is published, under the lifecycle lock, `start()` checks atomically the lifecycle, the generation, `start_failed`, the liveness (`task.done()`) of the supervisor and of every required component task, the READY boundary of every required component, the absence of a stop or a failed-start settlement, and the validity of the lock connection and the start resources; liveness is never decided from done-callbacks or the supervisor queue alone |

| D30-1 | Failed-start settlement (§9.1 SUP-19, item 4) | **applied as decided by the revision-30 instruction, not user-approved:** the cancellation, the wait and `_settle_failed_start` run inside the one shielded settle task that `_fail_start` awaits; `start()` does only the synchronous hand-off (the plain bool `_start_aborting` and the settling record); a second caller cancellation can never leave the Runner in `STARTING` |

| D30-3 | Start order (§9.1 SUP-19, SUP-31) | **applied as decided, not user-approved:** entry section, lock, self-test and capability upsert, and only then the supervisor and the components (a `RunnerAlreadyActive` start leaves no task); the sweeper's first pass is held until the startup mutation is done; `_loop_task` stays in the `RUNNING` publication section |

## 13. Test plan

**Status tag rule (introduced in revision 30, item C17):** every row of this table carries the status tag 'to be run, not run' (a row may follow the tag with a parenthetical note that a throw-away model ran; each row is a plan item and nothing in it has been run; the throw-away models of §13.1 are not these tests); the one row that no repository test can cover, the real-environment row at the end, carries 'not verified, not run'. Real-OS tests are marked per platform; a test that cannot run on the current OS is reported as **not run**, never as passed. POSIX real-environment tests are outside the proposed approval scope and listed as not run. **Approval boundary (proposed; nothing is approved):** tracking on Windows only; the untracked settlement hardening and the POSIX degrade and refusal contract are in scope; POSIX process tracking is not approved; POSIX real-execution verification has not been done; root process exit detected first by `returncode`; as a result the normal-exit outcome of untracked commands can differ from today's TIMEOUT or ALREADY_EXITED. Rows marked † in the handling table of §7.5 item 10 are **synthetic-DB-state tests, not production-normal-flow tests**. Every PostgreSQL test, `EXPLAIN`/`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and Windows Job Object test named in this section is **to be run and has not been run**. The PostgreSQL probes that were run are recorded once in §13.1.

**Revision-22 run (r22; PostgreSQL 18.4 as reported by `select version()` of the embedded server, `pixeltable-pgserver` 0.6.0, asyncpg 0.32.0 used directly, tiny stand-in `tasks`, `executions` and request tables, one throw-away reference simulation `sim22.py` in the session scratch directory `rev22`, with the block `<RISK_TARGET_LOCK>` written as in the SQL fence of this document (the binds `:project_id` and `:target_ids` as `$1` and `$2`); the simulation is a reference implementation written by the author for this revision, not production code and not a regression test; not committed).** 40 checks ran and all passed. (1) *Timeouts:* `set_config('statement_timeout', '300', true)` showed `300ms` and `pg_sleep(5)` was cancelled after 0.30 s with SQLSTATE `57014`; the next statement of the same transaction failed with `25P02`, and again on a second attempt; after `rollback()` a new query returned 1 and `statement_timeout` was `0`. A row held `FOR UPDATE` by another session: the ordered lock statement under `lock_timeout` 300 ms and `statement_timeout` 3000 ms ended with `55P03` after 0.32 s; with 3000 ms and 300 ms it ended with `57014` after 0.30 s (the smaller value fires first); `lock_timeout` 299 ms against `statement_timeout` 300 ms gave `55P03`. (2) *Restore:* with an upper transaction value of `7000` ms and `2500` ms the phase values read back as `2s` and `1s` during the phase and `7s` and `2500ms` after the restore with `set_config(name, previous, true)`, and with an upper `0` and `0` the restored values were `0` and `0`; the INSERT after the restore succeeded. (3) *Ordered lock:* the statement `… id = ANY($2::uuid[]) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` returned ascending ids for an unsorted input and its plan was `LockRows` over `Sort`; two sessions locking rows 1 and 2 one by one in opposite orders produced `40P01` for one of them, and in the same ascending order both finished; a takeover-style session that first ran `SELECT id … ANY(…) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` on an input in arbitrary order and then updated in the returned order against a session locking 1, 2, 3 in ascending order did not deadlock, while the mutation that updated in descending order without the ordered lock produced `40P01`. (4) *Re-evaluation and snapshot:* a statement that waited for rows held by a session that then settled two of them under READ COMMITTED returned the 6 remaining ids and the INSERT of the snapshot ran; when all eight were settled it returned no row and the simulated decision inserted nothing (the `409` path); with nothing settled all 8 ids were kept. (5) *uuid order:* PostgreSQL `ORDER BY id` on 500 random UUIDs equalled the Python sort. (6) *Pure Python:* a reference implementation of the transition table of §7.4 (rows 1 to 10: first versus current position, pending to stalled, replacement while pending, pinned while stalled with `first_failure_cursor` and `stalled_since` kept, success below the position without clearing, equality and beyond clearing, a failure candidate that vanished, a wrap-around with a `null` position, `SWEEP_NO_PROGRESS` never clearing, a restart) and 5000 randomized event sequences held every invariant; the backoff formula returned finite values within [30, 300] for counts 1, 2, 5, 16, 17, 1024, 1025 and integers of 100, 1329 and 33220 bits, saturated at 300 from the 5th failure on, and the naive `min * 2 ** (n - 1)` raised `OverflowError` for n = 1025 and for 10^4 (the detection power of the test). This run **did not** include production code, the real `LeaseService`, an HTTP layer, the Runner, `/health`, `alembic`, `EXPLAIN` or index use; the simulation is not an independent verification. (7) *Processes:* the script stops the server itself (`cleanup()`); an earlier attempt whose script the author stopped while it was blocked left the embedded server running and the author stopped it with `pg_ctl stop -m immediate`; after the final run the author ran `tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq postgres.exe"` in PowerShell, which printed `INFO: No tasks are running which match the specified criteria.`, and `(Get-Process -Name postgres -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object).Count`, which printed `0`.

**Revision-24 run (r24; throw-away pure-Python reference simulations, no PostgreSQL server started; written by the author for this revision, not independent of the author; not committed).** Two scripts in the session scratch directory `rev24`: `sim24.py` (150 checks, all passed) and `simpyd24.py` (17 checks, all passed; run with the project virtual environment, pydantic 2.14.1, Python 3.14.6). (1) *Cancel-reason state machine* (a model of the Runner field and of the sweeper handler with real `asyncio` tasks, not the production `Runner`): `Runner.stop()`-style and `_settle_failed_start`-style cancellations record `STOP` and `FAILED_START` before `task.cancel()` and count nothing; an external cancel while the lifecycle is `RUNNING` counts one `SWEEP_CANCELLED` and re-raises; a `STOP` recorded while an external cancel is already pending is read as `STOP`; an external cancel handled first and a stop afterwards count one failure and the stop is a no-op after the end; a changed generation without a recorded reason stays `EXTERNAL_OR_UNKNOWN`; a new task does not inherit the old reason and a reason bound to another task identity is ignored; with the record at the threshold minus one a normal stop and a failed start do not stall and an external cancel does; a cancel after the task ended is a no-op; the record-and-cancel function is synchronous. (2) *86,400 s ceiling:* the validator model accepts 86399.0 and 86400.0 and rejects 86400.000001, 86401.0, 3e11, 1e300, 0, negative values, NaN, infinity, a bool and a string for each of the interval, the two backoff values and the throttle, and rejects a minimum above the maximum and a minimum below the interval. (3) *`next_retry_at`:* valid delays give the sum; 86400.5, 3e11, 1e300, NaN, infinity, 0, a negative value and a bool give `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` with no `next_retry_at` and the ceiling as the wait; a clock within 100 s of `datetime.max` with a delay of 300.0 gives the same code; the unguarded `now + timedelta(seconds=3e11)` raised `OverflowError` ('date value out of range') and `timedelta(seconds=1e300)` raised `OverflowError`; no exception escaped a battery of 16 delay values, `10**400` included. (4) *Float backoff:* `sat` = 4; delays 30.0, 60.0, 120.0, 240.0, 300.0, 300.0; every result finite and within [30.0, 300.0] for counts up to `10**10000` and caps 0..62; the naive `min * 2 ** (n - 1)` with float limits raised `OverflowError` ('int too large to convert to float') at n = 1025, 1026, 2000 and 10000 while the integer-literal computation returned 300 silently; the cap-only mutant (no saturation, no maximum) differed when the cap was above `sat` and agreed when it was below; the cap boundaries and the saturation boundary (n = 4 gives 240.0, n = 5 gives 300.0) held. (5) *Lock budget:* a budget exhausted before a statement starts gave `TARGET_LOCK_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED` mapped to `TARGET_PAGE_TIMEOUT`, `retryable` true, no SQL executed and no write. (6) *`continue`:* the six combinations of U and A (none, U only, A only, both, `decode_error` only, an unproven absence) offered it only for U none and A none; a broken link, a stale gate and a failed safety condition never offered it. (7) *Clearing:* the per-kind and mixed-position model of table rows 5 to 12 held on hand-picked cases and on an exhaustive sweep of kind and position combinations: a record is cleared exactly when every recorded position is passed by its kind rule, a wrap-around always clears, and no branch is unreachable. (8) *Report runtime model* (a **local copy** of the shape of `app/schemas/reports.py:22-23, 202-205, 246-264`; `app/` was neither imported nor modified): the defaults are `warnings = []` and `SweeperStatusOut` (`stalled` false, 0, null, null, null: the five-field shape of r24, **superseded in r28**; the field set is the field plan of §14.2, whose default object is every boolean `false`, every count 0 and every other field `null`); `Field(default_factory=…)` instances are not shared; a legacy payload gets the defaults under strict validation and its serialised form differs from the old exact dict; a payload with `warnings` and a stalled sweeper is preserved; strict validation rejects a `str` for `warnings`, a `str` for `stalled`, an ISO string for a datetime, a float count and a non-string item; an unknown key and a cursor key inside `sweeper` are dropped by `extra=ignore` while the new fields survive; the revision-23 `RuntimeOut` silently drops `warnings` and `sweeper`, which is why the model must change. The scripts are reference implementations written by the author, not independent of the author. **Processes:** no PostgreSQL server was started in r24 and none was needed; the author ran `tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq postgres.exe"` in PowerShell before the scripts and again before this text was written, which printed `INFO: No tasks are running which match the specified criteria.` both times, and `(Get-Process -Name postgres -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object).Count`, which printed `0` both times (final process count 0). **The revision-23 run:** the notes of r23 do not preserve the output of a process check, so no process-check result is claimed for r23. **Not run in r24:** production code, the real `Runner`, the HTTP layer, the real `/health`, `alembic`, `EXPLAIN` for index use or cost, Windows, POSIX, Gradle and Maven. **Superseded in revision 25:** the stale-gate statement of this record (the stale gate of a DIRTY project and of a CLEAN project) is replaced by the CLEAN and DIRTY clauses of §7.5 item 1, and the config-guard wording 'null `next_retry_at`' and 'the wait is the ceiling' is replaced by §7.4 'Configuration guard and `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`'; the observations here are results of throw-away models and tiny scratch tables, not verification of production code.

**Revision-25 run (r25; a throw-away pure-Python reference simulation, no PostgreSQL server started; written by the author for this revision, not independent of the author; not committed).** One script in the session scratch directory `rev25`, `sim25.py`, run with the system Python 3.14.6 in isolated mode; its output is `sim25: 78001 checks, all passed` (the count includes a randomised run of 3000 event sequences; it is a count of assertion evaluations, not of distinct cases). (1) *`SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` replacement model* (a reference of the rows 1 to 11 and 22 to 26 mechanics): a failure recorded once and then replaced by the configuration failure leaves the count unchanged, keeps the position, first and current position and `pass_start_cursor`, sets `last_failure_code` to `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID` and keeps the trigger failure code in the internal field; `next_retry_at` is never null; five repeated passes count once each, `stalled` becomes true at the threshold 5 and both warnings are present while the warning `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` is already present at count 1 with `stalled` false; after the fix a pass that does not pass the position keeps the record and a pass that does clears it together with the warning; a failure-free pass that fails only the guard is counted once, with the position `PAGE_AFTER` at the committed cursor (strict `>` to clear) or the first undecided target (equality clears), never moves the cursor to 'no cursor', and the first-page `null` position clears only after an advance by at least one row or a wrap-around; a randomised run found no violation of 'at most once per pass', 'never null' and 'immediate warning at every count'. (4) *Supervisor and cancel-reason model* (real `asyncio` tasks, a model and not the production `Runner`): a stop recorded `STOP` before `task.cancel()`, counted nothing and caused no restart, a second stop after the end was a no-op; a failed start recorded `FAILED_START` with the same result; a child operation cancelled from outside while the sweeper task was not cancelled (`cancelling() == 0`) was recorded once as `SWEEP_CANCELLED` and the task kept running; an unexpected cancellation of the task itself was not recorded, the supervisor restarted it once, the reason field was empty afterwards and the pending record (count 2) was unchanged; an uncaught exception was restarted three times with the fixed delay name and then reported FAILED (4 tasks created; this model used a test-only override of the restart limit set to 3, the default limit is 5, and since revision 26 the exhausted state is DEGRADED and the budget is per component); a `STOP` recorded before the field was read won over a pending external cancel, the opposite order counted nothing and the following stop was a no-op, and a reason bound to another task identity was ignored; the record-and-cancel function is synchronous. (5) *Local check of an existing validator:* a local copy of the logic of `validate_recovery_timeouts` (`validators.py:21-33`, read, not imported) accepts `True` as a timeout and rejects `NaN`, which is the basis of the statement in §9.4. **Processes:** no PostgreSQL server was started in r25; the author ran `tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq postgres.exe"` in PowerShell at the start, before applying this text and again at the end, which printed `INFO: No tasks are running which match the specified criteria.` each time, and `(Get-Process -Name postgres -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object).Count`, which printed `0` each time (final process count 0). ### 14.1 `TRACKED_EXECUTIONS` diagnostics: causes, severity and aggregation (C-c)

The item returns **every applicable cause**, never only the first. The causes come from two independent evaluations whose results are merged: **row causes**, from the tracked rows of the project (U and A, §7.4, read through `<PROJECT_SCOPE>`) together with their Task, run and lease, which are loaded by separate queries by id and never by a `JOIN` of `tasks` and `executions` in one outer `FROM` (§7.4), and **request causes**, from the project's `process_risk_requests` and the capability state. The request causes are evaluated **even when U is empty** (a request can outlive the rows it was made for). The result is the additive field `DiagnosticItem.causes`, an internal tuple of `DiagnosticCause` (the API field `DiagnosticItemOut.causes` is a list) with the fields `{reason_code, severity, blocks_execution, cause, recommendation, related_execution_ids, related_request_ids}`; the cause `TRACKED_EXECUTION_ANOMALY` additionally carries `anomalies` (at most `DIAGNOSTIC_MAX_ANOMALIES` `TrackedAnomaly` items `{execution_id, task_id, project_id, anomaly_kind, sub_reason}` of §7.4, identifiers and fixed codes only; an internal tuple, an API list), `anomalies_returned`, `anomalies_truncated`, `anomalies_total` (`null` unless exact), `anomalies_total_is_exact` and `may_be_permanently_stuck` (the cause is the frozen dataclass `DiagnosticCause` and its API model `DiagnosticCauseOut`, §7.4; the defaults of a cause without anomalies are stated there). Duplicates by `reason_code` are removed (their ids are merged in ascending order); the list is ordered by severity (FAIL before WARN) and then by `reason_code` in ascending ASCII order, so the order is deterministic; the existing `cause` and `recommendation` strings are the same list joined in that order; `blocks_execution` of the item is the OR of the causes' flags; the item's `status` is the **highest severity** present (FAIL over WARN over PASS; no cause → PASS). **Normal progress is not a cause.** There is no Task state `RUNNING` (`TaskState`, `states.py:7-18`); the tracked commands run in `TESTING` (`_do_test` is the handler of `TESTING`, `workflow_service.py:957`; `collect_ids` for `ids_before` at `:746`, `tests.run` and `ids_after` inside `evaluate` at `:763-765`). A tracked execution is **running normally** only if **all** of the following hold: (1) the Task is `TESTING` and **not** `WAITING_APPROVAL` or terminal; (2) for `tests.run` and `ids_after` the Task's tester step is `RUNNING` (`StepState`, `states.py:21-29`; `ids_before` runs before the tester `_agent_step` call at `:784` (its `steps.begin` is at `:322`), so for that call no step of the current iteration exists yet, and because the row does not record which call it is, the item accepts a `TESTING` Task with a `RUNNING` TEST step or with no step in `INTERRUPTED`, `NEEDS_MANUAL_RECOVERY` or `WAITING_APPROVAL`); (3) a `task_runs` row with status `RUNNING` owns it (`RunStatus`, `states.py:32-35`); (4) its lease is valid (`lease_expires_at > now()`); (5) `executions.runner_id` equals the run's `runner_id`; (6) its age is within `TRACKED_EXECUTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`; (7) the project has no anomaly (A is empty). Anything else is **not** normal: `WAITING_APPROVAL` (even while the lease TTL is still valid), a terminal Task, an expired lease, no run, a Runner mismatch, a stale OPEN row, an anomaly, and the parking after `TerminationUnconfirmed` — `_park_for_recovery` keeps the run and its lease on purpose (`workflow_service.py:232-242`) and the gate sets the Task to `WAITING_APPROVAL` and the step to `NEEDS_MANUAL_RECOVERY` (`human_gate_service.py:82-102`), so for up to `LEASE_TTL_SECONDS` the lease still looks valid while nothing runs. A normal execution is reported only as information in the `cause` text ('N tracked executions running') and keeps PASS, because `Status` has no informational value (`diagnostics_service.py:48-52`). **`TASK_TERMINAL_WITH_UNRESOLVED` is defined once:** the owning Task is terminal **and** it has at least one normal-unresolved row (OPEN_UNPROVEN, CLOSED_UNPROVEN, or a U row under an unknown `detail.v`) **or** an anomaly row; it is not limited to OPEN rows. For a row of a terminal Task it is the only row cause besides the anomaly cause (the run-related causes would repeat the same fact). Revision 22: the cause also carries the optional `sweeper` (`None` unless the cause is a sweeper cause of the `RUNNER_STATE` item, described at the end of this section).

| `reason_code` | Severity | `blocks_execution` | Condition | `cause` text | `recommendation` | Related ids |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TRACKED_EXECUTION_ANOMALY` | FAIL | false | A is non-empty for the project | tracked executions are anomalous: an invalid proof or disposition, a wrong tracked marker or an undecodable `detail` (`decode_error`) (the kinds and sub-reasons are named; `may_be_permanently_stuck`) | repair is a manual, audited correction outside B2 (H11); a `decode_error` row has no automatic exit (§7.5 item 7); the project stays `DIRTY_UNRESOLVED` | execution ids of the returned anomalies, and the bounded `anomalies` list (execution, task and project ids, kind, sub-reason) with the truncation, total and `may_be_permanently_stuck` fields (§7.4) |
| `TASK_TERMINAL_WITH_UNRESOLVED` | WARN | false | the owning Task is terminal and (at least one normal-unresolved row or an anomaly row) | the Task ended while its executions are not proven terminated | wait for the sweeper, or decide at the `PROJECT_DIRTY` gate | execution ids, task id |
| `NO_OWNING_RUN` | WARN | false | an OPEN row of a non-terminal Task whose `run_id` is NULL or whose run is not `RUNNING` (also a parked Task whose lease was released) | no live run owns the execution | wait for the sweeper or recover the Task | execution ids |
| `TASK_NOT_EXECUTING` | WARN | false | an OPEN row of a non-terminal Task that is not in a state where a tracked command runs (the Task is not `TESTING`, in particular `WAITING_APPROVAL`, or its tester step is `INTERRUPTED`, `NEEDS_MANUAL_RECOVERY` or `WAITING_APPROVAL`), **whatever the lease says** (after `TerminationUnconfirmed` the parked run keeps its lease until `LEASE_TTL_SECONDS`) | the Task is parked or stopped while an execution is not proven terminated | decide at the RECOVERY gate, or wait for the sweeper or the registry re-check to prove the execution | execution ids, task id |
| `LEASE_EXPIRED` | WARN | false | an OPEN row whose run is `RUNNING` with `lease_expires_at <= now()` (also the 'heartbeat stale' test, `task_repository.py:71-79`) | the owning run's lease expired | wait for takeover or recovery | execution ids |
| `RUNNER_MISMATCH` | WARN | false | `executions.runner_id` differs from the run's `runner_id` | the execution belongs to another Runner incarnation | wait for takeover or recovery | execution ids |
| `EXECUTION_TOO_OLD` | WARN | false | the Task is not terminal, the row is OPEN and `now() - started_at > TRACKED_EXECUTION_MAX_AGE_SECONDS`; it is evaluated together with the run, lease, Runner and Task-state conditions and never replaces them (an old row of a `TESTING` Task with a `RUNNING` run, a valid lease and a matching Runner gives `EXECUTION_TOO_OLD` alone; with an expired lease it gives `LEASE_EXPIRED` **and** `EXECUTION_TOO_OLD`); a row within the limit is never `EXECUTION_TOO_OLD`, so a long-running normal command is not a stale execution; a terminal Task uses `TASK_TERMINAL_WITH_UNRESOLVED` | the execution runs longer than any command may | cancel the Task and check the host | execution ids |
| `CLOSED_UNPROVEN` | WARN | false | a CLOSED_UNPROVEN row of a non-terminal Task | a closing write was lost | wait for the sweeper | execution ids |
| `REQUEST_WITHOUT_WORKER` | WARN | false | a `REQUESTED` or due `RETRYABLE` request older than `PROCESS_RISK_REQUEST_STALE_SECONDS` (this includes an absent or failed worker, seen through the request) | no worker has claimed the request | check the `RUNNER_STATE` item | request ids |
| `REQUEST_CLAIM_TIMEOUT` | WARN | false | a `VERIFYING` request claimed longer than `PROCESS_RISK_CLAIM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` ago | a verification exceeds its claim | the request is reclaimed; check the Runner | request ids |
| `REQUEST_RETRY_STUCK` | WARN | false | the latest request ended `NEEDS_REDECISION(PROCESS_RECHECK_INCONCLUSIVE)` after the retries while U is non-empty, or a `RETRYABLE` request has `attempts >= PROCESS_RISK_MAX_ATTEMPTS - 1` | the automatic retries are exhausted or nearly so | decide again at the new gate | request ids |
| `CAPABILITY_MISMATCH` | WARN | false | an OPEN tracked row exists while the capability state is `UNAVAILABLE` or `UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM` (tracked rows are written only on a host that supports tracking) | the tracking capability of the host changed after the row was written | fix the host, then recheck | execution ids |

**`RUNNER_STATE` cause `SWEEPER_STALLED` (revision 21, CM-1; shapes revision 22).** Besides `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` (§9.1 item 6) the `RUNNER_STATE` item carries the cause `SWEEPER_STALLED` when the runtime snapshot of this process reports `sweeper.stalled = true`: severity WARN, `blocks_execution = false`, `cause` text 'the orphan sweeper is stalled at the position `current_failure_cursor` (first failure at `first_failure_cursor`) after `consecutive_failures` failed passes (last fixed failure code `last_failure_code`, counted since the Runner started); it skips no row and retries with a capped backoff', `recommendation` 'diagnose the failing page or classification (an operator action; B2 never skips the row)', and the `SweeperStallOut` of §14.2 as `sweeper` (its `next_retry_at` is informational and may lie in the past, §7.4 'Exposure'); a `DiagnosticCause` of any other reason carries `sweeper = None`. **Revision 25:** the `RUNNER_STATE` item also carries the cause `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` when `config_invalid_active` is true (§7.4 CI-1), even when `stalled` is false: severity WARN, `blocks_execution = false`, `cause` text conditional on `config_currently_valid` (§9.1 SUP-29): when it is false or `null`, 'the orphan sweeper configuration is invalid (the fixed code `SWEEP_CONFIG_INVALID`); the entry of a pass failed at the trigger position (`config_invalid_trigger_position`); the last entry-time snapshot failure set a wait of `ORPHAN_SWEEP_CONFIG_FALLBACK_SECONDS` that the wake-up of CI-7 ends once when the configuration is valid again; no row is skipped', `recommendation` 'correct the sweeper configuration (an operator action); the state clears when the failure position has been passed afterwards'; when it is true, 'an earlier orphan sweeper configuration error is not cleared yet; the configuration is valid now and the state clears when a pass has passed the position (`config_invalid_trigger_position`); no row is skipped', `recommendation` 'no correction is needed; wait for the sweeper pass', and the same `SweeperStallOut` as `sweeper`; the warning code `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` is added to `/health.warnings` and to the report `warnings`; `ready`, `runner_active` and `blockers` are unchanged. Each position is read by its kind (§7.4): a `CANDIDATE` position is a row, a `PAGE_AFTER` position is the boundary just before a page that could not be read, and the record clears only when a pass has passed it by the rule of its kind, so the text says 'position' and never 'failing row' for a page position. The same state is the fixed warning code `SWEEPER_STALLED` in the top-level `/health.warnings` (the diagnostics cause lifts a PASS item to WARN) and in `warnings` of the runtime part of the report. It is **not** a statement that the Runner stopped and not a Runner-wide failure: it does not change `ready`, `runner_active` or `blockers`, does not force a project CLEAN and changes no owner and no baseline; the affected projects stay blocked by the unresolved and anomaly guards. The record is in memory: it is reset when the process or the `Runner` object is replaced (§7.4 row 21) and is **kept** by a `stop()` followed by a `start()` of the same object (SUP-11, §7.4 row 31; superseded in r28: 'reset when the Runner restarts'); it is never a durable audit record. An instance that runs no Runner (an API-only instance, `ADVISORY_LOCK_HELD`) reports, in `/health` and in the report runtime part, the default `SweeperStatusOut` object (`stalled` false, counters 0, the other fields `null`) and an empty always-present `warnings` list; the diagnostics carry **no** sweeper object for it and no such cause, because the diagnostics add the `SWEEPER_STALLED` cause (with its `SweeperStallOut`) only when the sweeper is stalled. **Revision 26:** (1) the cause `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` appears **immediately** while `config_invalid_active` is true (`stalled` may be false) and also carries the additive `SweeperConfigInvalidOut` (its fields are listed in §14.2; the position kind and the trigger failure code stay internal, §7.4 CI-1), whereas the cause `SWEEPER_STALLED` appears only after the stall threshold (sustained no-progress at the same position, §7.4 STALL-1 to STALL-4); (2) the `RUNNER_STATE` item carries the cause `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` (WARN, `blocks_execution = false`, the component ids in the `cause` text, `recommendation` 'restart the Runner after diagnosing the component; it is not restarted automatically') for every DEGRADED component of §9.1 SUP-6 and carries the component detail list of §14.2 (for the supervisor the item is FAIL with `blocks_execution = true`, SUP-10); it replaces `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_FAILED`. **Revision 27:** the configuration cause is exposed immediately (the diagnostics add it whenever `config_invalid_active` is true) and the stall cause only after the threshold; the field plan of every object is §14.2.

**`RUNNER_STATE` severity of the background causes (revision 34, A5; it replaces the unstated severity of derived items in revision 33).** The `RUNNER_STATE` item has two **independent** sources, and the item keeps the **highest** severity of its base status and of every cause present: (1) the *real DEGRADED cause* `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` exists only while `background_degraded` is true (a component or the supervisor is really DEGRADED): WARN with `blocks_execution = false` for a component, FAIL with `blocks_execution = true` for the supervisor (SUP-6, SUP-10); (2) the *derived display source* `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` (the code is an **authoring choice, not user-approved**, §12 A33-1) exists, in the lifecycle `RUNNING` only (revision 35, D35-1), when at least one unit has a derived `display_state` (`BACKOFF_ORPHANED`, `EXITED_UNSUPERVISED` or `BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED`, table SUP-DS): always WARN with `blocks_execution = false`, and it carries only the derived items. A derived-only abnormal item lifts `RUNNER_STATE` from PASS to WARN; a higher existing severity is kept (the base FAIL of a blocker such as `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED` or `STOPPED` stays FAIL, the base WARN of `ADVISORY_LOCK_HELD` stays WARN); a derived item **never** creates a dispatch blocker, never changes `ready`, `runner_active` or `blockers`, never sets `background_degraded` and never adds the `/health` warning `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`. The four response shapes of the table below are the oracle of the §13 row of revision 34; the two derived shapes are case A and case B of SUP-17 and no other derived shape is an oracle: a derived-only item (no DEGRADED unit, `background_degraded` false) exists with a live supervisor as `EXITED_UNSUPERVISED` or as `BACKOFF_ORPHANED` (case A; revision 35, final decision Q1-1: a waiter-less BACKOFF unit is `BACKOFF_ORPHANED` whatever the supervisor state, and a live-supervisor example that can only be built by fault injection is an 'output test on a synthetic snapshot'), whereas `BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED` needs a dead supervisor by its definition (table SUP-DS row 4), and every derived item together with the DEGRADED supervisor has `background_degraded` true (case B; revision 35, D35-1).

**Table DIAG-BG: four `RUNNER_STATE` response examples (revision 34, A5; the keys are the fields of §14.2; nothing was run).**

| Example | `background_components` | `runner.background_degraded` and the `/health` warning | Causes of `RUNNER_STATE` | `status` and `blocks_execution` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | `[]` | false, no warning | none | PASS, false |
| case A (derived-only, the supervisor alive) | one item `{component: sweeper, reason_code: null, since: null, restart_exhausted: false, display_state: EXITED_UNSUPERVISED}` (case A1; a waiter-less BACKOFF unit with a live supervisor is case A2 with the same fields and `display_state: BACKOFF_ORPHANED`) | false, no warning | `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` (WARN) with that item | WARN, false |
| DEGRADED-only (a component, the supervisor alive) | one item `{component: risk-worker, reason_code: the reason code of the DEGRADED state (SUP-6), since: the time of the DEGRADED state, restart_exhausted: true, display_state: DEGRADED}` | true, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` | `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` (WARN) with that item | WARN, false |
| case B (the DEGRADED supervisor and a derived item) | two items: `{component: supervisor, reason_code: the reason code of the DEGRADED state (SUP-6, SUP-10), since: the time of the DEGRADED state, display_state: DEGRADED}` (`restart_exhausted` is not asserted for the supervisor) and `{component: sweeper, reason_code: null, since: null, restart_exhausted: false, display_state: BACKOFF_WAITER_DONE_UNSUPERVISED}` | true, `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED`, the blocker `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED` (`ready` false) | two causes, each with its own item: `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DEGRADED` (the supervisor item; FAIL, `blocks_execution` true) and `BACKGROUND_COMPONENT_DERIVED` (the derived item; WARN) | FAIL, true (a higher severity is kept; the derived item is still listed) |

### 14.2 Field plan of the snapshots and DTOs (revision 27, decision D27-2; ownership and output model revised in revision 28; the single list of fields)

This is the **only** place that lists the fields of the sweeper, configuration-invalid and background-component objects; every other section names the object and refers here. **Dependency direction:** `app/services/sweeper_stall.py` (the internal `SweeperStallState`, the frozen `SweeperStallSnapshot` and the frozen `SweeperConfigInvalidSnapshot`), `app/services/background_supervisor.py` (supervisor and component state) and `app/services/runtime_status.py` (the frozen `RuntimeSnapshot` and the frozen `BackgroundComponentStatus`) import nothing from `app/schemas`; `app/schemas/api.py` and `app/schemas/reports.py` define the DTOs; `DiagnosticsService` (`diagnostics_service.py`) returns frozen dataclasses (internal view models whose attribute names equal the DTO field names), `ReportService` (`report_service.py`) returns a plain dictionary (`report_service.py:325-329`, validated by `RuntimeOut` in `finalize`) and the `/health` body builder `RuntimeSnapshot.as_dict()` is a plain dictionary; the **routers and the FastAPI `response_model`** (`from_attributes`, `_Out` of `app/schemas/api.py:11-12`) convert them to the DTOs (superseded in r28: the r27 sentence that the services 'read the Runner-side state and convert it'); **no service imports `app.schemas`** (the existing rule `tests/architecture/test_rules.py:114` covers every service; the architecture test of §13 extends it: `runner.py`, `sweeper_stall.py`, `background_supervisor.py` and `runtime_status.py` import no API DTO).

| Object | Layer and module | Fields | Used by | Notes |

| `SweeperStatusOut` | API model, `app/schemas/reports.py` (its key set is also the `/health` `runner.sweeper` object) | `stalled`, `consecutive_failures`, `last_failure_code`, `last_failure_at`, `next_retry_at`, `config_invalid_active`, `clearance_pending` | `/health`, report runtime part | no cursor position; always present with the defaults `stalled` false, `consecutive_failures` 0, `config_invalid_active` false, `clearance_pending` false and `last_failure_code`, `last_failure_at`, `next_retry_at` `null`; `next_retry_at` is the **ordinary retry schedule** of the stall record (`null` without one); `config_invalid_active` and `clearance_pending` are taken from `SweeperConfigInvalidSnapshot.active` and `.clearance_pending`; `runtime_status.py` builds a plain dictionary with this key set (no service builds the Out object) |
| `SweeperStallOut` | API model, `app/schemas/api.py` | exactly the nine fields of `SweeperStallSnapshot`, with the same names: `stalled`, `stalled_since`, `pass_start_cursor`, `first_failure_cursor`, `current_failure_cursor`, `consecutive_failures`, `last_failure_code`, `last_failure_at`, `next_retry_at` (no `config_invalid_active` and no `clearance_pending`: they live only in `SweeperConfigInvalidOut` and `SweeperStatusOut`) | `DiagnosticCauseOut.sweeper`, the `SWEEPER_STALLED` cause (and the `SWEEPER_CONFIG_INVALID` cause) | equal attribute names make `from_attributes` work (r29: the r28 definition 'the fields of `SweeperStatusOut` plus four' had two fields that the snapshot does not have and is superseded); without a stall record, including the CI-only state, the default object (every boolean `false`, every count 0, every other field `null`); `next_retry_at` is the ordinary retry schedule |

| `RuntimeSnapshot` additions | internal frozen dataclass, `runtime_status.py` | `sweeper` (the `SweeperStatusOut` key set), `sweeper_stall`, `sweeper_config_invalid`, `warnings`, `background_degraded` (boolean), `background_components`, `background_revision` (int, §14.3; not in `as_dict()`) | `as_dict()` (`/health`: top-level `warnings`, `runner.sweeper`, `runner.background_degraded`) and the report runtime part (`RuntimeOut`: `warnings`, `sweeper`, `background_degraded`, each with a default) | `runner_active` is unchanged; `ready` and `blockers` change only by the blocker `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED` of §9.1 SUP-10 and SUP-17 |
| `RunnerRuntimeState` | internal frozen dataclass (the input bundle), `runtime_status.py` | `lifecycle`, `runner_active`, `sweeper_stall` (`SweeperStallSnapshot` or `None`), `sweeper_config_invalid` (`SweeperConfigInvalidSnapshot` or `None`), `background_degraded`, `background_components`, `supervisor_state`, `background_revision` | the fourth argument `state` of `runtime_snapshot`, built by `snapshot_of` from the Runner properties of the same names | the first argument `lifecycle` stays the authority for `runner_active` and `ready`; `supervisor_state` only drives the blocker `SUPERVISOR_DEGRADED`; the Runner exposes read-only properties `sweeper_stall`, `sweeper_config_invalid`, `background_degraded`, `background_components`, `supervisor_state` and `background_revision` (a Runner without one is read with a default) |
